area: Live video pipeline: IP camera (RTSP/ONVIF) to Web, Android, iOS and Windows clients
summary: Cameras speak RTSP and browsers cannot play it, so the product needs a gateway that repackages (remuxes) the camera stream into something each client can play. Remuxing costs very little CPU. Transcoding (decoding and re-encoding) costs a lot and is the thing to avoid. As of October 2026 the two strongest gateways are both MIT-licensed Go single binaries. go2rtc (v1.9.14, Jan 2026) is best for live viewing: it picks a format each client can play (WebRTC, MSE over WebSocket, HLS, MJPEG) from one camera connection and has the broadest two-way audio support (ONVIF RTSP backchannel plus Tapo, Hikvision ISAPI, Dahua DVRIP, Xiaomi and others). MediaMTX (v1.21.2, 8 Oct 2026) is best for recording and playback: segmented fMP4 with retention, hooks that fire when a segment completes (useful for uploading to Drive/OneDrive), and an HTTP playback API. It still cannot proxy two-way audio to cameras. Neither one does PTZ; that needs a separate ONVIF client. For delivery, use WebRTC (about 0.2-0.5 s latency) for single-camera view, PTZ and talk. Use MSE/fMP4 over WebSocket (TCP, no NAT setup, iPhone needs iOS 17.1+) for grids and as the fallback; Frigate made it its default for exactly these reasons. Keep LL-HLS (2-5 s) only for old iOS or CDN fan-out. H.264 is the only codec that plays everywhere. H.265 in 2026 is hardware-dependent in Chrome (WebRTC HEVC since Chrome 136), works in Safari 18+, is not offered by Edge over WebRTC, and works in Firefox only through MSE/HLS, not WebRTC. So set the camera substream to H.264 and send H.265 only to clients that report support. Grid views should use the camera substream (about 640x360 at about 512 kbps) and switch to the main stream only for fullscreen. Mobile phones only guarantee 2-6 hardware decoders at 720p, so phone grids must be small or paginated. A Raspberry Pi 5 has no hardware H.264 encoder (or decoder), so it is fine for remuxing many streams but poor for transcoding. An Intel N100-class mini PC with QuickSync is the cheapest box that can also transcode a few streams. Cameras sit behind the user's NAT, so the architecture that fits both self-hosted and SaaS is a local "edge agent" (go2rtc and/or MediaMTX on a PC, mini PC or NAS). The cloud handles only sign-in/signaling and TURN relay, so video does not normally pass through your servers.

facts.claim: go2rtc is MIT-licensed. Latest tagged release is v1.9.14 (2026-01-19). The dev branch had commits through 2026-09-06, but there has been no tagged release for about 9 months. About 14.4k GitHub stars; mostly a single maintainer (AlexxIT).
facts.source: https://github.com/AlexxIT/go2rtc ; https://github.com/AlexxIT/go2rtc/releases (tag dates checked with git ls-remote/fetch)

facts.claim: go2rtc browser codec matrix: WebRTC carries H.264, H.265* and PCMU/PCMA/Opus on Chrome 136+/Edge/Android Chrome/Safari. Firefox WebRTC is H.264 only. MSE carries H.264, H.265*, AAC, FLAC and Opus. MSE on iPhone needs iOS 17.1+. HTTP progressive streaming does not work on any Apple device. HLS is used only for iPhone and Apple apps. go2rtc rates latency: WebRTC best, MSE medium, HLS bad.

go2rtc supports two-way audio for RTSP (ONVIF backchannel), WebRTC, ISAPI (Hikvision), DVRIP, Tapo, Tuya, Ring, Roborock, Xiaomi, Wyze, Multitrans (TP-Link), DoorBird and exec. A browser can only grant microphone access on an HTTPS page. go2rtc's WHEP mode does not support two-way audio; its own WebRTC client format does.

go2rtc only remuxes by itself. Its built-in conversions are limited to packing PCMA/PCMU/PCM audio into FLAC for MSE/MP4/HLS and resampling G.711 for WebRTC. Real transcoding is delegated to an external FFmpeg (with hardware acceleration), and the author states there are no plans to embed complex transcoding.

go2rtc release binaries are about 4.3-7 MB for Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD (linux_arm64 4.43 MB, win64 7.04 MB). No Android or iOS builds are published. The project is meant to run as a standalone app driven by an HTTP API. Most of its logic is in Go 'internal/' packages, which other Go modules cannot import, so embedding it as a library means forking or using only the pkg/ packages.

go2rtc has had serious security flaws. CVE-2024-29192 (CSRF leading to arbitrary command execution through the exec source and api/config) was fixed in 1.9.0. ZDI-26-560/561 (Pwn2Own command injection, run as root) were fixed in 1.9.14. v1.9.12 added local_auth and allow_paths settings.

go2rtc WebRTC listens on port 8555 (TCP+UDP) by default and supports STUN hole punching and TURN through ice_servers. Its docs estimate that about 20% of users are behind symmetric NAT and cannot connect without a TURN relay, and that UDP is a poor fit for high-bitrate 2K/4K video over open networks.
go2rtc is bundled in Home Assistant 2024.11+ and in Frigate 0.12+, so it is very widely deployed.

MediaMTX is MIT-licensed. Latest release is v1.21.2 (2026-10-08), with releases every 2-4 weeks through 2026 (v1.19.0 Jun, v1.20.0 Aug, v1.21.0 Sep). About 20.4k stars. It is a single dependency-free binary for Linux, Windows and macOS.

MediaMTX accepts streams over Media-over-QUIC, SRT, WebRTC, RTSP, RTMP, HLS, MPEG-TS and RTP, and serves them over MoQ, SRT, WebRTC, RTSP, RTMP and HLS. WebRTC output codecs: AV1, VP9, VP8, H265, H264 video; Opus, G722, G711 audio. HLS output codecs: AV1, VP9, H265, H264 video; Opus, FLAC, AAC audio.

MediaMTX never transcodes; its docs tell you to run FFmpeg or GStreamer next to it. The docs also say browsers do not support H.264 with B-frames over WebRTC, and that Chrome plays H.265 over WebRTC only on Windows with a capable GPU. That platform claim conflicts with go2rtc's matrix, which lists Android Chrome 136+.

MediaMTX records to fMP4 or MPEG-TS segments with a crash-loss window equal to recordPartDuration (default 1s), plus recordSegmentDuration (default 1h) and recordDeleteAfter (default 1d). It has runOnRecordSegmentCreate/Complete hooks and a playback HTTP server (:9996) with /list and /get?path&start&duration endpoints.

MediaMTX cannot proxy two-way audio (RTSP backchannel). Issue #941 has been open since May 2022. Issue #4726 was closed as 'not planned' in July 2025, with the maintainer saying back-channel proxying is not supported and pointing to the gortsplib proxy-backchannel example instead.
MediaMTX HLS defaults to the low-latency variant, with 1s minimum segments and 200ms parts.

MediaMTX supports Media-over-QUIC drafts 16-19 through WebTransport and WebCodecs. It requires HTTPS and both TCP and UDP on port 8892. iOS Safari does not support serverCertificateHashes, so self-signed certificates fail there. Safari 26.4 (March 2026) shipped WebTransport.

The libraries behind MediaMTX can be embedded directly in a Go program. gortsplib (MIT, v5.6.7, 2026-10-08) is an RTSP client and server with UDP, multicast and TCP transport, RTSPS/SRTP, and a client-play-backchannel example. gohlslib and gortmplib are the HLS and RTMP equivalents.
WebRTC H.265 shipped in Chrome 136 (hardware decode only; no software fallback) and Safari 18. The IETF profile for HEVC in WebRTC was still a draft (draft-ietf-avtcore-hevc-webrtc-09, July 2026).

Microsoft Edge does not advertise or send H.265 over WebRTC, even though Chromium has the code behind flags. A Microsoft Q&A moderator said there is no public roadmap for it and recommended H.264 or a dual H.264/H.265 strategy.

HEVC playback outside WebRTC (caniuse): Safari is supported from 13 and iOS Safari from 11. Chrome is 'partial' from 107 (needs a hardware decoder). Edge is partial (goes through Windows Media Foundation and the HEVC Video Extension). Firefox is partial from 137 (hardware decoding on Windows 134+, macOS 136+, Linux 137+). Frigate's docs (Oct 2026) also say only a limited set of H.265 profiles play.

Frigate's docs (updated Oct 2026) recommend H.264 + AAC on the camera. They say to avoid 'smart codecs' (H.264+/H.265+) because they remove keyframes, and to set the I-frame interval equal to the fps. MSE needs PCMA/PCMU or AAC audio; WebRTC needs PCMA/PCMU or Opus. Frigate uses MSE by default (TCP, every frame delivered, no NAT setup) and WebRTC only when needed, such as two-way talk.

Frigate's example camera setup uses a main stream of 2688x1520 at 15 fps H.264 for recording and an H.264 substream for detection (default 5 fps). It recommends giving the substream the same aspect ratio as the main stream, e.g. 640x360 for a 16:9 main stream.

Android Media3 ExoPlayer RTSP (media3-exoplayer-rtsp 1.11.1) plays only H.264 (with SPS/PPS in the SDP), AAC and AC3. It supports UDP unicast and RTP over TCP (interleaved), but not multicast. H.265 over RTSP is not supported.
iOS AVPlayer does not play RTSP. A native iOS app needs a gateway that converts to HLS or WebRTC, or an FFmpeg/VLC-based player (VLCKit has reported slow-start and cellular problems).
iPhone Safari got MSE-style playback through ManagedMediaSource in iOS 17.1 (Nov 2023). This is what makes MSE/fMP4 players (and hls.js 1.5+) work on iPhone.

WebCodecs support: Chromium since 94; Firefox desktop since 130 (not Firefox for Android); Safari had only VideoDecoder for a long time, with full audio support reportedly arriving in Safari 26. Chromium WebCodecs HEVC decoding needs hardware.

LiveKit server is Apache-2.0 (v1.13.10, 2026-10-14). The current source enables H265, PCMU and PCMA by default, even though the public codec docs still list only H264, VP8, VP9 and AV1. LiveKit Ingress (Apache-2.0, v1.5.0 Apr 2026) accepts RTMP, WHIP and URL pull (http/srt/udp) but not RTSP. It transcodes by default (default cost: 2 CPUs per RTMP/WHIP ingress); WHIP input can skip transcoding.

mediasoup is ISC-licensed (v3.30.1 on 2026-10-17; Rust crate 0.31.0). It ships as a Node.js module or Rust crate. Supported video codecs are VP8, VP9, H264 and AV1; H.265 was removed in 3.16.6. It has no RTSP client, so camera ingest needs an external FFmpeg or GStreamer sending plain RTP.

Janus is GPL-3.0 (v1.4.3, 2026-10-12). Its Streaming plugin can pull RTSP through libcurl, but the RTSP SETUP request only asks for RTP/AVP/UDP (unicast or multicast); RTP over TCP (interleaved) is not implemented in janus_streaming.c.
Pion WebRTC is an MIT-licensed pure-Go library (v4.2.24, 2026-10-16) with an H.265 payloader in its media engine. go2rtc is built on Pion.

GStreamer core is LGPL. 1.28.0 shipped 2026-01-27 and 1.28.8 on 2026-10-08. 1.28 added webrtcsink renegotiation, VA hardware encoders, a WHEP client/server signaller, and rtspsrc2 improvements (SRTP, auth, HTTP tunnelling, TLS). webrtcsink lives in gst-plugins-rs, which is licensed MPL-2.0.

FFmpeg is LGPL-2.1+, but configuring it with --enable-gpl (needed for libx264) puts the whole build under GPL. FFmpeg 8.0 (2025-08-22) contains a WHIP muxer (whip.c, LGPL). FFmpeg 9.0 shipped 2026-08-03 and 9.0.2 on 2026-09-18.
WHIP (WebRTC ingest over HTTP) is a standard, RFC 9725 (January 2025). WHEP (the playback counterpart) is still an Internet-Draft (draft-ietf-wish-whep-04, June 2026).

Raspberry Pi 5 has no hardware H.264 encoder. Raspberry Pi's own white paper says software libx264 encodes 1080p30 in real time using about 60% of one core in low-latency mode. The Pi 5 has a hardware HEVC decoder, but H.264 decoding is done in software.

Remuxing is cheap. One blog reports a Raspberry Pi 4 handling about 10 streams, with roughly 5% CPU for an RTSP-to-WebRTC proxy versus roughly 40% when converting H.265 to H.264. Home Assistant/Frigate CPU spikes are usually traced to unintended H.265 transcoding.
An Intel N100 mini PC with QuickSync is commonly estimated at 4-8 simultaneous 1080p hardware transcodes. These are unverified community figures, not benchmarks.

Using substreams for grids cuts NVR CPU dramatically. Blue Iris users report drops such as 94% to about 35% across 20+ cameras. The usual practice is the main stream for recording and single-camera view, and the substream for multi-camera grids and motion detection.
Typical Hikvision guidance (third-party guide): substream 640x360 or 640x480 at about 512 kbps; 4MP main stream at about 4096 kbps. Some 4MP models cap the substream at 640x360.

Android phones advertise how many hardware decoders can run at once through getMaxSupportedInstances(). Android media performance classes only guarantee 2, 4 or 6 concurrent decoders at 720p30 (class 10/20/30), so a 9- or 16-tile grid can exceed hardware decoders on many phones.
Vendor latency ranges: WebRTC 0.2-0.5 s glass-to-glass; LL-HLS about 2-5 s; classic HLS 6-30 s.

MJPEG has very low latency and is trivial to decode, but uses roughly 5x the bandwidth of H.264 and has no audio. Multipart MJPEG in browsers has had bugs (Firefox freezes, iOS showing only the first frame when loaded as a main resource).

Cloudflare Realtime TURN/SFU costs $0.05 per GB of egress, with the first 1,000 GB per month free (shared between SFU and TURN). Example: a 4 Mbps main stream relayed for one hour is about 1.8 GB, or about $0.09 per viewer-hour; a 512 kbps substream is about 0.23 GB/h.

HEVC patents: the Access Advance pool licenses HEVC software sold separately from devices. Access Advance acquired Via LA in December 2025. Shipping your own software HEVC decoder (FFmpeg/libmpv/VLC) in a commercial app can trigger royalties; using the OS or browser decoder generally does not.

Chrome 92 briefly blocked pages with more than 75 playing media elements (WebMediaPlayer limit), then raised the limit enough to effectively disable it. Large grids are still memory- and decoder-bound.

options.name: go2rtc (AlexxIT)
options.description: Go camera streaming gateway. Pulls RTSP/ONVIF/RTMP/HTTP and many vendor-specific camera protocols, and serves WebRTC, MSE (fMP4 over WebSocket), HLS, MJPEG, RTSP and MP4. Picks the right codec per client automatically and handles two-way audio.
pros: MIT license, about 5-7 MB static binary, runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, ARM and Pi
Broadest camera coverage: RTSP/ONVIF plus native Tapo, Hikvision ISAPI, Dahua DVRIP, Xiaomi, Wyze, Tuya, Ring, Reolink HTTP-FLV H.265
Best two-way audio support (RTSP backchannel, WebRTC and vendor APIs)
Picks the codec and format each client can play (WebRTC, MSE, HLS, MJPEG) from one camera connection; its JS player falls back automatically
Proven at scale through Home Assistant 2024.11+ and Frigate
Repackages G.711 into FLAC for MSE and resamples it for WebRTC, so no transcoding is needed for most audio
cons: No continuous segmented recording, retention or playback server (MP4 export only); you need MediaMTX or FFmpeg for the recording side
Mostly one maintainer; no tagged release since 2026-01-19 (dev branch active until Sep 2026)
Not a clean Go library: the core is in internal/ packages, so integration is through its HTTP API, a fork or pkg/ packages
Security history (CVE-2024-29192, ZDI-26-560/561 command injection); exec/ffmpeg sources and the API must be locked down
No PTZ control (ONVIF PTZ needs a separate client)
options.license: MIT
options.maturity: High adoption, active through 2026 (v1.9.14, Jan 2026), about 14.4k stars

options.name: MediaMTX (bluenviron)
options.description: Go media server/router. Takes in and serves MoQ, SRT, WebRTC, RTSP, RTMP and HLS (including LL-HLS), records fMP4/MPEG-TS segments, has a playback API, hooks, an auth API (internal/HTTP/JWT), a control API and Prometheus metrics.
pros: MIT license, very active (v1.21.2 on 2026-10-08, releases every 2-4 weeks), about 20.4k stars
Ready-made recording: segments, retention, hooks on segment create/complete (to trigger uploads to Drive/OneDrive/S3), and an HTTP playback /list and /get
Built-in JWT/HTTP auth and forwarding to other servers (RTSP/RTMP/SRT), which suits an edge-to-cloud setup
Its RTSP, HLS and RTMP libraries (gortsplib, gohlslib, gortmplib) are importable MIT Go libraries
Early Media-over-QUIC support (drafts 16-19) for future WebTransport/WebCodecs delivery
cons: Cannot proxy two-way audio (issue #941 open since 2022)
No transcoding at all; codec mismatches must be fixed with FFmpeg or GStreamer
No MSE-over-WebSocket output; browsers get only WebRTC, HLS or MoQ
Less vendor-specific camera support than go2rtc (mostly RTSP/RTMP/HLS/SRT/WebRTC sources)
Release binaries are larger (about 26-29 MB archives)
options.license: MIT
options.maturity: High; very active 2025-2026 with regular security fixes

options.name: Pion WebRTC + gortsplib (custom Go gateway)
options.description: Build your own gateway from MIT Go libraries: gortsplib to pull RTSP (including backchannel), Pion to serve WebRTC, plus your own fMP4/MSE muxer. This is the stack go2rtc and MediaMTX are built from.
pros: Full control and embeddable in your own agent binary; MIT throughout
Pion is very active (v4.2.24, 2026-10-16) and supports H.265 packetization
gortsplib supports TCP/UDP/multicast transport, RTSPS/SRTP and the ONVIF backchannel
cons: Months of streaming work (jitter, timestamps, codec quirks, NAT) that go2rtc and MediaMTX already solved
You own the camera-compatibility long tail yourself
options.license: MIT
options.maturity: Libraries are mature; your integration would not be

options.name: LiveKit (server + Ingress)
options.description: Apache-2.0 WebRTC SFU (a server that forwards each stream to many viewers) with client SDKs for Web, Android, iOS, Flutter, React Native and Unity. Ingress takes RTMP, WHIP and URL pull and re-encodes for WebRTC.
pros: Excellent cross-platform client SDKs and production-grade SFU scaling; managed cloud option
Default codec list in the current source includes H265, PCMU and PCMA
Fits a SaaS where many people watch the same camera
cons: No RTSP ingest; you need go2rtc/MediaMTX/GStreamer in front to push WHIP
Ingress transcodes by default (default cost 2 CPUs per stream), which is too expensive for many cameras
Built for rooms and conferencing, not NVR timelines; adds Redis and an Ingress service to operate
Overkill for 1-3 viewers per camera, which is the typical camera-viewing pattern
options.license: Apache-2.0

options.name: mediasoup
options.description: Low-level WebRTC SFU shipped as a Node.js module or Rust crate; can take in plain RTP.
pros: Permissive ISC license; very efficient C++ worker; active (3.30.1 on 2026-10-17)
Good fit if the backend is Node/Rust and you need custom fan-out
cons: No RTSP client; needs FFmpeg or GStreamer to bridge each camera
No H.265 (removed in 3.16.6)
Media layer only: no recording, HLS or MSE; you build signaling and the app layer
options.license: ISC
options.maturity: High for the SFU role

options.name: Janus WebRTC Server (Meetecho)
options.description: C WebRTC server with plugins. The Streaming plugin can pull RTSP and serve it over WebRTC.
pros: Mature, still active (v1.4.3, 2026-10-12)
Built-in RTSP mountpoints
cons: GPL-3.0: a problem for closed-source distribution (e.g. bundling it in a Windows app or edge agent); hosted-only SaaS use is less affected
Source shows RTSP pull over UDP only (no RTP-over-TCP), which is fragile across NAT/VPN
WebRTC only; no MSE/HLS or recording timeline; C codebase is harder to extend
options.license: GPL-3.0
options.maturity: High, but not camera-focused

options.name: GStreamer (rtspsrc/rtspsrc2 + webrtcsink, hlssink, splitmuxsink)
options.description: Pipeline framework for complex media processing, hardware transcoding (VA, NVENC, QSV, V4L2) and WebRTC (webrtcsink from gst-plugins-rs), plus native mobile SDKs.
pros: Most flexible option for transcoding, mosaics, overlays and analytics pipelines
Core is LGPL and webrtcsink is MPL-2.0; 1.28 (2026) added a WHEP signaller and hardware encoders
Builds for Android, iOS and Windows, so it could be the shared native player or recorder
cons: Steep learning curve and heavier footprint than go2rtc/MediaMTX
GPL plugins (e.g. x264) and the 'ugly' plugin set create licensing and patent obligations when distributed
You still build signaling, auth and the HTTP layer
options.license: LGPL-2.1+ core; MPL-2.0 for gst-plugins-rs webrtc; some plugins GPL

options.name: FFmpeg (helper process or library)
options.description: General-purpose decode/encode/remux tool. Used next to go2rtc/MediaMTX for audio conversion (AAC to Opus), H.265 to H.264 transcoding, snapshots, and segment muxing for recordings and uploads.
pros: Universal codec support and hardware acceleration (QSV, VAAPI, NVENC, VideoToolbox, D3D11, Vulkan)
Has a WHIP muxer since 8.0; current version 9.0.x (Aug-Sep 2026)
go2rtc and MediaMTX both use it as their transcoding backend
cons: LGPL only if built without GPL parts (libx264 forces GPL); mobile static linking needs care to stay LGPL-compliant
Process-per-stream model costs memory; transcoding is CPU/GPU-heavy
Shipping its software HEVC decoder can create patent royalty exposure
options.license: LGPL-2.1+ (GPL if built with --enable-gpl)
options.maturity: Very high

options.name: Delivery: WebRTC
options.description: UDP/SRTP real-time delivery with P2P via STUN or relay via TURN; signaling through go2rtc's API or WHEP.
pros: Lowest latency (about 0.2-0.5 s); needed for responsive PTZ and two-way talk
Works in every browser and has native libraries on Android, iOS and Windows
Can deliver H.265 to Chrome 136+ (hardware) and Safari 18+
cons: NAT traversal: about 20% of users need TURN, which costs money (e.g. $0.05/GB at Cloudflare)
Drops late frames, so video degrades on poor networks; no B-frames; AAC audio needs transcoding to Opus
No H.265 in Firefox or Edge WebRTC
options.license: n/a (open standard)
options.maturity: Mature

options.name: Delivery: MSE/fMP4 over WebSocket (go2rtc 'mse')
options.description: Fragmented MP4 sent over a WebSocket and played through Media Source Extensions (ManagedMediaSource on iOS).
pros: TCP over HTTPS: goes through any proxy or firewall, no TURN, every frame arrives
Sub-second to about 1 s latency with a tuned player; carries AAC and H.265 where the browser supports it
Frigate's default for live view
cons: iPhone needs iOS 17.1+; older iPhones need HLS
Latency can build up on slow links, so the player needs catch-up logic
Through a cloud relay, every byte passes your servers (bandwidth cost)
options.license: n/a
options.maturity: Mature

options.name: Delivery: LL-HLS / HLS
options.description: Segmented HTTP delivery (MediaMTX defaults: 1s segments, 200ms parts).
pros: Universal, especially native iOS AVPlayer; cacheable on a CDN
Simple to secure with signed URLs
cons: 2-5 s latency for LL-HLS, 6-30 s for classic HLS; too slow for PTZ
CDN caching rarely helps because cameras usually have 1-2 viewers
options.license: n/a
options.maturity: Mature

options.name: Delivery: MJPEG / JPEG snapshots
options.description: Multipart JPEG stream or periodically refreshed JPEG snapshots.
pros: Trivial to decode; works anywhere; ideal for thumbnails and large grids on phones (no hardware decoder limits)
cons: About 5x the bandwidth of H.264 for continuous video; no audio; browser quirks
options.license: n/a
options.maturity: Legacy but useful

options.name: Delivery: WebCodecs / Media-over-QUIC
options.description: Raw H.264/H.265 frames over WebTransport or WebSocket, decoded in the page with VideoDecoder (MediaMTX MoQ drafts 16-19).
pros: Very low latency without WebRTC complexity; supports B-frames; full control of codecs per frame
WebTransport has been in all major browsers since Safari 26.4 (Mar 2026)
cons: MoQ is still an IETF draft that changes often; Firefox for Android lacks WebCodecs; Safari WebCodecs audio is recent
You own jitter buffering and audio/video sync; iOS self-signed certificate limitation
options.license: n/a
options.maturity: Emerging (2026); watch, do not depend on it yet

recommendation:
1. Use an edge-gateway architecture that works for both business models. Ship a small "agent" next to the cameras: a Windows service, Docker or Pi/mini-PC image, or NAS app.
   - It contains go2rtc for live view and two-way audio, and MediaMTX for recording and playback.
   - MediaMTX should pull from go2rtc's local RTSP restream, so each camera gets only one connection per profile.
   - Run ONVIF discovery and PTZ in your own agent code; neither project does PTZ.
   - In self-hosted mode, clients reach the agent on the LAN or over a tunnel.
   - In SaaS mode, the cloud handles accounts, signaling and TURN only. WebRTC goes P2P from agent to client, with TURN fallback for the roughly 20% behind symmetric NAT. A WebSocket/MSE relay through the cloud is the last resort.
   - Do not have the cloud pull RTSP directly from users' cameras; that means port-forwarding cameras to the internet.

2. Pick the delivery format by situation, and let go2rtc's negotiation do the selection.
   - Single camera, PTZ and talk: WebRTC with H.264 video and Opus or G.711 audio.
   - Grids and poor networks: MSE/fMP4 over WebSocket.
   - Thumbnails and large mobile grids: JPEG snapshots or MJPEG.
   - iOS below 17.1 and any CDN use: LL-HLS.

3. Treat H.264 as the baseline codec.
   - During onboarding, use ONVIF to set the substream to H.264 (about 640x360, 10-15 fps, about 512 kbps, I-frame interval equal to fps, no H.264+/H.265+ "smart codecs").
   - Keep the main stream at native quality for recording.
   - Send H.265 only to clients that report it: Chrome 136+ with hardware decode, or Safari 18+. Never to Edge or Firefox WebRTC.
   - Transcode only audio (AAC to Opus) by default. Allow video transcoding only on agents with QuickSync/VAAPI/NVENC, and never on a Raspberry Pi 5.

4. For native apps, use the same gateway outputs rather than raw RTSP. Android Media3 RTSP is H.264-only, and iOS AVPlayer has no RTSP.
   - Use libwebrtc (flutter_webrtc, react-native-webrtc, or the native SDKs) plus an fMP4 player.
   - Avoid bundling a software HEVC decoder (FFmpeg/libmpv/VLC) in commercial builds until LGPL compliance and HEVC patent exposure are reviewed.

5. Cap concurrent decodes per client.
   - Phones: 4-tile pages by default, up to about 9 tiles with substreams. Desktop: 16+ tiles of substreams.
   - Switch to the main stream only in fullscreen.

6. Capacity planning (benchmark before committing):
   - Remuxing is limited by network more than CPU: about 10 streams at low CPU even on a Pi 4.
   - Network math: N cameras x (main about 4 Mbps + sub about 0.5 Mbps) in, plus per-viewer egress.
   - An N100-class box with QuickSync handles roughly 16-32 cameras of remux and recording, plus a few hardware transcodes.
   - Lock both gateways' APIs to localhost and wrap them behind your own authenticated API. Pin and patch versions promptly, given the go2rtc exec CVEs and MediaMTX CORS/playback-auth fixes in 2025-2026.
risks: H.265 support is fragmented. Many cameras default to H.265 or H.265+, but WebRTC H.265 is hardware-only in Chrome, absent in Edge and Firefox, and limited to certain profiles elsewhere. Without forcing an H.264 substream or transcoding, some users will get black tiles or high CPU.
'Smart codecs' (H.264+/H.265+) drop keyframes, and H.264 B-frames are unsupported in WebRTC. Both cause slow start or no playback. Detect and warn during camera onboarding.
Two-way audio: MediaMTX cannot proxy the backchannel (open since 2022), so talk has to go through go2rtc or your own gortsplib code. Many cameras use proprietary talk APIs that only go2rtc covers.
go2rtc depends mostly on one maintainer and has gone about 9 months without a tagged release. Plan to vendor or fork it, or keep MediaMTX/gortsplib as a fallback path.

Security: go2rtc has had RCE-class bugs (CVE-2024-29192, ZDI-26-560/561 via exec), and MediaMTX shipped CORS and playback-auth fixes in 2025-2026. Exposing either API directly to the internet or to an untrusted LAN is dangerous.

NAT traversal: about 20% of users need TURN relay, which is a recurring cost in SaaS (e.g. $0.05/GB, or about $0.09 per viewer-hour for a 4 Mbps main stream). Symmetric NAT and carrier-grade NAT on mobile networks make P2P unreliable.

Mobile hardware decoder limits (2-6 concurrent at 720p guaranteed by performance class) and Android Media3 RTSP being H.264-only. Large grids on phones will stutter or fail unless paginated or shown as snapshots.
Raspberry Pi 5 has no hardware H.264 encoder or decoder. Marketing a Pi as the edge box is fine for remuxing and recording, but not for transcoding H.265 cameras.

Licensing: Janus is GPL-3.0. FFmpeg built with x264 is GPL. GStreamer 'ugly' and GPL plugins are restricted. Distributing these in Windows, Android or iOS apps or in an edge agent can force source disclosure. LGPL static linking on iOS needs care.
HEVC patents: bundling software HEVC decoders in commercial apps may require Access Advance/VCL Advance licensing. OS/browser decoders are safer.

Some sources here are possibly outdated or conflicting. MediaMTX docs say Chrome WebRTC H.265 is Windows-only, while go2rtc and IETF slides say Chrome 136 broadly (hardware-gated). Safari WebCodecs audio support and WebTransport details rest on single secondary sources. N100 and Pi capacity figures are community estimates. Validate on real devices.
Media-over-QUIC/WebCodecs is moving fast (IETF drafts 16-19 in MediaMTX). Building primary playback on it in 2026 risks breaking changes.
Cheap cameras often allow only 1-4 simultaneous RTSP sessions. If the app, recorder and other NVRs each open their own connection, streams will fail. Always restream through one gateway connection.
questions_for_product_owner: Is the first version a self-hosted/personal tool, or a multi-tenant SaaS? May users' video pass through our cloud (cost, GDPR/privacy), or must it stay P2P or local?
Will users run an always-on device at home (Windows PC, mini PC, NAS, Raspberry Pi) for 24/7 recording, or do you expect phone-only setups? Recording from a phone or browser is unreliable.

Which camera brands and protocols must work on day one: ONVIF Profile S/T only, or also Tapo, Reolink, Hikvision, Dahua, Xiaomi, Wyze and other cloud-only cameras that go2rtc covers with vendor-specific code?
Is two-way audio (talk to the camera) a launch requirement? It decides whether go2rtc is mandatory.
What live latency is acceptable? Under 0.5 s for PTZ and talk means WebRTC with TURN costs; 1-3 s allows MSE/HLS through simpler infrastructure.
How many cameras per user, and how many tiles in a grid on phones versus desktop? How many people watch the same camera at once (family versus business)?
Are we willing to require or force H.264 substreams on cameras, or must we support H.265-only cameras, accepting transcoding hardware or reduced browser support?

Licensing posture: is it acceptable for any shipped component (desktop app, edge agent) to be GPL? Will native apps bundle FFmpeg/libVLC/libmpv (LGPL/GPL and HEVC patents) or rely only on OS/browser decoders and WebRTC?
Should the Windows app be a native app with local LAN access (e.g. also running the edge agent), or just a wrapped web app?
What budget per user per month is there for TURN/relay bandwidth, if the product is SaaS?

area: Camera discovery, onboarding and control (ONVIF, vendor APIs, P2P/cloud-only cameras, client libraries, auth/time quirks)
summary: ONVIF plus RTSP is the only practical cross-vendor baseline, but real-world support is uneven. Hikvision has shipped with ONVIF off since firmware 5.5.0, and on Reolink, EZVIZ, Imou, Dahua and Tapo RTSP/ONVIF must be switched on, or a separate camera account created, before it works. A guided per-vendor onboarding wizard is therefore a core feature. Standards are changing: ONVIF announced on 2025-10-09 that it is ending Profile S over weak authentication, recommends Profile T, has published a WebRTC streaming spec (24.06 to 26.06), and released Profile V as a release candidate (2026-07-09) for outbound cloud connections over WebRTC. Matter 1.5 (2025-11-20) added cameras over WebRTC. Neither Profile V nor Matter cameras are in the field at scale yet. PTZ is the least consistent area. Basic Continuous/Absolute moves and presets usually work, but Hikvision does not update MoveStatus, Reolink lacks FOV RelativeMove, Uniview claims RelativeMove but the camera does not move, and Foscam and Sunba are incomplete. Probe capabilities per camera and do not trust advertised features. A large consumer segment is cloud-only or P2P-only: Ring, Blink, most Arlo, new Nest, Xiaomi, Tuya/Smart Life, many EZVIZ and Imou models, and battery cameras in general. These need either official cloud APIs (Nest Device Access, EZVIZ Open, Imou Open, Tuya Cloud) or reverse-engineered protocols such as go2rtc's xiaomi, tapo, wyze and tuya sources, each with its own legal and stability risk. Browsers cannot do WS-Discovery (UDP multicast), cannot talk SOAP or RTSP to cameras (CORS, mixed content, Chrome Local Network Access prompt), and cannot reach cameras behind NAT. iOS needs an Apple-approved multicast entitlement, and Android 17 (target SDK 37) requires the ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK runtime permission. The architecture therefore needs a local edge agent that does discovery, control, events and credential custody, whether the product is self-hosted or a multi-tenant SaaS. Permissive (MIT) building blocks are available and active in 2026: go2rtc, kerberos-io/onvif and 0x524a/onvif-go (Go), agsh/onvif (Node, v1 TS rewrite at rc), onvif-zeep-async (Python, used by Home Assistant), SharpOnvif (.NET), easy_onvif (Dart/Flutter, but no events service) and oxvif and lumeohq/onvif-rs (Rust). Licenses to avoid or audit: python-amcrest (GPLv2) and gSOAP-based C++ stacks (GPLv2 or commercial). Auth and time quirks are a frequent cause of failed onboarding. WS-Security UsernameToken depends on clock skew, so compute the offset from an unauthenticated GetSystemDateAndTime. Newer firmware may default to SHA-256 digest, while FFmpeg releases up to 9.0 and go2rtc only do MD5 digest.

facts.claim: ONVIF announced on 2025-10-09 that it will end support for Profile S because its authentication mechanisms (WS UsernameToken) no longer meet current cybersecurity recommendations. It recommends Profile T. The June 2026 conformance test tools, valid for 9 months, are the last that let manufacturers claim Profile S conformance. Deployed Profile S systems keep working.

Profile T covers H.264 and/or H.265 (a device must support at least one, so H.265 is not strictly mandatory), HTTPS streaming, imaging settings (focus, exposure, WDR), motion and tampering alarm events, PTZ configuration, digital I/O and bidirectional audio. OSD and metadata streaming are mandatory for devices, and PTZ control is mandatory for clients.

ONVIF published a WebRTC streaming spec in 24.06 (configured via Media2), added reflexive/relay ICE candidates in 24.12, and released further versions 25.06, 25.12 and 26.06. Sending PTZ, events or metadata over WebRTC data channels is out of scope, and client-to-signaling-server communication is shown only as an example.

ONVIF Profile V Release Candidate (2026-07-09) is a draft standard for cloud video surveillance. The device opens a secure outbound connection to a conformant cloud VMS and streams over WebRTC, with no port forwarding or VPN. As of 2026-10 I found no final release.

ONVIF Profile G specification v1.1 was published around November 2025. In practice, Profile G (edge recording search and replay) is rarely and inconsistently implemented on consumer cameras, so per-model testing is required.

Profile M standardizes analytics metadata and events (object classification, face, vehicle, licence plate, counting) and allows events as JSON over MQTT. The source material dates from 2020-2021, so it may be outdated.

Matter 1.5 (released 2025-11-20) added a camera device type using WebRTC with STUN/TURN, multi-stream, PTZ, detection and privacy zones, and continuous or event recording to local or cloud storage. Matter 1.5.1 (about March 2026) adds multi-stream improvements.

Hikvision IP camera firmware has shipped with ONVIF disabled since v5.5.0 (2017), and upgrading also disables it. To enable it: Configuration > Network > Advanced > Integration Protocol > Enable ONVIF, then create an ONVIF user (max 32) with a level such as Media User or Administrator.

Hikvision RTSP paths are /Streaming/Channels/101 (main), 102 (sub) and 103 (third stream). Some newer Hikvision cameras need RTSP and WEB authentication set to digest/basic with MD5 digest before third-party clients work.

Hikvision ISAPI is a RESTful HTTP/XML API. Official ISAPI developer guides are on the Hikvision TPP portal and need a Materials License Agreement. Events stream over the long-lived multipart endpoint /ISAPI/Event/notification/alertStream, and PTZ continuous move is PUT /ISAPI/PTZCtrl/channels/{n}/continuous.

Per Frigate's community list, Hikvision PTZs do not update ONVIF MoveStatus even on the latest firmware, so they cannot autotrack. Reolink (including TrackMix) lacks ONVIF FOV RelativeMove. Uniview IPC672LR-AX4DUPK claims FOV RelativeMove but does not move. Axis Q-6155E lacks MoveStatus. Dahua/EmpireTech PTZs are the most consistently working, while Dahua lite/picoo series and Vikylin and Sunba have incomplete ONVIF.
Typical ONVIF service ports differ by vendor: Reolink 8000, Tapo 2020, Amcrest/Axis/Dahua 80. Frigate defaults to 8000. The port must be discovered or configured; it cannot be assumed.
Dahua/Amcrest RTSP path is /cam/realmonitor?channel=1&subtype=0 (main); subtypes 1-3 are the sub and mid streams. go2rtc's author rates Dahua as the 'reference implementation' for streaming.

Dahua HTTP API (CGI) supports Basic and Digest (MD5). eventManager.cgi?action=attach holds the connection open and streams multipart events. Newer Dahua hardware moved some functions to a JSON RPC2 interface, and some old CGI calls stopped working. Public Dahua/Amcrest API docs are old (Amcrest rev 2.12 from 2017).

In 2022 Nozomi Networks disclosed that Dahua's ONVIF WS-UsernameToken handling allowed replay of sniffed credentials. Dahua patched it, and the advice was to use HTTPS. In 2026, CVE-2026-88278 (GeoVision) showed the same class of freshness and nonce failure.

A Dahua forum report and a GitHub issue show cameras advertising MaxPullPoints=5 (5 simultaneous event subscriptions). ONVIF conformance tests check the max pull-point count, so clients should read capabilities, call Unsubscribe and renew well inside TerminationTime.

Reolink: on most models the RTSP and ONVIF ports are disabled by default and must be enabled in the app or client (port settings). Firmware 3.1+ on some models disabled ONVIF by default for security reasons.

Reolink ports are HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, RTMP 1935, RTSP 554, ONVIF 8000 and proprietary TCP 9000 (Baichuan). Some models (B400/B500/B800/D400/D800/E1 etc.) have no HTTP API and work only through a Reolink NVR or Home Hub. Battery cameras are reachable via Home Hub/NVR. LTE models (Go series, TrackMix LTE) cannot be integrated. 'Account device' mode, which binds the camera to a Reolink cloud account, blocks local login. Reolink cannot push ONVIF events to HTTPS endpoints and supports only a limited number of simultaneous connections.

Reolink event delivery used by the official Home Assistant integration, in order of preference: TCP push (Baichuan), ONVIF push, ONVIF long-poll, then fast polling every 5 seconds. Reolink 4K main streams are H.265, and RTMP/FLV do not carry 4K. Frigate recommends HTTP-FLV for 5MP and below and RTSP or enhanced-FLV H.265 (ffmpeg 8) for 6MP and above.

Reolink HTTP API: POST to api.cgi with cmd=Login returns a token (leaseTime 3600 s) used for later JSON commands such as PtzCtrl. The path is /api.cgi or /cgi-bin/api.cgi depending on firmware. The reolink_aio library (MIT, 0.21.18, 2026-10-10) is the Reolink-authorized implementation behind the Home Assistant platinum integration.

Reolink Wi-Fi QR provisioning: generate an ISO-8859-1 QR code containing ssid

password

last4 (last4 = last 4 digits of the camera's printed QR) and show it to the camera at power-up. The camera joins Wi-Fi in about 1 minute.

Tapo: wired cameras support RTSP (554, /stream1 and /stream2) and ONVIF Profile S (port 2020) after a separate 'Camera Account' is created in the Tapo app. Battery cameras and doorbells (e.g. C410/C420/C425/D230) do not support RTSP. ONVIF exposes only the wide lens on dual-lens models and has no two-way audio. Tapo Care cloud, microSD and NVR recording cannot all run together; only 2 of the 3 can.

Some Tapo/Kasa firmware requires enabling 'Third-Party Compatibility' (Tapo Lab) before local third-party access works. Newer Tapo devices need TP-Link cloud credentials for local auth, plus camera-account credentials for live view.

go2rtc's proprietary tapo:// source authenticates with the Tapo cloud password (or its uppercase MD5 hash, or SHA-256 hash on newer firmware), not the RTSP password, and supports two-way audio. vigi:// covers TP-Link VIGI. TP-Link says VIGI supports ONVIF Profile S/G/T, and Frigate recommends setting VIGI main streams to H.264 with Smart Coding off.

EZVIZ: local RTSP is off by default and is enabled in the app (Settings > LAN Live View > scan > camera > Local Server Settings > enable RTSP). Username is admin and the password is the 6-character verification code on the sticker. Users report RTSP turning off after reboot on the C3X and missing entirely on some 2023+ models (BC1, BC2, BM1). Home Assistant's EZVIZ integration is cloud_polling via the unofficial ezvizlife API.

go2rtc's author rates EZVIZ RTSP as an 'awful RTSP protocol implementation, many bugs in SDP', some Reolink models as having an 'unusable RTSP implementation', and TP-Link as having 'few streaming clients, packet loss'.

The EZVIZ Open Platform offers HLS/RTMP/FLV stream URLs via AppKey/AppSecret to accessToken. I found no published quota. The Imou Open Platform (open.imoulife.com) offers cloud live URLs, alarms and PTZ with regional hosts, and Home Assistant docs state 30,000 free API requests per month per App ID.

Imou: many models have an RTSP/ONVIF toggle in Imou Life. Which credential works (a separate ONVIF/RTSP password or the Safety Code on the label) is inconsistent across models and reports. Local RTSP sometimes works only after the Imou app has connected.

Xiaomi Mi Home cameras expose no standard RTSP. go2rtc v1.9.13 (2025-12-14) added a native xiaomi:// source for the proprietary 'miss' protocol over cs2/TUTK P2P. It needs a Mi account login, needs Internet on every connection to fetch encryption keys, streams locally, and does not support all cameras.

go2rtc v1.9.14 (2026-01-19, latest tag on proxy.golang.org) added a native Wyze P2P source (needs Wyze API key and DTLS firmware). v1.9.13 added Tuya (needs a Tuya Smart account; Smart Life accounts are not supported, or a Tuya Cloud project with the IoT Video Live Stream service). go2rtc also has dvrip (XMEye/Sofia), eseecloud, kasa, ring, nest, homekit, isapi (two-way audio) and roborock sources. License is MIT.

Cheap Xiongmai-based cameras (XMEye/iCSee) use the DVR-IP/Sofia protocol on TCP 34567, with RTSP URLs like /user=X_password=Y_channel=1_stream=0.sdp. The ONVIF port is non-standard (8899 is often reported). Security record: XMEye P2P cloud IDs are derived from the MAC address, cloud traffic is unencrypted, and an undocumented 'default' account exists (CVE-2018-17919). CVE-2022-45045 is an authenticated RCE via port 34567, exploited in the wild. SEC Consult advised not using XMEye P2P products.
ThroughTek Kalay (TUTK) P2P SDK below 3.1.10 allowed UID impersonation (CVE-2021-28372, CVSS about 9.6). Kalay claimed more than 83M devices across many OEM camera brands.

Google Nest Device Access charges a one-time US$5 fee per account (commercial and individual). New Nest cameras stream via GenerateWebRtcStream (SDP offer/answer). GenerateRtspStream is limited to legacy Nest Cam, Nest Hub Max and legacy doorbell. A stream URL can be used by only one application at a time and is valid for 5 minutes unless extended.

Ring and Blink offer no RTSP/ONVIF and no official third-party streaming API. Arlo is largely cloud-first. Eufy offers RTSP only on some models, and officially not when the camera is linked to HomeBase 3. Most of these sources are third-party guides or forums, some predating 2025.

Axis devices ship with VAPIX and ONVIF disabled and no root password at factory default. AXIS OS 11.6+ removed the default 'root' user. Axis recommends dedicated, limited service accounts for integrations.

Uniview's own guide suggests disabling RTSP/HTTP authentication (Setup > Security > Authentication) when live view fails on third-party recorders. Forum reports show switching RTSP auth from Digest to Basic, which is a security trade-off the app should not recommend by default.
FFmpeg HTTP/RTSP digest auth supports only MD5 and MD5-sess in every release branch up to release/9.0. SHA-256 and SHA-512-256 digest exist only on master (9.1-dev) as of 2026-10-17.

go2rtc's RTSP/HTTP digest implementation (pkg/tcp/auth.go, request.go) is MD5-only. Its ONVIF client builds WS-Security PasswordDigest from local time.Now() without compensating for device clock offset.
TP-Link states that SHA-256 RTSP digest is more secure but most third-party clients do not support it, so MD5 is the default for compatibility.

WS-Security UsernameToken includes a Created timestamp and nonce, so clock skew between client and camera causes auth failures. agsh/onvif calls GetSystemDateAndTime first (unauthenticated, retrying with credentials for some Panasonic and Digital Barriers models) and keeps a timeShift. Frigate added ignore_time_mismatch as an escape hatch. I found no normative ONVIF skew tolerance.

The Home Assistant ONVIF integration selects only H.264 profiles. It fails with 'No usable cameras' on H.265-only cameras unless a substream is set to H.264. It uses PullPoint (with optional webhooks) and maps topics such as Motion alarm, Cell motion, Field detection, Human shape and Tamper. IR lamp and autofocus use ONVIF Imaging (IrCutFilter, AutoFocusMode).

WS-Discovery uses UDP multicast 239.255.255.250:3702, which routers do not forward across VLANs or subnets. Manual add-by-IP is the standard fallback. go2rtc notes its ONVIF autodiscovery requires the same subnet, and Docker 'network host'.

iOS: sending or receiving multicast/broadcast (needed for WS-Discovery probes) requires the restricted com.apple.developer.networking.multicast entitlement, which the Account Holder requests from Apple per team, plus an NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription Local Network prompt.

Android local network permission: opt-in in Android 16 (uses NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES). For apps targeting SDK 37 (Android 17), LAN TCP and UDP unicast/multicast/broadcast are blocked by default and need the ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK runtime permission (or a system picker). Apps targeting below 37 with INTERNET get a temporary implicit grant. A WifiManager.MulticastLock is still needed to receive multicast on many devices.

Browsers: Chrome's Local Network Access permission gates public-origin requests to private IPs. Google described it on 2025-06-09 (flag in Chrome 138), and it shipped as a user prompt around Chrome 141/142 (sources disagree). Browsers also cannot send UDP, so no WS-Discovery. easy-onvif-web states WS-Discovery is unsupported and SOAP needs a CORS-friendly proxy in front of the camera.

Windows: Dart's RawDatagramSocket fails to join 239.255.255.250:3702 on Windows 10/11 (errno 10049). easy_onvif works around it with an FFI discovery.dll. UWP/MSIX-packaged apps need the privateNetworkClientServer capability for LAN sockets.

Go ONVIF libraries: use-go/onvif (MIT) last commit 2024-09-29, last tag v0.0.9 (2022-07-26), so effectively unmaintained. kerberos-io/onvif (MIT fork) is v1.2.3 (2026-10-02) with Device/Media/PTZ/Event/Discovery and UsernameToken/Digest/both auth fallback. IOTechSystems/onvif (MIT, EdgeX fork) is v1.3.0 (2026-09-07). 0x524a/onvif-go (MIT) is v1.2.0 (2026-10-10), with 200+ typed operations plus a virtual camera server.

Node: npm 'onvif' (agsh, MIT) has latest = 0.8.3 (2026-09-07) and rc = 1.0.0-rc.3 (2026-09-24), a TypeScript rewrite with Profiles S/T/G/M/C/A, Digest MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256, WS-Discovery, pull-point and base-notification events, and a preserveAddress option for wrong XAddr hosts behind NAT. Master was updated 2026-10-17. futomi/node-onvif (MIT) last commit 2018, abandoned.

Python: onvif-zeep-async (MIT) 4.3.0 (2026-09-28) is asyncio-based with PullPoint and Notification managers, and Home Assistant core pins it (onvif-zeep-async==4.3.0, WSDiscovery==2.1.2). The original onvif-zeep's last PyPI release was 0.2.12 (2018). onvif-python (nirsimetri, MIT) 0.4.4 (2026-10-05) is a newer alternative.

.NET: SharpOnvifClient/Server/Common (MIT, jimm98y) 0.11.3 (2026-10-15) target net481, netstandard2.0, net8.0 and net10.0. Version 0.10 replaced WCF/CoreWCF with HttpClient and ASP.NET Core. The client supports PullPoint and Basic event subscriptions and WS-Discovery. OnvifDiscovery (MIT) is 3.0.0. Onvif.Core 3.0.0 (2025-03-18) declares no license in its nuspec.

Dart/Flutter: easy_onvif (MIT) 3.1.5 (2026-07-28) is tagged for Android, iOS, Windows, Linux, macOS and web, and covers Device, Imaging, Media1/2, PTZ (helper falls back from Relative to AbsoluteMove), Recording, Replay, Search and WS-Discovery. Its README documents no Events/PullPoint service, so motion events would have to be built in-house.

Rust: lumeohq/onvif-rs (MIT) is git-only (not on crates.io), last commit 2026-08-12, types generated from schema but not all operations. oxvif (MIT) 0.17.0 (2026-09-14), first published 2026-04, has 34 versions with source-breaking changes, covering discovery, Media1/2, PTZ, imaging, events, recording, search, replay and a mock device. retina (MIT/Apache-2.0, 0.4.21, 2026-10-04) is a Rust RTSP client.

Licensing traps: python 'amcrest' (Dahua/Amcrest HTTP API wrapper) is GPLv2 (1.9.9, 2025-07). gSOAP, the base of many C/C++ ONVIF stacks, is GPLv2 or commercial (the gSOAP Public License covers only parts). libonvif (sr99622) is Apache-2.0. pytapo, pyHik and reolink-aio are MIT, and pyezvizapi is Apache-2.0.
