facts.claim: ONVIF access classes: PRE_AUTH is open to all levels, READ_MEDIA to Administrator, Operator and User, and ACTUATE (PTZ moves) only to Administrator and Operator. A dedicated Operator-level ONVIF user is therefore enough for viewing plus PTZ without granting WRITE_SYSTEM or UNRECOVERABLE rights. The matrix is reproduced by easy_onvif docs, not the spec itself.

Hik-Connect (Hikvision P2P) 'Platform Access' is disabled by default on NVRs and needs a 6-12 character, case-sensitive verification code. Stream encryption then requires that code for remote live view.

Common consumer Wi-Fi provisioning methods are: phone-generated QR shown to the camera lens (Reolink, many others), AP/hotspot mode, BLE provisioning, and SmartConfig/EZ broadcast. SmartConfig works only on 2.4 GHz and fails with hidden SSIDs and AP isolation.

options.name: A. Local edge agent (recommended core): Go service embedding go2rtc + an ONVIF client library + vendor adapters
options.description: A single Go binary (or a Windows service, Docker container, NAS package or Raspberry Pi image) on the camera LAN. It does WS-Discovery and subnet scanning, ONVIF control (kerberos-io/onvif or 0x524a/onvif-go), event subscriptions, vendor adapters (Hikvision ISAPI, Dahua CGI/RPC2, Reolink api.cgi/Baichuan, Tapo), and stream ingest and repackaging via go2rtc (RTSP, WebRTC, MSE, HLS). It holds camera credentials locally. Web, iOS, Android and Windows clients talk to the agent directly on LAN or through an outbound tunnel/WebRTC when remote. The Windows desktop app can bundle the agent.
pros: Avoids every client-platform restriction: browser UDP/CORS/mixed content/LNA, the iOS multicast entitlement and Android 17 local-network permission. Only the agent needs LAN access.
go2rtc (MIT) already covers RTSP/ONVIF plus proprietary tapo, vigi, xiaomi, wyze, tuya, dvrip, isapi, kasa, ring and nest sources, and outputs WebRTC/MSE/HLS for all client platforms.
Camera credentials never leave the LAN, which matters for SaaS liability and GDPR (the user is Romanian/EU).
The same agent serves the self-hosted and multi-tenant SaaS models; the SaaS only brokers signalling and metadata.
Event subscriptions (PullPoint, Baichuan TCP push, ISAPI alertStream, Dahua attach) need a long-lived process near the camera anyway.
cons: Needs an always-on device on the user's network (Windows PC, NAS, Pi or old Android phone), which adds install friction for pure-consumer users.
go2rtc's ONVIF client is minimal (MD5-only digest, no clock-skew compensation), so a fuller ONVIF library is still needed for PTZ, imaging and events.
Reverse-engineered vendor protocols (xiaomi, tapo, wyze) can break on firmware updates and may conflict with vendor ToS.
Remote access requires a relay/TURN or tunnel infrastructure, which costs money at SaaS scale.
options.license: go2rtc MIT; kerberos-io/onvif MIT; 0x524a/onvif-go MIT; IOTechSystems/onvif MIT
options.maturity: go2rtc v1.9.14 (2026-01), widely deployed (Frigate, Home Assistant); kerberos-io/onvif v1.2.3 (2026-10); onvif-go v1.2.0 (2026-10, young)

options.name: B. Client-direct control inside a Flutter app (easy_onvif) with no agent
options.description: Each native client (Android, iOS, Windows) discovers and controls cameras itself using easy_onvif for ONVIF and per-vendor HTTP calls, and plays RTSP via a native player. Web would be view-only through some relay.
pros: No extra hardware; the simplest story for a single user on home Wi-Fi.
easy_onvif is MIT, actively maintained (3.1.5, 2026-07) and tagged for all Flutter platforms.
Lower latency for local viewing and PTZ.
cons: Does not work for web: no UDP, CORS and LNA prevent direct SOAP or RTSP.
Needs the iOS multicast entitlement (Apple approval) and Android 17 ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK. Windows Dart multicast needs an FFI DLL.
easy_onvif has no Events/PullPoint support, so motion-triggered recording would have to be rebuilt per platform.
Recording only runs while the app is open (mobile background limits), and every device needs camera credentials, which widens exposure.
Breaks when the phone is off-LAN unless ports are forwarded, which is insecure.
options.license: easy_onvif MIT
options.maturity: easy_onvif 3.1.5 (2026-07-28); single-maintainer project

options.name: C. Cloud-side connectors to vendor clouds (for cloud-only/P2P cameras)
options.description: Server-side integrations with official vendor clouds: Google Nest Device Access (WebRTC), EZVIZ Open Platform (HLS/RTMP/FLV), Imou Open API, Tuya Cloud (IoT Video Live Stream). Optionally go2rtc's reverse-engineered sources run in the agent for Xiaomi, Wyze and Tapo.
pros: Only path to cameras with no RTSP/ONVIF (Nest, many EZVIZ/Imou/Tuya models) and to battery cameras.
No LAN access needed; works from SaaS directly.
Official APIs give vendor-sanctioned access with stable contracts.
cons: Quotas, fees and per-vendor app approval (Imou 30,000 free requests/month per App ID; Nest US$5 per account plus Google project review for commercial use; Tuya service subscription).
Streams are short-lived (Nest 5 minutes unless extended) and often lower quality; PTZ and events vary.
Ring, Blink and Arlo have no official third-party streaming API, so only unofficial reverse-engineering is possible (legal and ToS risk).
Video transits vendor clouds, which raises privacy and GDPR considerations.
options.license: Vendor ToS; go2rtc MIT for reverse-engineered sources
options.maturity: Varies: Nest SDM stable; EZVIZ/Imou/Tuya stable but thinly documented in English; go2rtc xiaomi/wyze/tuya sources new (2025-12 to 2026-01)

options.name: D. Direct cloud-to-camera (port forwarding, DDNS) from a central SaaS
options.description: The SaaS backend connects to each camera's public IP over RTSP/ONVIF/HTTP via user-configured port forwarding.
pros: No agent and no vendor APIs; conceptually simple.
cons: Exposes cameras with weak, replay-prone auth (UsernameToken, Basic/MD5 digest, Xiongmai history) to the Internet. ONVIF and vendors explicitly recommend VPN or TLS instead.
WS-Discovery is impossible; onboarding is entirely manual; CGNAT breaks it on many mobile and ISP links.
High liability for a multi-tenant SaaS.
options.license: n/a
options.maturity: Legacy pattern; not recommended

options.name: E. Standards-forward: ONVIF Profile V and Matter 1.5 camera support (watch, then add)
options.description: Support cameras that connect outbound to the cloud (ONVIF Profile V, WebRTC) or expose Matter camera clusters (WebRTC Transport Provider, PTZ, zones).
pros: Removes NAT and agent problems by design and is vendor-neutral.
Matter brings large ecosystems (Apple, Google, Amazon, SmartThings) and standard PTZ and zone control.
cons: Profile V is only a release candidate (2026-07); few if any shipping devices.
Matter cameras are only starting to ship (spec 2025-11, 1.5.1 in 2026-03); the full spec needs CSA registration and certification costs to act as a commissioner.
Cannot serve the existing installed base.
options.license: ONVIF specs free to read; Matter spec via CSA (membership for certification)
options.maturity: Emerging (2025-2026)

recommendation:
Build camera access around a local edge agent (Option A) and treat client-direct ONVIF (Option B) only as an optional LAN fast path in native apps. Add official vendor-cloud connectors (Option C) selectively, and track Profile V and Matter (Option E) for a 2027+ roadmap.

Concretely:
(1) Agent in Go. Embed go2rtc (MIT) for stream ingest and WebRTC/MSE/HLS out, and use kerberos-io/onvif (MIT, active, UsernameToken/Digest fallback) as the ONVIF control and events library. Evaluate 0x524a/onvif-go as a richer but younger alternative, and avoid use-go/onvif (unmaintained). If the team prefers TypeScript or .NET for the agent, agsh/onvif v1 (MIT) or SharpOnvif (MIT) are the equivalents. Do not use GPL code (python-amcrest, gSOAP) in a closed product.

(2) Onboarding wizard:
- Run WS-Discovery plus a fallback unicast subnet scan of the known ports: 80/443, 554, 8000 (Reolink), 2020 (Tapo), 8899 and 34567 (Xiongmai), 37777 (Dahua), 9000 (Reolink Baichuan). Always offer add-by-IP.
- Call unauthenticated GetSystemDateAndTime and store a per-camera clock offset. Prefer HTTPS when offered.
- Try WS-UsernameToken, then HTTP Digest, then Basic only over TLS. Detect SHA-256-only digest and tell the user to switch to MD5, or ship a digest implementation that supports SHA-256, since FFmpeg ≤9.0 and go2rtc are MD5-only.
- Fingerprint the vendor with GetDeviceInformation and show vendor-specific instructions for enabling ONVIF/RTSP: Hikvision Integration Protocol, Reolink port settings and 'Local device' mode, Tapo Camera Account and Third-Party Compatibility, EZVIZ LAN Live View with the verification code, Imou toggle.
- Prefer an H.264 substream for web and mobile live view and keep the H.265 main stream for recording.

(3) Control: probe capabilities and do not trust what the camera advertises.
- PTZ: test ContinuousMove with an explicit Stop rather than relying on Timeout, test AbsoluteMove/RelativeMove (including whether FOV RelativeMove really works), and handle presets via GetPresets/GotoPreset/SetPreset. Treat MoveStatus as unreliable on Hikvision.
- Imaging: IrCutFilter, focus and exposure via the Imaging service.
- Events: start with ONVIF PullPoint (respect MaxPullPoints, renew early, Unsubscribe on shutdown), then vendor-native events (Reolink Baichuan push, Hikvision alertStream, Dahua eventManager attach), with agent-side motion detection on the substream as the universal fallback.

(4) Credentials: store them only in the agent, encrypted with the OS keystore (DPAPI/Credential Manager on Windows, Android Keystore, iOS Keychain). Encourage a dedicated Operator-level ONVIF user, never the admin account. Never send credentials to browsers or the SaaS backend.

(5) Support tiers for marketing and QA:
- Tier 1: ONVIF Profile S/T wired cameras from Dahua/Amcrest, Hikvision, Axis, Uniview, TP-Link VIGI, Reolink wired and Tapo wired.
- Tier 2 (beta, may break): proprietary local protocols via go2rtc, i.e. Tapo two-way audio, Xiaomi, Wyze, Tuya, XMEye/DVRIP with a security warning.
- Tier 3: official cloud APIs (Nest first, then EZVIZ/Imou if demand exists).
- Explicitly unsupported at launch: Ring, Blink, Arlo, battery-only and LTE cameras.

(6) Before committing, build a small hardware lab of about 8-10 cameras (Hikvision, Dahua/Amcrest, Reolink wired and Reolink battery with Home Hub, Tapo C2xx, VIGI, EZVIZ, Imou, a Xiongmai/iCSee unit and one Axis or Uniview). Run an automated conformance smoke test against them: discovery, auth modes, time skew, stream URIs, PTZ modes, events.
risks: Vendor firmware drift: defaults change silently (Hikvision ONVIF off since 5.5.0; Reolink 3.1+ ONVIF off; EZVIZ RTSP resets on reboot; Dahua moving from CGI to RPC2). Integrations need continuous regression testing on real hardware.

Many cameras have a small concurrent-stream or connection budget (Reolink drops connections from the same host IP; Tapo allows only 2 of cloud/SD/NVR). The app must multiplex one upstream connection per camera through the agent, not one per viewer.

PTZ and events are inconsistent despite ONVIF conformance claims (Hikvision MoveStatus, Reolink and Uniview RelativeMove, MaxPullPoints=5). The UI must degrade gracefully, which raises support-ticket volume.

Security and liability: UsernameToken replay (Dahua 2022, GeoVision CVE-2026-88278), Xiongmai backdoors and P2P flaws (CVE-2018-17919, CVE-2022-45045), and TUTK Kalay CVE-2021-28372. Supporting cheap cameras or P2P protocols can expose users. Never port-forward cameras; keep camera traffic on LAN through the agent.

Legal and ToS risk of reverse-engineered protocols (Xiaomi miss/cs2, Tapo cloud-password auth, Wyze P2P, Ring, Eufy). These can break or be blocked by vendors at any time and should not be core to a paid SLA.
Copyleft contamination: python-amcrest (GPLv2) and gSOAP (GPLv2 or commercial) must not be linked into a closed-source commercial product.

Platform permission hurdles: the iOS multicast entitlement needs Apple approval (can delay App Store launch). Android 17 targetSdk 37 needs ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK, a runtime prompt that can be denied. The Chrome Local Network Access prompt blocks web-to-LAN calls. All of these push toward the agent architecture.

Codec mismatch: many cameras default to H.265 main streams, which some browsers and the Home Assistant-style H.264-only logic cannot play. Requires substream selection or transcoding (CPU cost on the agent).

Auth incompatibilities: SHA-256-only digest on newer firmware vs MD5-only FFmpeg (≤9.0) and go2rtc; clock-skew failures with UsernameToken; vendor confusion over which password to use (Imou Safety Code, EZVIZ verification code, Tapo camera account vs cloud password).

Cloud API dependencies: Imou 30,000 requests/month free quota per App ID, Nest 5-minute stream lifetime and Google commercial review, undocumented EZVIZ quotas. Costs and limits scale with SaaS usage.

Standards transition: Profile S is being retired (conformance claims end around Q1 2027) while Profile V and Matter cameras are immature. The integration layer must abstract protocols so new transports (WebRTC/Profile V/Matter) can be added without a rewrite.

Several facts here come from community forums or third-party guides (Imou credentials, XMEye ports, Tapo connection limits, Chrome LNA version). Validate them against the hardware lab before relying on them in product messaging.
questions_for_product_owner: Business model: personal/self-hosted tool, prosumer one-time purchase, or multi-tenant SaaS with subscriptions? This decides whether an always-on edge agent (PC/NAS/Pi/old phone) is acceptable for target users and who pays for remote-access relay (TURN) bandwidth.

Target camera segment: professional/prosumer ONVIF cameras (Hikvision, Dahua, Reolink wired, VIGI, Axis), consumer Wi-Fi brands popular in Romania/EU (Tapo, EZVIZ, Imou, Xiaomi), or cloud-only brands (Ring, Nest, Arlo, Blink)? Which 5-10 models must work at launch?
Are you willing to ship reverse-engineered vendor protocols (Xiaomi, Tapo cloud-password, Wyze, Eufy) given ToS and stability risk, or only standards (ONVIF/RTSP) plus official vendor APIs?

Which 'control' features are must-have for v1: PTZ (continuous, presets, patrol), imaging (IR, day/night, exposure), two-way audio, siren/floodlight, reboot/firmware, motion-zone configuration? Two-way audio and siren often need vendor-specific APIs.
Is battery-camera support required? Battery cameras rarely expose RTSP and drain when streamed; most need a vendor hub (Reolink Home Hub, Eufy HomeBase) or cloud.
Should the app recommend or sell certified cameras (a compatibility list), or promise 'any IP camera'? The latter implies heavy support cost.
Remote access expectation: should viewing outside home work with zero router configuration (needs relay or tunnel infrastructure), or is VPN/Tailscale-style setup acceptable for power users?
Motion-triggered recording: rely on camera events (fast, inconsistent) or run server/agent-side motion or AI detection (consistent, costs CPU/GPU)? This affects agent hardware requirements.
Data residency and GDPR: may video or metadata transit or be stored on non-EU vendor clouds (EZVIZ, Imou, Tuya, Google) for cloud-only cameras?
Is App Store presence on iOS required at launch? The multicast entitlement request to Apple should start early if on-device discovery is needed.

area: Cross-platform client framework (Web + Android + iOS + Windows) for live video grids, playback timelines and PTZ: Flutter vs React Native vs Kotlin/Compose Multiplatform vs .NET MAUI(+Blazor) vs web-first (SPA + Capacitor + Tauri/Electron), including per-platform video stacks, background-execution limits, push, and store-review constraints
summary: The most important finding is that the framework choice matters less than the video architecture. Browsers cannot play RTSP, iPhone AVPlayer cannot play RTSP, and Android's built-in Media3 RTSP is H.264-only. Viewing remotely or on the web therefore always needs a media gateway that converts RTSP to WebRTC, with MSE or LL-HLS as fallbacks. Both go2rtc and MediaMTX are MIT-licensed and do this. Once the gateway exists, WebRTC can be the common live transport on all four targets. Native players (libmpv, libmdk, libVLC) remain useful for direct RTSP on the local network and for H.265 decoding where the browser cannot help (Firefox has no H.265 in WebRTC or MSE; Chrome needs 136+ and Safari 18+). Phones cannot be the recorder. iOS suspends apps seconds after backgrounding, and Android 15+ caps dataSync/mediaProcessing foreground services at 6 hours per 24 hours. Recording has to run on an always-on component: a gateway/NVR box, a Windows service, or the cloud, which then uploads to Drive, OneDrive, S3 or local disk. In October 2026, Flutter (stable 3.47.x) is the only option where one UI codebase has a working, maintained video path on all four targets: flutter_webrtc (MIT, libwebrtc m150 on Windows, released 2026-10-07) for live WebRTC, and media_kit (MIT) or fvp (libmdk, free for commercial Flutter apps) for native RTSP, H.265 and recorded playback. Flutter's weakest target is the web, where each video tile is an HTML platform view. A 9–16 tile grid spike on Flutter web is the first de-risking task. Web-first (React/Svelte + Capacitor 8.5 + Tauri 2.12) is the strong alternative if the web dashboard is the main surface and the team writes TypeScript. Its trade-off is no direct RTSP anywhere without custom native plugins. React Native lacks WebRTC and video players on Windows. Compose Multiplatform for web is still Beta and lacks a WebRTC library on desktop. MAUI has no web target and only short support windows. Note: the shared web-search budget ran out near the end, so WebView2 HEVC support and Chrome's exact Local Network Access enforcement version could not be checked independently.

facts.claim: Flutter stable line is 3.47.x (latest listed patch 3.47.7); 3.41 shipped Feb 11 2026, 3.44 May 18 2026, 3.47 Aug 12 2026; 3.50 planned for November 2026.

Flutter 2026 roadmap: WebAssembly intended to become the default for web builds; desktop multi-window support driven by Canonical; finish Impeller migration on Android. The roadmap calls itself aspirational, not a guarantee.

media_kit (MIT) supports Android 5+, iOS 9+, macOS, Windows 7+, Linux and Web. On web libmpv is NOT used: playback is an HTML <video> element and format support is 'extremely limited as compared to native platforms'.
media_kit native builds list the FFmpeg 'rtsp' and 'hls' demuxers and use GPU hardware-accelerated decoding by default. No documented limit on simultaneous players ('handles multiple FHD videos').
media_kit maintenance: commits on main through Aug 30 2026 (memory-leak fix), but pub releases are infrequent (media_kit_video 2.0.1 was ~10 months old when checked); ~340 open issues.

media_kit's Android libmpv build repo has 'default'/'full' flavors under a permissive license and an 'encoders-gpl' flavor under GPLv3, so a commercial closed-source app must avoid the GPL flavor. The LGPL/GPL status of the bundled FFmpeg/libmpv binaries is not stated and must be verified.

fvp (BSD-3-Clause, v0.39.x) implements the official video_player platform interface on Windows (x64/arm64), Linux, macOS, iOS, Android and HarmonyOS, but not web. It enables hardware decoders by default (e.g. D3D11/NVDEC/MFT on Windows), has a 'lowLatency' option for network streams, and adds record() and snapshot() extensions.
libmdk (the engine behind fvp) is proprietary-keyed: 'Free for Flutter users. A key is already included. Can be commercial softwares.' Other commercial users need a paid license.

flutter_webrtc (MIT) 1.6.2+hotfix.4 was released 2026-10-07. Audio/video and data channels are supported on Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux and Web. Windows/Linux moved to libwebrtc m150, and 2026 releases include several Windows/Linux crash fixes. Insertable streams are not supported, and MediaRecorder is only partial on mobile.
The official Flutter video_player (2.14.1) supports Android, iOS, macOS and web only, not Windows. Formats depend on ExoPlayer, AVPlayer or the browser.
Android Media3 ExoPlayer RTSP supports only H.264, AAC (ADTS) and AC3. There is no H.265 and no multicast. Transport is RTP over UDP unicast or interleaved TCP, with Basic/Digest auth.
iOS AVPlayer/AVURLAsset does not support the RTSP scheme. Apps use FFmpeg/VLC/mpv-based players or a gateway that converts RTSP to HLS or WebRTC.

go2rtc (MIT) takes RTSP/ONVIF/RTMP and many vendor protocols and outputs WebRTC, MSE (fMP4), HLS and MJPEG. Its browser matrix: H.265 over WebRTC needs Chrome/Edge 136+ or Safari 18+; desktop Firefox has no H.265 in WebRTC or MSE; iPhone Safari gets MSE only from 17.1. Latency ranks WebRTC best, MSE medium, HLS worst. Two-way audio is supported for many sources.

MediaMTX (MIT) ingests and serves RTSP, WebRTC, LL-HLS/HLS, SRT, RTMP and Media-over-QUIC. It records to fMP4 or MPEG-TS with playback, supports internal, HTTP or JWT auth, and has a Control API and Prometheus metrics.

Flutter web embeds native HTML (e.g. <video>) via HtmlElementView platform views. The docs warn that many HTML elements under CanvasKit can hurt performance. No documented hard cap on the number of platform views was found.
react-native-webrtc (MIT, WebRTC M155) supports Android, iOS and tvOS; macOS is 'not actively supported'; react-native-windows is explicitly NOT supported; web only via a separate shim.

React Native for Windows removed the legacy Paper renderer in 0.82. RNW 0.84 shipped June 30 2026 (aligned with RN 0.84.1, requires Visual Studio 2026), while core React Native had moved to 0.86/0.87 with a 0.88 RC in Sept 2026, so RNW trails core by several versions.
react-native-video v7 (Nitro modules, New Architecture) is still beta, and v6 is recommended for production. It lists iOS/Android and basic web support, with no Windows.

react-native-vlc-media-player (MIT wrapper over libVLC) is iOS and Android only and supports RTSP/RTP/RTMP/HLS. Its README still references RN 0.59–0.62 and says nothing about New Architecture support. VideoLAN calls it unofficial.

Kotlin Multiplatform docs list Compose Multiplatform as Stable on Android, iOS and Desktop (JVM), and Beta on Web (Kotlin/Wasm). The latest is Compose Multiplatform 1.12.2 (Oct 2026), and no announcement of a stable web target was found.
The KMP WebRTC library webrtc-kmp supports Android, iOS and JS/WasmJS only, with no desktop JVM (Windows). The vlcj desktop video binding is GPLv3, with a paid commercial license.

In ComposeMediaPlayer (MIT; Android/iOS/desktop/web), the maintainer reports the Wasm target broken since 0.8.3. Chaintech's CMP media player has only experimental wasmJs support. Neither documents RTSP.
.NET MAUI 10 (released Nov 11 2025; latest patch 10.0.110 on Sept 22 2026) is the only supported MAUI version, and its support ends May 11 2027, so yearly major upgrades are effectively mandatory.
.NET 11 (GA planned Nov 2026) switches MAUI on Android, iOS and Mac Catalyst from Mono to CoreCLR. Blazor WebAssembly stays on Mono. Previews lacked a CoreCLR mobile debugger.

LibVLCSharp is LGPLv2.1, with commercial licenses via VideoLabs. Its MAUI MediaPlayerElement covers Android, iOS and Windows, with no web/WASM. LibVLCSharp.MAUI 3.10.2 was updated 2026-10-13 with net10.0-android36.0, ios26.0 and windows10.0.19041 targets.
CommunityToolkit.Maui.MediaElement 10.0.0 targets .NET 10 on Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst and Windows. On Android it requires single-task launch mode. RTSP support is not documented.
Capacitor's latest release is 8.5.3 (2026-10-07). Capacitor 8 defaults new iOS projects to Swift Package Manager, and the CocoaPods Specs repo becomes read-only in Dec 2026.
Tauri (MIT or Apache-2.0, latest 2.12.4) uses WebView2 (Chromium) on Windows, WKWebView on iOS and Android System WebView on Android. Minimums are Windows 10+ and Android 8+.
WKWebView gained WebRTC/getUserMedia support in iOS 14.3. Capacitor's custom capacitor:// scheme has caused secure-context issues in some reports.
iPhone Safari got ManagedMediaSource (MSE-compatible) in iOS 17.1, and hls.js plays through it. Before 17.1, iPhone web playback was limited to native HLS or WebRTC.

Chrome's Local Network Access shows a permission prompt when a public website connects to the user's local network (e.g. a camera's private IP). Private-IP or .local targets, or fetch with targetAddressSpace:'local', are exempt from mixed-content blocking. The exact default-enforcement version (cited as 142 by a third party) was not verified.

iOS gives applicationDidEnterBackground five seconds before the app is suspended. beginBackgroundTask grants only limited extra time, and the app is terminated if it doesn't end the task. BGAppRefreshTask and silent pushes get up to 30 s, and silent pushes are rate-limited above roughly 3 per hour.

BGContinuedProcessingTask (iOS/iPadOS 26+) starts in the foreground and can continue in the background with a Live Activity progress UI the user can cancel. The system can terminate it abruptly under resource constraints, prioritizing tasks with little progress. It is meant for finite jobs, not indefinite recording.

App Review 2.5.4: background services may only be used for their intended purposes (VoIP, audio playback, location, task completion, local notifications, etc.). Keeping streams alive by abusing the audio background mode would violate this.

App Review 2.1 requires a demo account or a fully featured demo mode, and the 'Before You Submit' checklist asks for any hardware or resources needed. A camera app should give reviewers a reachable demo camera or stream.

App Review 3.1.1/3.1.2: features or subscriptions unlocked in-app (e.g. cloud-recording plans) must use In-App Purchase, and SaaS or cloud subscriptions are allowed. 3.1.3(f) exempts free companion apps to paid web cloud-storage services only if the app has no purchasing and no calls to action.

iOS 15+ supports Picture in Picture from an AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer content source. This lets a user keep watching a live camera feed in PiP after leaving the app, but it does not enable background recording.

iOS 14+: any app using the local network (unicast to local hosts, Bonjour, multicast) should declare NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription. Sending or receiving IP multicast or broadcast requires the com.apple.developer.networking.multicast entitlement, which needs Apple's approval. This is relevant to ONVIF WS-Discovery, which uses multicast probes.

The Critical Alerts entitlement (sound plays through mute and Do Not Disturb) requires a request form approved by Apple. Time-sensitive notifications (iOS 15+) break through Focus without special approval.

Android (apps targeting 15+): dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services are each capped at 6 hours per 24 hours. The cap resets when the app comes to the foreground. At timeout the service must stop within seconds, otherwise it crashes or ANRs.

No Android foreground-service type is meant for recording network IP cameras. connectedDevice covers network interactions with external devices (with prerequisites such as CHANGE_NETWORK_STATE). specialUse needs a manifest justification that Google Play reviews. Apps targeting 14+ must declare FGS types in the Play Console.

Android 17: ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK (NEARBY_DEVICES group) is mandatory for apps targeting SDK 37. It gates TCP, UDP unicast/multicast/broadcast, mDNS/SSDP and .local resolution, and also OkHttp/Cronet and WebViews.
Google Play: from Aug 31 2026, new apps and updates must target Android 16 (API 36). An extension to Nov 1 2026 is possible.
Since Android 9 (API 28) cleartext HTTP is blocked by default. Talking to cameras' HTTP/ONVIF endpoints needs a Network Security Config domain-config exception.
Some Android devices expose a single hardware decoder or a few, and a second player can fail or show black. The number of simultaneous tiles depends on the device.

firebase_messaging (17.0.0) supports Android, iOS, macOS and web, but not Windows. Windows push needs WNS via the Windows App SDK, which requires an Azure AD app registration; packaged apps also need a PFN mapping requested by email, processed weekly.
iOS/iPadOS web push (16.4+) works only for web apps added to the Home Screen with a manifest, and the prompt must follow a user gesture.

Google Play's stalkerware policy allows surveillance or monitoring apps only for parental or enterprise use, with a persistent notification and a clear icon. It targets covert monitoring of people. The cited text dates from 2020 and may have been revised.

options.name: Flutter (3.47.x) single codebase + gateway (RECOMMENDED)
options.description: One Dart/Flutter UI for Android, iOS, Windows and Web. Video stack by platform. ANDROID: flutter_webrtc for WebRTC from the gateway (hardware MediaCodec); media_kit (libmpv) or fvp (libmdk) for direct RTSP on the local network, including H.265, recorded MP4/HLS playback and snapshots; video_player/ExoPlayer is HLS only, and its RTSP is H.264-only and not exposed. iOS: flutter_webrtc; media_kit or fvp for RTSP and H.265, since AVPlayer has no RTSP; PiP needs a small native AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer bridge. WINDOWS: flutter_webrtc (libwebrtc m150); media_kit (libmpv, D3D/ANGLE) or fvp (D3D11/NVDEC/MFT); the official video_player has no Windows support, and fvp fills that gap. WEB: flutter_webrtc web (browser RTCPeerConnection rendered as an HtmlElementView <video>); media_kit web is a plain HTML <video>, with HLS native only in Safari, so MSE or hls.js needs JS interop; no RTSP and no fvp. Low latency: WebRTC under 1 s everywhere; native RTSP is low-latency with tuned buffers; LL-HLS is a fallback only. Multi-stream grids: native textures on mobile and Windows, limited by hardware decoder count, so use camera substreams for tiles. On web each tile is a platform view, which is the main risk. PTZ, presets and timelines are ordinary Flutter widgets calling the backend ONVIF/PTZ API.
pros: The only candidate with a maintained, documented video path on all four targets in one UI codebase (flutter_webrtc lists all six platforms, released 2026-10-07).

Native RTSP and H.265 decoding on Android, iOS and Windows via media_kit or fvp, so the app works on the local network without a gateway and is not limited by browser codecs (Firefox, older Chrome/Safari).
Licensing works for a commercial product: Flutter BSD-3, flutter_webrtc MIT, media_kit MIT (avoid the GPL libmpv flavor), and libmdk is free for commercial Flutter apps.
The Windows desktop build can also host the always-on recorder (sidecar go2rtc, MediaMTX or FFmpeg), which covers the 'local storage' and self-hosted use cases.
Consistent pixel-level UI for dense grids, timelines and PTZ joysticks across mobile and desktop.
Active 2026 roadmap (Wasm default on web, multi-window desktop) and a fast release cadence.
cons: Flutter web is the weakest target: larger bundles, and each live tile is an HtmlElementView, which the docs warn costs performance under CanvasKit. 16-tile grids must be proven in a spike.
Two player stacks to maintain: WebRTC for live via the gateway, and libmpv or libmdk for RTSP and recordings.
Pub releases of media_kit are infrequent (main branch is active, the last pub release is about 10 months old), so you may need to pin or fork.
fvp depends on a closed-source engine (libmdk) under a key-based license, which is a vendor risk even though it is free for Flutter.
Push on Windows is not covered by firebase_messaging; it needs WNS or an in-app socket.
H.265 over flutter_webrtc native (libwebrtc) is undocumented; do not assume it, and test it.
options.license: Flutter BSD-3-Clause; flutter_webrtc MIT; media_kit MIT (bundled libmpv/FFmpeg: use the non-GPL flavors and verify LGPL obligations); fvp BSD-3 + libmdk proprietary key (free for Flutter, commercial OK); video_player BSD-3
options.maturity: Android, iOS and Windows: stable and production-used. Web: stable framework, but video-heavy grids are the least proven. flutter_webrtc very active (monthly releases in 2026); media_kit active main branch with slow pub cadence.

options.name: Web-first: React or Svelte SPA/PWA + Capacitor 8.5 (iOS/Android) + Tauri 2.12 or Electron (Windows)
options.description: One TypeScript UI running in the browser engine everywhere. Video stack: the gateway serves WebRTC (WHEP), MSE fMP4 over WebSocket, or LL-HLS, played with go2rtc's player or hls.js; WebCodecs is an advanced option. ANDROID: Android System WebView (Chromium): WebRTC, MSE and HLS via hls.js. iOS: WKWebView, with WebRTC since 14.3 and MSE only through ManagedMediaSource from iOS 17.1; native HLS otherwise. WINDOWS: Tauri on WebView2 (Chromium, evergreen) or Electron with bundled Chromium. WEB: the same code as a PWA. RTSP direct: impossible in any webview without a custom native plugin, so the gateway is mandatory even on the local network. Low latency: WebRTC under 1 s; MSE around 1–2 s; LL-HLS a few seconds. Grids: browsers handle many <video> elements with hardware decode; codec coverage follows the browser (H.265 WebRTC needs Chrome 136+ or Safari 18+, none on Firefox).
pros: The best web experience, since web is the native target, and ideal if desk operators are the main users.
A single player code path on every platform (WebRTC, MSE, HLS), and go2rtc ships a ready browser player.
Huge ecosystem and easy hiring in TypeScript; React/Svelte, Capacitor, Tauri and Electron are all MIT or Apache.
Tauri sidecars or Electron can embed the recorder on Windows; Capacitor gives native push, local network and HTTP plugins.
cons: No direct RTSP and no native H.265 fallback: a gateway is required even for a camera on the same Wi-Fi, which hurts a 'personal, no server' mode.
iPhone MSE needs iOS 17.1+; WKWebView WebRTC has historical quirks with Capacitor's custom scheme.
Native features (PiP, ONVIF multicast discovery, background behavior, Critical Alerts) need custom Swift/Kotlin plugins.
Risk under App Review 4.2 ('repackaged website') unless native value is clearly added.
Webview memory and battery use with many tiles on low-end Android.
options.license: React/Svelte MIT; Capacitor MIT; Tauri MIT or Apache-2.0; Electron MIT; hls.js Apache-2.0; go2rtc and MediaMTX MIT
options.maturity: Very mature. Capacitor 8.5.3 (Oct 2026), Tauri 2.12.4; browser WebRTC and MSE are production-grade.

options.name: React Native (0.86/0.87) + react-native-web + react-native-windows (0.84)
options.description: ANDROID/iOS: react-native-webrtc (MIT, M155) for WebRTC; react-native-vlc-media-player (libVLC) for RTSP and H.265, though its README is stale (RN 0.59–0.62) and New Architecture status is unclear; react-native-video v6 for HLS (v7 is still beta). WEB: react-native-web with browser WebRTC, MSE and hls.js, which works well. WINDOWS: react-native-webrtc explicitly does not support react-native-windows, react-native-video lists no Windows, and no Fabric video module was found. You would write C++/WinRT native modules (XAML MediaPlayerElement island, libVLC, or a WebView2 host) yourself. Low latency and grids are good on mobile and web; on Windows they are custom work.

recommendation:
Choose Flutter (stable 3.47.x) as the single client codebase for Web, Android, iOS and Windows, built around a mandatory gateway and recorder component. Reasoning:

(1) A gateway is unavoidable. Browsers cannot play RTSP, iPhone AVPlayer cannot play RTSP, Android Media3 RTSP is H.264-only, remote access needs NAT traversal, and Chrome's Local Network Access blocks or prompts web pages that reach camera IPs. Deploy go2rtc or MediaMTX (both MIT) as the gateway: in Docker on a NAS, mini-PC or Raspberry Pi for self-hosted users, as a Windows service, or in the cloud for SaaS. Use WebRTC (WHEP) as the universal live transport, MSE or LL-HLS as fallback, and fMP4 segments for recordings.

(2) Flutter is the only framework with maintained players on all four targets in one UI. Use flutter_webrtc (MIT, released Oct 2026) for live view everywhere. Use media_kit (MIT) or fvp (libmdk, free for commercial Flutter) on Android, iOS and Windows for direct RTSP on the local network, H.265 and recorded playback. Use HTML <video> plus MSE/hls.js on web for recordings.

(3) Never record on phones. iOS suspends apps about 5 s after backgrounding and BGContinuedProcessingTask is finite and killable. Android 15+ caps dataSync/mediaProcessing foreground services at 6 h per 24 h, and other foreground-service types need Play justification. Recording, motion detection and upload to Google Drive, OneDrive, S3 or local disk run on the gateway, the Windows app's background service, or the cloud. Phones do live view, PiP (iOS 15+ AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer), short foreground clips, PTZ and push.

(4) Push: firebase_messaging covers Android, iOS and web (iOS web only as an installed PWA, 16.4+); Windows needs WNS. Use time-sensitive notifications on iOS, and request Critical Alerts only if you can justify it.

(5) De-risk in week 1 with a spike: a 9/16-tile WebRTC grid using substreams on Flutter web (Chrome, Safari, Firefox), Windows and a mid-range Android, plus one H.265 camera through each path. If the Flutter web grid fails, keep Flutter for Android, iOS and Windows, and ship the web viewer as a thin TypeScript page reusing go2rtc's browser player against the same API.

Switch to web-first (React/Svelte + Capacitor + Tauri) instead if the web dashboard is the main product surface, the team is TypeScript, and you accept that every camera must go through a gateway. Avoid React Native (no WebRTC or video on Windows), Compose Multiplatform (web Beta, no desktop WebRTC, GPL vlcj) and MAUI (no web target, support ending May 2027) for this product.

Store checklist:
- iOS: NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription, the multicast entitlement request for ONVIF discovery, ATS NSAllowsLocalNetworking, a demo camera for reviewers (2.1), no audio-mode abuse (2.5.4), and IAP for in-app cloud plans (3.1.1).
- Android: target API 36 now and ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK when targeting 37, a cleartext network-security-config for camera IPs, foreground-service type declarations, and a non-covert, property-monitoring positioning versus the stalkerware policy.
risks: Flutter web performance with many concurrent HtmlElementView video tiles under CanvasKit or skwasm is unproven at 9–16 tiles. Platform views have known costs, and DOM moves can restart players.

Codec mismatch: many cameras default to H.265. Browsers handle it only partly (Chrome 136+ and Safari 18+ over WebRTC, no Firefox), Media3 RTSP has no H.265, and flutter_webrtc's native H.265 support is undocumented. Transcoding on the gateway is CPU/GPU-expensive per stream.
Hardware decoder limits on phones (some Android devices have one or a few decoder instances). Grids must use low-resolution substreams and cap simultaneous decoders.

The licensing of bundled media binaries needs a legal check: libmpv and FFmpeg build flavors (avoid GPL/'encoders-gpl'), LGPL static linking on iOS (libVLC, FFmpeg), libmdk's proprietary key model (vendor lock-in to one maintainer), and vlcj's GPLv3.

Dependency maintenance: media_kit's pub releases are slow (fork risk), react-native-vlc is weakly maintained, and RNW lags core RN. Single-maintainer packages (fvp/libmdk, go2rtc) carry bus-factor risk.

Background expectations: users will expect phones to keep recording or streaming in the background. iOS and Android policies make that impossible or reviewable, so product messaging must say that recording happens on the hub or cloud.

Network permission changes: Android 17's ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK (targetSdk 37), iOS local-network prompts and the multicast entitlement approval, and Chrome Local Network Access prompts for web pages reaching LAN devices. Any of these can break camera discovery or connection if handled late.
App Review: reviewers need a working camera or demo stream (2.1). In-app subscriptions for cloud recording must use IAP (3.1.1), which affects margins. A thin webview app risks a 4.2 rejection.
Windows push requires an Azure AD registration and a WNS PFN mapping by email with weekly processing; unpackaged apps have limited functionality.
Fast-moving platforms: Flutter 3.50 (Nov 2026), .NET 11 CoreCLR switch, and the Play target-API ratchet every August all need ongoing upgrade budget.

Research gap: the shared web-search budget ran out before WebView2/Edge HEVC support and the exact Chrome version that enforces Local Network Access by default could be confirmed. Treat both as unverified.
questions_for_product_owner: Which surface matters most to paying users: a desktop or browser dashboard watched by operators, or a mobile app for owners checking alerts? This decides between Flutter and web-first.

Business model: personal or self-hosted (a hub at home or the office, possibly running offline on the local network) or multi-tenant cloud SaaS? Will you ship or require an always-on box (Docker image, NAS app, Raspberry Pi, Windows service) to do recording?
What languages does the team already know well (Dart, TypeScript, C#, Kotlin)?
Which camera brands and protocols must work on day one (ONVIF Profile S/T/G, Hikvision ISAPI, Dahua, Reolink, Tapo, RTSP-only)? What share use H.265 by default?
What is the maximum number of simultaneous tiles in a grid, and on which minimum devices (low-end Android, iPhone version, Windows hardware)?
Minimum OS and browser support: is iOS 17.1+ acceptable (MSE on iPhone)? Do you need Firefox, which has no H.265?
Do you need two-way audio (talk-back) and the microphone permission and review implications that come with it?
Monetization: will cloud-recording or storage plans be sold inside the iOS and Android apps (IAP fees) or only on the web?
Windows distribution: Microsoft Store (MSIX, packaged identity, easier WNS push) or direct installer? Should the Windows app double as the 24/7 recorder?
Alerting requirements: are motion or AI events pushed in real time with snapshots? Is Critical Alerts-level urgency (security/alarm use case) needed on iOS?
Which markets are you launching in? EU/GDPR applies to video of people (privacy policy, retention, consent), plus app-store privacy labels.

area: Remote access and system topology (NAT/CGNAT traversal, hub vs cloud vs direct, relay economics, cloud backend for auth/pairing/signaling/presence/push)
summary: The most robust and cheapest topology for this product is a hub-centric hybrid. A small on-premise agent (one Go binary, runnable as a Windows service, in Docker on a NAS/Linux/Raspberry Pi, or on a spare Android phone) talks RTSP/ONVIF to the cameras, records locally, and uploads straight to the user's Google Drive, OneDrive, S3 or local disk. Clients reach the hub through WebRTC, with your cloud doing only accounts, pairing, signaling, presence, push and TURN credentials. Browsers can't use RTSP and can't freely reach LAN devices: Chrome 142 (Oct 2025) added a Local Network Access permission prompt. iOS can't run a 24/7 hub either. So WebRTC is the one transport that works the same on web, Android, iOS and Windows, and a WebRTC data channel can carry the control API (PTZ, presets, playback, settings) too. NAT is the main cost driver. Over 90% of cellular networks use CGNAT (IMC 2016, dated), residential CGNAT keeps growing (Starlink, 5G home), and IPv6 is only about 43-50% of traffic. Expect 10-25% of sessions to need a TURN relay. Tailscale reports more than 90% direct connections, and libp2p measurements show about 70% hole-punch success overall but only about 40% for symmetric NAT. Relay cost differs by up to 100x depending on the provider. Cloudflare Realtime TURN is $0.05/GB with 1,000 GB/month free, Twilio is $0.40/GB, and self-hosted coturn on a Hetzner EU server is about €1/TB after 20 TB included. So start on Cloudflare TURN and add self-hosted coturn/pion-turn in the EU as you grow. Relaying all video through a cloud media server costs about 5x more bandwidth than P2P with TURN fallback, and it decrypts the footage, which matters for GDPR. Use it only for multi-viewer sharing or a paid cloud-recording tier. Reverse tunnels and mesh VPNs fit poorly for consumers. Cloudflare's policy forbids serving video over its proxied bandwidth without a paid video product. ngrok bills per GB. Embedding Tailscale (tsnet) means every user needs a tailnet, and Headscale serves only one tailnet. NetBird's servers moved to AGPLv3 in Aug 2025, and ZeroTier's SDK is under BSL. For the backend, a Go + Postgres + WebSocket stack on an EU VPS costs about €10-20/month at 100 users and about €150-400/month at 10k users, before TURN bandwidth. Supabase is the fastest MVP path at $25+/month, but keep high-frequency presence and signaling off its per-message Realtime billing. Avoid Firebase's Spark plan (hard cap of 100 RTDB connections), and keep PocketBase for a self-hosted or personal edition.

facts.claim: Chrome 142 (released 2025-10-28) enforces Local Network Access: requests from a public website to local or loopback addresses need an explicit user permission prompt. Chrome 145 split the setting into 'Apps on device' and 'Local Network'. A web app served from https://app.example therefore cannot silently fetch from cameras or a hub at 192.168.x.x, so the web client should reach the hub over WebRTC, not direct HTTP.

iOS apps must declare NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription and get user consent before reaching LAN devices, including when the user types an IP/RTSP URL. If the user denies it, the app cannot connect to local devices.

iOS 26 BGContinuedProcessingTask allows only user-initiated, progress-reporting work that the system may terminate under pressure. It is not a way to run a 24/7 recording/streaming hub on iOS, so iOS should be a client only.

For apps targeting Android 15+, dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services are limited to 6 hours total per 24h (tracked separately per type). After timeout, onTimeout() fires and the service must stop. An Android 'hub' must not rely on these FGS types for 24/7 recording.

Android 14+ requires declaring a foreground service type per service. The connectedDevice type covers interaction with external devices over Bluetooth/NFC/IR/USB/network. Google Play requires a per-type declaration on the App content page, including a demo video and a use-case selection.

CGNAT prevalence (IMC 2016, now dated): more than 90% (about 92%) of cellular ASes deploy CGN, 17-18% of non-cellular eyeball ASes do, and about 40% of 75 surveyed ISPs deployed CGN with another 12% considering it. Deployment correlates with IPv4 scarcity. No rigorous 2025-2026 replacement study was found, and current prevalence is likely higher.

Starlink residential service is behind CGNAT by default (public IP only on Business/Priority plans), and T-Mobile Home Internet uses CGNAT/IPv6 translation. Inbound IPv4 to a home hub is therefore impossible for a growing share of users, so outbound-initiated connectivity (WebRTC/ICE, tunnels) is required.

IPv6 carried 50.1% of Google traffic on 2026-03-28, but the cross-source average is about 43% (Cloudflare 40.1%, APNIC 43.13%) and it varies widely by country (France 73%, India 72%, Italy 17%, Spain 10%). Some carriers also filter inbound IPv6, so IPv6 helps ICE but cannot be relied on for inbound reachability.

Digi (RCS&RDS, AS8708, Romania's largest fixed ISP) was an early IPv6 adopter: all Digi Net Fiberlink customers had IPv6 from May 2012, and in 2012 the company planned to avoid CGN as long as possible. No current data on whether Romanian residential lines are behind CGNAT was found, so this must be measured in a beta.

Share of WebRTC sessions needing a TURN relay: estimates range from about 10-15% (EasyRTC docs) to 'up to 17.7%' (small Hancke study cited by OpenVidu, 2026) to 15-25% (Fora Soft, May 2026). No authoritative recent large-scale figure exists. UDP-blocking corporate networks can need relay for nearly all traffic.
Tailscale reports that direct (non-relayed) connection success is 'well north of 90%' in typical conditions, falling back to peer relays and then DERP relays when hard NAT blocks hole punching.

A large-scale measurement of decentralized NAT traversal (libp2p DCUtR) found about 70% hole-punch success overall, about 83% for port-restricted cone NAT, and only about 40% for symmetric NAT (small sample). When both camera hub and viewer sit behind CGNAT or mobile symmetric NAT, relay need rises well above the average.

Cloudflare Realtime TURN costs $0.05 per GB of egress from Cloudflare to the TURN client. A 1,000 GB/month free tier is shared between SFU and TURN, and TURN is free when used together with the Cloudflare Realtime SFU. It is served over anycast (nearest PoP), and Cloudflare cannot read relayed WebRTC media because DTLS is end-to-end.

Cloudflare TURN ports: TLS 5349/tcp (alternate 443/tcp), TCP 3478 (alternate 80), UDP 3478 (alternate 53, not recommended because browsers and ISPs block it). Credentials are short-lived and must be minted by your backend through Cloudflare's API.
Twilio Network Traversal Service: TURN costs $0.40/GB (US, Europe), $0.60/GB (Singapore, Mumbai, Tokyo) and $0.80/GB (Sydney, São Paulo). STUN is free.
Metered TURN plans: Free tier with 500 MB/month; Growth $99/month for 150 GB (overage $0.40/GB); Business $199/month for 500 GB ($0.20/GB); Enterprise $499/month for 2 TB ($0.10/GB).

AWS Kinesis Video Streams WebRTC (managed signaling plus STUN/TURN) costs about $0.03 per active signaling channel per month, $2.25 per million signaling messages and $0.12 per 1,000 TURN minutes (US), plus standard AWS data transfer out. It has no free tier. Wyze and Abode are published customers.

AWS KVS WebRTC quotas: 1 master per channel (hard limit), 10 concurrent viewers per channel (soft), 1-hour maximum connection duration, 10-minute idle timeout, 10,000 channels per region in us-east-1/us-west-2 and 5,000 elsewhere, and 50 TURN allocations per channel (hard).
AWS internet egress costs about $0.09/GB for the first 10 TB/month after 100 GB free, falling to $0.085, $0.07 and $0.05/GB at higher tiers. Inbound traffic is free.

Hetzner Cloud EU servers include 20 TB/month of traffic, with overage around €1/TB (US locations include only about 1 TB). Hetzner raised prices twice in 2026: about +30-37% on 1 Apr, then on 15 Jun CX23 went from €3.99 to €5.49 and CPX22 from €7.99 to €19.49 for new orders. Some cost-optimized lines were reported 'currently not available'.

Derived cost per relayed stream-hour at 2 Mbps (about 0.9 GB/h): Cloudflare about $0.045; Twilio about $0.36 (up to 2x if both legs are metered); Metered $0.09-0.36; AWS KVS about $0.007 in TURN minutes plus about $0.08 egress; self-hosted coturn on Hetzner about €0.001 (within the 20 TB allowance it is effectively the server price). A mobile substream at about 0.5 Mbps (0.23 GB/h) costs about a quarter of these figures.

Typical IP camera bitrates: 1080p H.264 about 2-5 Mbps and H.265 about 1-3 Mbps (H.265 is roughly 30-50% smaller). Data volume in GB/hour is about Mbps × 0.45. Most cameras use VBR, so real usage often falls below the configured maximum.

WebRTC H.265: Chromium enabled H.265 send/receive by default from Chrome 136 (Apr 2025, hardware-dependent), and Safari also supports it. Edge does not enable it by default (Microsoft, May 2026), and Firefox status is unverified. An IETF draft (Jul 2026) defines the interop profile. H.265-only cameras may still need hub-side transcoding for some browsers.

coturn is BSD-3-Clause and actively maintained in 2026 (4.14.0 Jun 2026; 4.15.0 in Fedora Aug 2026). Recent releases include security fixes (CVE-2026-40613 DoS fixed in 4.10.0), and 4.13.1 denies link-local/ULA relay peers by default (anti-SSRF). Keep it patched.

Pion WebRTC v4 is MIT-licensed pure Go with data channels and a TURN client (UDP/TCP/DTLS/TLS). It suits a cross-compiled hub binary for Windows, Linux/ARM and Android (via gomobile), and pion/turn can embed a TURN server.

go2rtc is MIT-licensed (v1.9.14, 2026-01-19). It supports RTSP, WebRTC, ONVIF and two-way audio and converts camera streams for browsers (WebRTC/MSE). Its documented remote options are port-forward + STUN or ngrok, and users report WebRTC failing on some mobile networks without TURN.

MediaMTX is a zero-dependency Go media server and proxy. It publishes and reads SRT, WebRTC (WHEP), RTSP, RTMP, HLS and RTP, records and plays back, and converts protocols automatically. It is MIT per the upstream repo (verify the LICENSE file); a third-party listing shows 1.19.2 (Jul 2026).
LiveKit server (SFU) is Apache-2.0 and free to self-host. LiveKit Cloud tiers in 2026 are Build (free), Ship ($50/month), Scale ($500/month) and Enterprise.

Home Assistant Cloud (Nabu Casa) is a working precedent for the hub + WebRTC + TURN model. The subscription includes a TURN relay for WebRTC camera streaming, enabled by default and possible to disable for P2P-only. The Open Home Foundation hosts free STUN for all users.

Matter 1.5 (CSA, 2025-11-20) adds cameras: WebRTC live streaming, two-way audio, local and remote access through STUN/TURN, PTZ, multi-stream, and detection/privacy zones. Storage, clip playback and analytics are left to manufacturers and platforms, so a WebRTC-native hub/backend is aligned with where consumer cameras are going.

Camera-vendor P2P SDKs are a security liability. ThroughTek Kalay CVE-2021-28372 (CVSS 9.6-9.8) let attackers who knew a device UID compromise it remotely, including live audio/video, and ThroughTek claimed more than 83M active Kalay devices. Do not build on vendor P2P clouds.

Cloud-only (camera-initiated) connectivity exists only for specific vendors. Hikvision ISUP/EHome (ISUP 5.0 needs an encryption key and a platform-issued Device ID) lets a third-party platform do live view, playback and PTZ, and enabling ISUP disables other platform access. Dahua Auto Register has the device open an outbound connection to a registration server with no port forwarding. Generic ONVIF/RTSP cameras have no push-to-cloud mechanism.

Cloudflare policy says it has prohibited streaming video over its bandwidth from the start. On Free, Pro and Business plans it may redirect or limit apps that serve video without a paid service (Stream). Tunnel public hostnames go through that proxy, and community and staff interpretations conflict, so it is not a safe base for a commercial camera product.

Cloudflare Zero Trust limits are 1,000 cloudflared tunnels per account and 25 replicas per tunnel (seen on a preview mirror of the docs). Tunnels can be created and configured through the API, but a per-customer tunnel model caps at about 1,000 hubs per account unless the limit is raised.

ngrok (2026): the free tier includes about 1 GB of data transfer; Hobbyist is about $8-10/month with 5 GB; pay-as-you-go is from about $18-20/month with data transfer at about $0.10/GB. 'Bandwidth' was renamed 'data transfer' in April 2026. This is uneconomic and awkward per end user for video.
frp (fatedier/frp), the self-hostable reverse proxy, is Apache-2.0. Alpine ships 0.65.0 (2026), and a third-party index shows v0.70.x upstream.

tailscale.com/tsnet is BSD-3-Clause (v1.98.2, May 2026). It embeds a full Tailscale node in a Go process using a userspace gVisor netstack, with no root needed, but each node must authenticate to a tailnet through an auth key or a login URL.

Tailscale pricing reportedly changed on 2026-04-08: the free Personal plan now covers up to 6 users with unlimited user-owned devices (previously 3 users/100 devices); Standard about $8 and Premium about $18 per user/month. Sources conflict, so verify on tailscale.com/pricing.

Headscale (BSD-3, v0.28-0.29 in 2026) implements a single tailnet by design ('suitable for personal use or a small open-source organisation'), so multi-tenancy is out of scope. It cannot serve as a multi-tenant SaaS control plane without running one instance per customer.

NetBird moved its server-side components (management, signal, relay; dashboard reported too) from BSD-3 to AGPLv3 from v0.53.0 (announced 2025-08-04). Client code stays BSD-3, and a commercial license is sold (a third party reports €2,000/year for its Starter tier).

The ZeroTier SDK (libzt/libztcore) is under BSL 1.1 and needs a commercial license for closed-source apps and devices. A 2025 ZeroTier Source-Available License treats the controller as non-commercial, while the agent is MPL-2.0.

iroh (n0-computer) reached 1.0 in mid-2026. It is a Rust QUIC P2P stack that dials by public key, hole-punches when possible and falls back to relay servers, dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0. It is an alternative to WebRTC data channels between native apps and the hub, but browser support is unverified.

flutter_webrtc's README lists Android, iOS, Web, macOS, Windows and Linux with data channel support. However, pub.dev analysis of v1.2.0 does not declare Web support, so verify web support for the chosen version (or use browser-native WebRTC on web).

RFC 8628 (OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant) is the standard pattern for pairing input-constrained devices. The device shows a short user_code and verification URI, the user approves on a phone, and the device polls. Short codes have low entropy and need rate limiting and brute-force protection. A hub 'claim code' or QR flow can be built on this.

Supabase Pro costs $25/month per org and includes 100k MAU, 250 GB uncached egress and a $10 compute credit (Micro). Compute is Micro $10, Small $15, Medium $60 and Large $110 per month. Egress overage is $0.09/GB and MAU overage $0.00325.

Supabase Realtime: Pro includes 500 peak connections and 5M messages, then $10 per 1,000 peak connections and $2.50 per million messages. Pro allows 500 messages/sec, rising to 10,000 connections and 2,500 msg/s with the spend cap off. Free allows 200 connections and pauses projects after 7 days of low activity. Per-hub heartbeat traffic through Realtime adds up quickly (10k hubs × 1 msg/30 s ≈ 864M msgs/month ≈ $2.1k).

Firebase: Auth is free up to 50k MAU for email/social sign-in; phone/SMS is always paid and needs Blaze (since Sept 2024). Realtime Database on Spark has a hard cap of 100 simultaneous connections that cannot be raised. Blaze allows 200k per database, $1/GB downloaded after about 10 GB/month and $5/GB stored.
FCM is free. Its downstream quotas are per-minute message counts (HTTP 429 when exceeded), and iOS delivery goes through APNs, with per-platform APNs overrides in the HTTP v1 API.

PocketBase (MIT, v0.39.x, Jul 2026) is still pre-1.0: a single binary with embedded SQLite and realtime subscriptions. Its docs say it is not recommended for production-critical apps unless you follow the changelog and apply manual migrations.

EMQX moved to BSL 1.1 from v5.9.0 (announced 2025-05-07). A single node is free in production, but clusters of more than one node need a license file. Each version reverts to Apache-2.0 after 4 years. This matters if MQTT is chosen for hub presence and signaling.

Cloudflare Durable Objects with WebSocket Hibernation do not bill duration while idle, and incoming WebSocket messages bill at a 20:1 ratio to requests. This fits a low-cost serverless signaling and presence layer if Cloudflare is used for TURN as well.

options.name: Topology A: On-premise hub/agent (recommended core)
options.description: A single Go binary (Pion WebRTC + RTSP/ONVIF client, built on go2rtc/MediaMTX components) runs on a Windows service, in Docker on a NAS/Linux/Raspberry Pi, or on a spare Android phone. It discovers and controls cameras (ONVIF PTZ/presets/settings), records locally (segmented MP4), and uploads to Google Drive, OneDrive, S3 or local disk with the user's OAuth tokens. It holds an outbound WebSocket to the cloud for presence and signaling, and serves clients over WebRTC: video tracks plus a data channel carrying the control and playback API. The cloud never touches media or camera credentials.
pros: Works with any RTSP/ONVIF camera; no vendor cloud required
Only outbound connections, so it works behind CGNAT; ICE finds direct paths most of the time and TURN covers the rest
Media is end-to-end DTLS-encrypted, so relays can't see footage and GDPR exposure is low (you are not processing video)
Your bandwidth bill covers only the relayed share (about 10-25%); cloud-drive uploads go hub to provider directly
The same binary can run 'cloud-less' for a self-hosted/personal edition
Matches Home Assistant/Nabu Casa's proven model and Matter 1.5's WebRTC direction
cons: Needs an always-on device on each site; iOS cannot host it, and Android hosting has foreground-service limits (6h cap on dataSync/mediaProcessing on Android 15+, plus OEM battery killers and a Play FGS declaration)
Remote viewing is limited by the home upload bandwidth; several remote viewers can saturate ADSL/cable uplinks
Packaging, auto-update and support across Windows, ARM Linux, NAS and Android
