recommendation:
Build a hub-centric hybrid and make WebRTC the single remote transport.

1) Topology: the on-premise hub (Topology A) is the core. Ship one Go binary built on Pion (MIT) with RTSP/ONVIF handling based on go2rtc/MediaMTX (MIT), packaged as a Windows service, a Docker image (NAS, Linux, Raspberry Pi 4/5 arm64) and an Android 'hub mode' app. For Android, test the connectedDevice FGS type and the Play declaration early, and avoid dataSync/mediaProcessing because of the 6h cap. iOS and web are clients only. The hub records locally and uploads directly to Google Drive, OneDrive, S3 or local storage, so media never touches your cloud and camera passwords never leave the site.

2) Remote access: one RTCPeerConnection per viewing session, carrying video and audio tracks (sub-stream by default on mobile, main stream on demand) plus a reliable data channel for the RPC API (PTZ, presets, settings, recording index, playback, chunked clip download). ICE handles the LAN fast path automatically. For STUN, use Cloudflare's or your own. For TURN, start on Cloudflare Realtime TURN (free up to 1 TB/month shared with SFU, then $0.05/GB, TLS on 443 for strict networks). Past roughly 2-5 TB/month, add self-hosted coturn or pion/turn on 2-3 EU VPSes from two providers, keep Cloudflare as overflow, and mint short-lived credentials from the backend. Log ICE selected-candidate-pair types from day one so you learn your real relay ratio; budget 25% until measured, especially for Romanian and other mobile carriers.

3) Do not build on Cloudflare Tunnel (video policy), ngrok (cost and UX), Tailscale or Headscale embedding (no multi-tenancy), NetBird servers (AGPL) or the ZeroTier SDK (BSL) for the commercial product. Do offer 'bring your own VPN' (Tailscale or WireGuard to the hub IP) as a zero-cost option in the self-hosted edition.

4) Cloud relay (Topology D) is a later add-on, used only for 3 or more concurrent viewers, wide sharing, or a paid cloud-recording tier: LiveKit (Apache-2.0) or the Cloudflare SFU, where TURN is then free. Cloud-only cameras (Topology B, via Hikvision ISUP, Dahua Auto Register or Matter 1.5) also come later, as a premium connector, because you then pay ingest and egress.

5) Backend: if you are going commercial, use Go + Postgres + a WebSocket gateway on EU hosting. Estimated cost is about €10-20/month at 100 users and about €150-400/month at 10k users, plus TURN at €0-50 self-hosted or about $1k on Cloudflare at about 20 TB/month relayed. If speed matters most, start with Supabase Pro for auth, Postgres and RLS sharing ($25 to about $300/month), but run hub presence and signaling in a small Go service rather than per-message Supabase Realtime. Either way, keep the backend containerized so the same stack doubles as the self-hosted edition. PocketBase is fine only for that personal edition.

6) Pairing and security: hub pairing follows RFC 8628 (code or QR on the hub, approve in the app, rate-limited codes), then issue a per-hub credential (mTLS client cert or rotating refresh token). Shares are ACL rows in Postgres, and the backend authorizes each signaling offer. Keep TURN credentials short-lived and deny private/ULA peers. Push goes through FCM (Android and web) and APNs (iOS); the hub emits motion and offline events, and the backend detects presence loss. Never integrate vendor P2P SDKs.

7) Clients: browsers use native WebRTC. For Android, iOS and Windows, use flutter_webrtc or libwebrtc (verify web support per version if you pick Flutter). Plan for H.264 everywhere, with H.265 passthrough only where the browser advertises it, otherwise sub-stream or transcode on capable hubs.
risks: The relay ratio could run higher than modelled (CGNAT and symmetric NAT on both the mobile viewer and the hub's ISP), which pushes TURN cost up. Mitigate with measurement, a sub-stream default, idle-session timeouts, self-hosted TURN and paid tiers for heavy remote viewing.

Home upload bandwidth is a hard ceiling. Several remote viewers or remote playback of main streams can saturate ADSL/cable uplinks and degrade recording uploads to Drive/OneDrive at the same time. This needs adaptive stream selection and upload throttling.

Android-as-hub reliability: foreground-service type policy (Play review with demo video), the 6h caps on dataSync/mediaProcessing, OEM battery optimizers killing services, and thermal limits on 24/7 phones.
iOS cannot host; web cannot reach the LAN directly (Chrome LNA prompt, no RTSP in browsers), so feature parity depends on the hub and WebRTC working everywhere.

Codec compatibility: H.265-only cameras may not decode in Edge or Firefox via WebRTC, and transcoding on a Raspberry Pi or low-end NAS is CPU-bound. If FFmpeg is used for transcoding, confirm an LGPL-only build (no GPL x264/x265) for a closed-source commercial product.
License traps: AGPLv3 (NetBird servers), BSL (EMQX clusters since 5.9.0, ZeroTier SDK) and vendor SDK terms (Hikvision ISUP). Keep a license allowlist (MIT/BSD/Apache/MPL/LGPL) in CI.

Vendor and policy risk: Cloudflare's video-delivery policy (Tunnel/CDN), AWS KVS quotas (1-hour max connection, 10 viewers per channel), Supabase per-message Realtime billing, the Firebase Spark 100-connection cap, and Hetzner's two 2026 price increases and capacity shortages.

Security: the hub stores camera credentials and a long-lived cloud credential, so a compromised hub means compromised cameras. Pairing codes can be brute-forced without rate limiting, an open TURN relay can be abused or used for SSRF, and the data channel API needs per-share authorization. Vendor P2P SDK history (Kalay CVE-2021-28372) shows the cost of getting this wrong.

GDPR: video of identifiable people is personal data. P2P/E2E keeps you out of media processing, but Topology D (cloud relay or recording) or cloud-only cameras make you a processor, which needs a DPA, EU data residency and retention controls.

Data quality: the CGNAT figures date from 2016, the TURN-ratio figures are vendor or small-sample estimates, and several 2026 prices (Tailscale, ngrok, Hetzner, MediaMTX/LiveKit versions) come from third-party trackers. Verify on the official pages before committing budgets.
questions_for_product_owner: Is the first target a personal/self-hosted tool, a commercial multi-tenant SaaS, or both (a free self-hosted hub plus a paid cloud for remote access)? This decides between Supabase and a custom Go backend, and whether remote relay is a paid feature.

Can you require every customer to have an always-on device for the hub (Windows PC, NAS, Raspberry Pi, spare Android phone), or must 'cameras only, no extra device' setups work? The latter forces cloud-only connectors for specific brands.

Which camera brands and protocols must be supported at launch (generic ONVIF Profile S/T/G + RTSP, Hikvision, Dahua, Reolink, TP-Link Tapo, Matter 1.5)? Are H.265-only cameras common among target users?
How many people typically watch the same camera remotely at the same time (family vs installer vs business with many guards)? Above about 2 viewers we need a cloud SFU to protect the home uplink.
Where are the users: Romania and the EU only at first, or global? This sets TURN PoP placement, latency, and GDPR/data-residency requirements.

Is recording continuous 24/7 or event/motion-based, and must recordings be uploaded to Google Drive/OneDrive continuously or only as clips? This affects the home upload budget and API quotas on those providers.
Should the web client have full parity (live view, playback, PTZ, settings, downloads) or be view-only?
Is a dependency on Cloudflare (TURN/SFU) or AWS acceptable, or must the entire stack be self-hostable from day one?
Will remote viewing through relay be metered or tiered in pricing (e.g. X GB/month relayed included)? Can we cap or downgrade stream quality when users are on relay?
What languages is the team strongest in (Go, .NET/C#, Node/TypeScript, Dart/Flutter)? This affects the hub and backend stack and code sharing.
Is a cloud-recording tier (footage stored by us, not the user's drive) on the roadmap? It changes the topology, cost and GDPR posture significantly.

area: Pluggable storage destinations for recordings (Local/NAS, Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, S3-compatible, Box, pCloud, WebDAV/Nextcloud, FTP/SFTP)
summary: The storage layer should be built around your own capability-based "destination driver" interface. Treat third-party engines as implementations behind it, not as the architecture itself. The providers differ in ways that leak into product behaviour: upload chunk alignment (Google 256 KiB, OneDrive 320 KiB and under 60 MiB per request, Dropbox 4 MiB for concurrent sessions, S3/R2 5 MiB minimum with equal-size parts on R2), whether direct playback links exist (S3 presigned URLs up to 7 days, OneDrive pre-authenticated downloadUrl lasting minutes, Dropbox temporary link lasting 4 h, none for Google Drive), whether deletes free quota (OneDrive Personal keeps deleted items in a recycle bin that counts against quota), and how OAuth refresh tokens behave (Box single-use, Microsoft SPA tokens last 24 h, Google tokens in Testing mode last 7 days). rclone (MIT, v1.75.2 released 9 Oct 2026, 71 backend directories) is the best tool for the long tail and for NAS/SMB. It can be imported in-process from Go, but librclone is marked "experimental", is untested on iOS, and its internal Go API is not a stable SDK. So use it for WebDAV, SFTP, FTP, pCloud, Box and SMB, and write native drivers for the four providers that matter most: S3-compatible, Google Drive, OneDrive and Dropbox. Apache OpenDAL (Apache-2.0, v0.59.4) is a weaker fit here. It has no SMB, NFS or Box support, its OneDrive service supports Personal accounts only, and its gdrive docs ask for the full `drive` scope, which is restricted. For Google Drive the key decision is to use only `drive.file` (plus optionally `drive.appdata`). These are non-sensitive scopes that need no CASA security assessment, and they also work with the TV/limited-input device flow for headless recorders. The full `drive` scope is restricted and triggers verification plus a recurring paid security assessment. Google changed Drive API quotas in 2026: usage is now counted in quota units, a download costs 200 units, and there is a per-project daily billing threshold of 400M units, with billing details to come later in 2026. A SaaS that streams playback through Drive should keep its own segment catalog and avoid listing calls. Recordings should be written as closed fMP4/MP4 segments into a local spool with a SQLite catalog, then uploaded by resumable per-destination workers whose session state is persisted. Retention runs in the app for Drive, OneDrive and Dropbox, and through server-side lifecycle rules for S3. Client-side encryption should be optional and seekable (for example the rclone-crypt format with 64 KiB authenticated blocks), with the trade-off that playback then needs decryption on the client. Research limitations: web search was unavailable (the session search budget was used up), and developers.google.com, learn.microsoft.com, dropbox.com and rclone.org could not be reached directly. Google, Microsoft, Dropbox, AWS and Cloudflare facts were therefore taken from the official docs via Context7 or from the vendors' GitHub doc repos. CASA pricing could not be verified and is marked low confidence.

facts.claim: rclone is MIT licensed (COPYING: 'Copyright (C) 2012 by Nick Craig-Wood ... Permission is hereby granted, free of charge'), so it can be embedded in a commercial closed-source product.
Latest rclone release is v1.75.2 (09 Oct 2026); previous releases were v1.75.1 (04 Sep), v1.75.0 (31 Jul) and v1.74.4 (08 Jul).

The rclone repo has 71 backend directories, including drive, onedrive, dropbox, s3, b2, box, pcloud, webdav, ftp, sftp, smb, local, crypt, chunker, union, protondrive, iclouddrive and others. There is no NFS client backend.

librclone exports RcloneInitialize, RcloneRPC (method + JSON in, JSON + status out), RcloneFinalize and RcloneFreeString. It builds as c-shared (.so/.dll) or c-archive, and as an Android AAR via gomobile. iOS is 'not tested' ('should probably work'), and the interfaces are 'experimental' and 'may change in the future'. Windows apps must not unload the DLL.

Go package librclone (module v1.75.2) exposes Initialize(), RPC(method, input string) (output string, status int) and Finalize(). 'operations/uploadfile and core/command are not supported' through it.
The rclone issue 'librclone integration with iOS' (#6784, opened Feb 2023) is still open. The maintainer said gomobile is 'probably the correct solution' but iOS builds are not set up in CI.

rclone PR #9740 (merged 8 Sep 2026) adds rc operations/getfile for in-process use via librclone. It supports offset/count but has a 2 MiB cap, so it is not suitable for video streaming. Maintainers point to --rc-serve, which serves files with Range support.

rclone RC API: config/create and config/update support opt.nonInteractive/continue/state/result, which drive the backend config (including OAuth) as a question/answer state machine. Other relevant calls: operations/copyfile, deletefile, list, about (quota), publiclink, cleanup, purge, plus job/status and _async. The docs warn that 'Access to the rc API is equivalent to shell access', so keep it bound to loopback.

rclone headless OAuth works in three ways: run 'rclone authorize <backend>' on a machine with a browser and paste the token blob into the headless config, copy the config file (which holds token/client_id/client_secret), or SSH-tunnel the localhost:53682 callback.

rclone's Google Drive docs say the shared rclone client_id 'is being retired and will stop working during 2026', so creating your own client is now 'required rather than merely recommended'. The docs also say Testing-mode apps get grants that 'expire after a week'.

rclone documents an undocumented Google Drive limit of 750 GiB uploaded per day (--drive-stop-on-upload-limit) and a practical rate of 'about 2 files per second'. Its default Drive chunk size is 8 MiB ('power of 2 >= 256k').

The Google Drive scope table lists drive.file, drive.appdata/drive.appfolder and drive.install as 'Non-sensitive (recommended)'. One older passage on the same site calls drive.file 'sensitive', but either way it 'doesn't require a security assessment'. Restricted Drive scopes (e.g. full 'drive') 'require a Google review and a security assessment', and the app needs a privacy policy and terms of service.

Google scope categories: non-sensitive scopes need basic app verification only, sensitive scopes need additional verification, and restricted scopes need additional verification plus a security assessment. Internal-only Workspace apps are exempt from review.

The CASA security assessment for restricted scopes is done by an App Defense Alliance-authorized assessor at the developer's cost and must be renewed periodically (commonly cited as every 12 months). Commonly reported prices range from a few hundred USD (Tier 2) to several thousand USD per year (Tier 3). I could not open Google's or the ADA's pages to confirm current tiers or prices.

Google Drive API quotas (2026): 1,000,000 quota units per minute per project and 325,000 per minute per user per project. Per-method cost: files.get 5, files.list 100, download 200, update 50, other 5. Exceeding the quota returns 403 userRateLimitExceeded or 429.

Google Drive has a new daily billing threshold of 400,000,000 quota units per project per day, which cannot be increased. 'Full billing details will be shared later in 2026 with at least 90 days' notice.' The same page also lists a 1 TB per-day per-project egress line, which looks inconsistent. Both should be re-checked before launch.
Drive API release note of May 01, 2026: quotas are now measured in quota units instead of requests, a new tiering model is rolling out, and Workspace users 'can now only egress 1 TB per day'.
Google Drive: 750 GB per user per day upload limit (copies included). After hitting it, no uploads for 24 h. Maximum upload file size is 5 TB.

Google Drive resumable uploads: the session URI expires after one week, and chunks must be multiples of 256 KiB except the last. To resume, send an empty PUT with 'Content-Range: bytes */<size>' and read the 308 response's Range header; a 404 means the session expired. The total size can be '*/*' if unknown.

Google Drive supports partial downloads with a 'Range: bytes=500-999' header on files.get?alt=media, but the request needs an Authorization: Bearer header. The API has no S3-style presigned URL. A newer files.download long-running operation returns a downloadUri, but whether that URI works without auth is not documented in what I reviewed.

Google Drive files.delete permanently deletes a file, skipping trash (owner only). Trashed files are auto-deleted after 30 days. about.get storageQuota returns usage, usageInDrive and usageInDriveTrash.
A Google shared drive can hold at most 500,000 items, and trashed items count toward that limit. A user can create up to 500 million items in total.

Google's OAuth device flow (TVs and limited-input devices) supports the Drive scopes drive.file and drive.appdata, and refresh tokens are always returned for devices. This allows a headless recorder to be linked by showing a code.

Google refresh tokens: 7-day expiry for External apps in 'Testing' status, a limit of 100 refresh tokens per Google Account per OAuth client ID (the oldest is silently revoked), expiry after 6 months unused, and possible revocation by the user or an admin.

Microsoft Graph upload sessions: each request must be under 60 MiB, and fragments must be multiples of 320 KiB (327,680 bytes) sent in order. Do not send the Authorization header on PUTs to uploadUrl (it can cause 401). Each fragment extends expirationDateTime. Resume with GET uploadUrl to read nextExpectedRanges. conflictBehavior is fail/replace/rename. fileSize pre-check returning 507 Insufficient Storage works on OneDrive Personal only.
OneDrive simple upload (PUT /content) supports files only up to 250 MB. The maximum file size is 250 GiB for both Personal and Business (per rclone docs).

OneDrive download: GET /content returns a 302 to a pre-authenticated URL (the same as @microsoft.graph.downloadUrl) that needs no Authorization header. The URL 'might expire within minutes', Range is supported (206), and browser JS can fetch it without a CORS preflight.

OneDrive DELETE moves items to the recycle bin. The quota resource exposes 'deleted' bytes in the recycle bin. rclone notes 'OneDrive personal accounts do not support the permanentDelete API' (Business/SharePoint only).

Graph throttling returns 429 with Retry-After, and requests keep counting against limits while throttled. SharePoint/OneDrive for Business per-user limits are 3,000 requests per 5 min, 50 GB/h ingress and 100 GB/h egress. Per-app per-tenant limits start at 1,250 resource units/min and 1.2M/24 h for tenants under 1,000 licenses. Upload costs 2 resource units and download costs 1. The docs also recommend an 'ISV|Company|App/version' User-Agent.

The Files.ReadWrite.AppFolder delegated permission is labelled '(preview)' and is 'available for consent in personal Microsoft accounts'. The app folder is created at Apps/{Entra app name} through /special/approot.

Microsoft publisher verification is free and requires a Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program (Partner One) account, a matching verified domain and MFA. With risk-based step-up consent, users generally cannot consent to unverified multitenant apps registered after 8 Nov 2020 that request more than basic permissions.

Microsoft refresh tokens last 24 hours for SPA redirect URIs and 90 days for other scenarios. A browser-only web client therefore cannot keep a long-lived OneDrive connection; tokens must be held by a backend or native agent.

Dropbox upload sessions: at most 150 MiB per request, a maximum file size of 2^41-2^22 bytes (about 2 TiB), and sessions valid for 7 days. Concurrent sessions need appends in multiples of 4 MiB. finish_batch_v2 takes up to 1,000 entries per request.

Dropbox returns 429 too_many_write_operations because writes take a lock on the user's namespace, so parallel writers contend. It also returns too_many_requests with Retry-After. Dropbox recommends batch endpoints.

Dropbox apps in Development status can link at most 500 users. Once 50 users are linked, you have 2 weeks to obtain Production approval or new linking is frozen. Approval requires following the branding guidelines.

Dropbox: with token_access_type=offline you get short-lived access tokens (expires_in 14400 s) plus a refresh token that does not expire automatically. PKCE is recommended for public clients. get_temporary_link returns a streaming link valid for 4 h, but the docs say it 'should not be used to display content directly in the browser'.

Box: chunked uploads use upload sessions where the server dictates part_size and total_parts and the total file size must be declared up front. Each refresh token 'is valid for one use in 60 days' (per rclone's Box docs), so concurrent refreshes from two processes invalidate each other.

Amazon S3 multipart limits: maximum object size 48.8 TiB, 10,000 parts, part size 5 MiB to 5 GiB (no minimum for the last part). Presigned URLs are valid for up to 7 days with SigV4 and long-term IAM keys, and expire earlier if created with temporary credentials.

Cloudflare R2: multipart parts must be 5 MiB to 5 GiB, all non-trailing parts must be the same size (error 10048), and incomplete multipart uploads expire after 7 days by default. Bucket lifecycle rules support expiration by prefix/days and aborting multipart uploads.

Wasabi has a minimum storage duration policy (90 days by default, or 30 days if changed). Objects deleted earlier incur a 'Timed Deleted Storage' charge, which penalises short CCTV retention such as 7 or 30 days.
The MinIO GitHub repository (AGPLv3) was archived on 25 Apr 2026 and states 'THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED'. The community edition is now source-only with no prebuilt binaries.

rclone's S3 backend supports 50+ S3-compatible providers, including AWS, Cloudflare R2, Wasabi, MinIO, Ceph, SeaweedFS, Hetzner, OVHcloud, Scaleway, IDrive e2, Storj and Synology C2. Backblaze B2 also has its own native b2 backend.

rclone crypt encrypts with NaCl SecretBox (XSalsa20-Poly1305) in 64 KiB chunks, each with a 16-byte authenticator, plus a 32-byte header (8-byte magic and 24-byte nonce). Overhead is about 0.03% for large files. Keys are derived with scrypt (N=16384, r=8, p=1). File names can be encrypted with EME/AES-256.

rclone crypt supports seeking and range reads. calculateUnderlying() maps a plaintext offset to an underlying block offset and advances the nonce by the block count (DecryptDataSeek/RangeSeek), so encrypted segments can still be range-read for playback.

rclone OneDrive docs: chunk size must be a multiple of 320k (default 10 MiB). Business apps commonly fail with 'publisher of the App is not verified'. The refresh token expires after 90 days unused. Folders with about 100,000 files can cause listing errors. QuickXorHash is the default hash.
rclone's SMB backend uses the go-smb2 library with NTLM (default) or Kerberos auth. Anonymous login is not supported (use 'guest' with an empty password).

Apache OpenDAL is Apache-2.0 licensed, latest release v0.59.4 (05 Oct). Its services include s3, b2, gdrive, onedrive, dropbox, pcloud, webdav, ftp, sftp and fs, but not box, smb or nfs. It has 17 language bindings (C, C++, Dart, .NET, Go, Java, Node.js, Python, Swift and others), each versioned independently.

OpenDAL's OneDrive service: 'Currently, OpenDAL supports OneDrive Personal only'. OpenDAL's gdrive docs say the OAuth scope must contain the full 'https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive' (a restricted scope). Neither service supports presign, and OpenDAL does not perform the initial OAuth authorization itself.
The OpenDAL Go binding wraps opendal-c without CGO (purego + libffi), and libffi must be installed. Each service is a separate companion Go module.

Official SDK licenses: google-api-go-client is BSD-3-Clause and msgraph-sdk-go is MIT. dropbox-sdk-go-unofficial is MIT but 'not a formally supported Dropbox product' and covers only 'a practical subset' of the API.

options.name: A. Own capability-based Destination interface: native drivers for the top providers, rclone for the long tail (RECOMMENDED)
options.description: Define a Go (or Rust) Destination interface that exposes capabilities, not just put/get. Implement native drivers for S3-compatible storage (aws-sdk-go-v2 or minio-go), Google Drive (google-api-go-client with drive.file), OneDrive (raw Graph REST or msgraph-sdk-go), Dropbox (REST) and Local/SMB. Add one generic 'rclone' driver that imports rclone backends in-process (Go import of fs/operations, or librclone RPC) for WebDAV/Nextcloud, SFTP, FTP, pCloud, Box and others. All drivers sit behind the same upload-session, playback-URL, retention and quota contracts. The engine runs inside the edge recorder (Windows/Linux/NAS/Docker) and in the SaaS backend. Mobile and web clients only configure destinations and play recordings back.
pros: Full control of the cases that matter: resumable sessions persisted in SQLite, provider-specific chunk alignment, presigned/pre-authenticated playback URLs, permanent delete and quota semantics
Google can use drive.file only (non-sensitive, no CASA). OneDrive can use the app folder and the right token lifetimes
Long-tail coverage of about 70 backends from day one through MIT-licensed rclone, which is commercially safe
Only the native drivers are on the critical path, so rclone's experimental embedding API can be swapped out later
Capability flags let the UI tell users honestly what each destination supports (e.g. 'Google Drive: no direct links, playback is proxied', 'Wasabi: 90-day minimum billing')
cons: You implement and maintain four or five provider drivers yourself (OAuth, retries, Retry-After/backoff, error mapping)
Two code paths (native and rclone) make testing and behaviour less uniform
rclone embedded in-process adds tens of MB to the agent binary (not measured here; trim by importing only the needed backends)
On iOS rclone/librclone is untested, so long-tail destinations stay agent-side only
options.license: Own code; rclone MIT; google-api-go-client BSD-3; msgraph-sdk-go MIT; aws-sdk-go-v2 Apache-2.0 (not re-verified here)
options.maturity: All components are production-grade. Embedding librclone is labelled experimental.

options.name: B. rclone for everything (in-process Go import, librclone FFI, or 'rclone rcd' sidecar)
options.description: Use rclone as the single storage engine. Configure remotes through the rc config/create state machine (which handles OAuth), move segments with operations/copyfile or movefile, read quota with operations/about, rotate with deletefile, and serve playback with Range support through --rc-serve or 'rclone serve http'.
pros: Fastest path to supporting Local, SMB, Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, S3 (50+ providers), Box, pCloud, WebDAV, SFTP, FTP and more
Mature, battle-tested provider quirk handling (chunking, Drive 750 GB/day detection, Dropbox batching, OneDrive hashes)
Built-in crypt (seekable, documented open format), chunker and union backends
MIT license; very active project (v1.75.2, Oct 2026)
cons: librclone is 'experimental' and the internal Go API is not a semver-stable SDK, so upgrades may break you
operations/uploadfile is not available over librclone; getfile is capped at 2 MiB, so streaming needs rc-serve/serve http
rclone's OAuth model is built around a local loopback (127.0.0.1:53682) or 'rclone authorize'. A multi-tenant SaaS needs its own token broker anyway
No presigned-URL abstraction in the docs reviewed. publiclink creates public share links, which is the wrong security model for CCTV
iOS not supported or tested (issue #6784 open)
The RC API is 'equivalent to shell access', so a sidecar must stay on loopback with auth
options.license: MIT
options.maturity: rclone itself is very mature. Embedding via librclone is experimental.

options.name: C. Apache OpenDAL as the single abstraction
options.description: Use OpenDAL (Rust core) through Rust directly or via its Go/Swift/Java/Dart bindings as a unified Operator API over s3/b2/gdrive/onedrive/dropbox/pcloud/webdav/ftp/sftp/fs.
pros: Apache-2.0, an ASF project with frequent releases (v0.59.x, Sep-Oct 2026)
Clean library-first API with capability introspection (op.info().capability) and presign for object stores
Bindings for many languages, including Swift and Dart (Flutter), which helps if the client stack is Flutter/Rust
cons: No Box, SMB or NFS support
OneDrive service supports Personal only, not Business
gdrive docs require the full 'drive' scope (restricted), which brings Google verification and a recurring CASA assessment
No presign for gdrive or onedrive. You still own the OAuth authorization step
The Go binding needs libffi at runtime; binding maturity varies by language
options.license: Apache-2.0
options.maturity: Pre-1.0 (0.59.x). Object-store services are mature; SaaS drive services are less proven.

options.name: D. Per-provider SDKs only (no rclone/OpenDAL)
options.description: Write every driver yourself on top of official SDKs or REST: S3, Google Drive, Graph, Dropbox, Box, WebDAV (generic client), SFTP (golang.org/x/crypto/ssh + pkg/sftp), FTP.
pros: Smallest binary and no third-party engine semantics
Full control and the best fit to product behaviour
cons: Highest engineering cost. The long tail (pCloud, Box, FTP quirks, SMB) is expensive for little revenue
The Dropbox Go SDK is officially 'not a formally supported Dropbox product'
Re-implements years of edge-case handling that rclone already has
options.license: Mostly MIT/BSD/Apache SDKs
options.maturity: Depends on the SDK

options.name: E. Cloud relay for the SaaS tier (record to your own object storage, then copy asynchronously to the user's cloud)
options.description: In a SaaS deployment, cloud-recorded or edge-uploaded segments first land in the operator's own S3/R2 bucket, which handles lifecycle, presigned playback and CORS. A background job copies them to the user-linked Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox as 'archive/export' destinations.
pros: Playback always comes from S3/R2 with presigned Range URLs, so it is fast and predictable
User-cloud outages, quota exhaustion and throttling don't stop recording
Opens a revenue line (managed cloud retention)
cons: You pay storage and egress (R2 has no egress fees). GDPR processor obligations for video of people
Double transfer. User-cloud copies are not real-time
Does not fit the self-hosted/privacy-first version of the product
options.license: n/a
options.maturity: Standard pattern

recommendation:
Adopt option A, with option E as an optional SaaS add-on.

1) Interface. `Destination` should expose `Capabilities()`: resumable upload, chunk alignment and min/max part size, whether total size is required up front (Box, OneDrive), max object size, server-side lifecycle (S3/R2/B2), playback link type (presigned / pre-authenticated / temporary link / proxy-only), Range read, permanent delete versus recycle bin, quota query, app-scoped folder, hash types. Operations:
- `BeginUpload(key, size, meta)` returning a serialisable `UploadState` (Drive session URI, Graph uploadUrl, Dropbox session_id+offset, S3 uploadId+parts)
- `PutChunk` and `Resume(state)`, then `Commit`, which returns provider object ID, size and hash
- `OpenRange`
- `PlaybackURL(objectRef, ttl)`, returning either a URL or `ErrProxyRequired`
- `Delete(objectRef, permanent)`
- `Quota()`
- `List(prefix)`, used only for reconciliation and never for the timeline

2) Pipeline.
- The recorder writes closed fMP4/CMAF segments into a local spool. Use 5–10 min segments for cloud destinations and 1–2 min locally; 1-min segments create 14,400 files/day for 10 cameras, which hits Drive's ~2 files/s and quota-unit costs and fills a shared drive's 500k-item cap in about 35 days.
- A SQLite catalog tracks each segment: recorded → queued(dest) → uploading(UploadState) → verified(remote id, hash) → local-evictable.
- Workers run per destination with bandwidth caps and provider-specific concurrency: Dropbox runs one writer per account plus finish_batch, Graph honours Retry-After, Drive keeps file creation under about 2/s.
- Verify each upload by size and provider hash (Drive md5, OneDrive QuickXorHash, Dropbox content_hash, S3 ETag/checksum).
- Use day folders, e.g. `/{App}/{site}/{camera}/YYYY-MM-DD/`, which avoids OneDrive's ~100k-items-per-folder listing errors.

3) Retention and quota.
- Policy combines max age, max bytes and a minimum-free-quota floor.
- On S3/R2/B2, also set bucket lifecycle rules so expiry still happens when the agent is offline.
- On Drive, use files.delete, which is permanent.
- On OneDrive Business use permanentDelete. OneDrive Personal goes through the recycle bin, so count `quota.deleted`.
- On Dropbox use delete_batch.
- Poll quota (Drive about.storageQuota, Graph drive.quota, Dropbox space usage). Pre-flight with OneDrive's fileSize check (507).
- Handle Drive's 750 GB/day limit by pausing that destination for 24 h. Sizing: a 4 Mbps camera is about 43 GB/day, so one Google account can take roughly 17 such cameras.
- Warn when Wasabi's 30/90-day minimum is longer than the retention period.
- When quota runs out, the user chooses: rotate the oldest early, pause and buffer locally, or alert only. Never silently drop segments that have not been uploaded.

4) OAuth and token broker.
- Register your own clients with every provider; rclone's shared Drive client ends in 2026.
- Google: one Cloud project, scopes drive.file (+ drive.appdata), web, Android and iOS clients plus a 'TV/limited-input' client so headless boxes can be linked with the device flow. Publish the app (Testing mode gives 7-day tokens) and do basic or brand verification. Do not request the full `drive` scope unless the product truly needs to browse arbitrary folders, because that means CASA every year.
- Microsoft: one multi-tenant + personal app registration with publisher verification (free, needs Partner Center), Files.ReadWrite (or AppFolder for Personal), offline_access.
- Dropbox: an App Folder app, PKCE, offline tokens, and apply for Production before reaching 50 users.
- SaaS: refresh tokens live encrypted in the backend (envelope/KMS). Agents fetch short-lived access tokens from the broker, which also serialises refreshes because Box refresh tokens are single-use.
- Self-hosted: tokens are kept on the agent, encrypted with DPAPI, Keychain or Keystore.
- Never hold OneDrive tokens in a browser SPA (24 h refresh-token lifetime).

5) Playback.
- S3-family: short-TTL presigned Range URLs (5–15 min) with bucket CORS. These can be written directly into an HLS playlist that the server builds from the catalog.
- OneDrive: downloadUrl fetched on demand (lasts minutes, Range supported, CORS-friendly).
- Dropbox: temporary link (4 h) for native players. For web, test it first or proxy, because Dropbox advises against direct browser display.
- Google Drive: always proxy through the agent or backend with Range pass-through, or let a native client fetch with its own token. Budget against the 2026 daily quota-unit threshold, since each download request costs 200 units.
- Local/NAS: the agent serves the files over HTTPS with Range support.

6) Encryption. Make client-side encryption optional per destination and default it on for consumer clouds. Use a seekable chunked AEAD. Prefer the documented rclone-crypt format (64 KiB blocks, XSalsa20-Poly1305) so users can always recover footage with stock rclone, which avoids lock-in. Use per-file random data keys wrapped by a user key (passphrase via scrypt/Argon2id, or device-held keys). The cost: no provider previews, and playback must decrypt in the app (native player, or a WASM/Service Worker plus MSE on web), though presigned URLs still deliver the ciphertext ranges.

7) Phasing.
- MVP: Local disk + SMB/NAS (rclone smb or OS mount), S3-compatible (AWS/R2/B2/Wasabi/self-hosted), Google Drive (drive.file), OneDrive.
- Phase 2: Dropbox, WebDAV/Nextcloud and SFTP through the rclone driver.
- Phase 3: Box, pCloud, FTP and the rest.

Do not bundle MinIO as the self-hosted object store (archived Apr 2026, AGPL). Point self-hosters at any S3-compatible server instead.
risks: Google Drive API cost uncertainty: since May 2026 quotas are counted in quota units (download = 200, list = 100), with a 400M units/day per-project billing threshold and billing terms still to be announced 'later in 2026'. A SaaS that proxies playback or lists folders on Drive at scale could start incurring charges.

If any feature needs the full Google 'drive' scope (e.g. 'pick any existing folder' without the Picker, or showing files the app didn't create), the scope becomes restricted. That means Google review plus a paid CASA assessment that recurs (commonly yearly), and verification can take weeks.

drive.file only sees files the app created or the user picked. Files uploaded under a different Cloud project or client (e.g. a self-hosted build using the user's own client ID, then a move to the SaaS) are invisible to the other app. Keep one Cloud project for every first-party client.

Google Testing-mode apps get 7-day refresh tokens, and there are at most 100 refresh tokens per account per client. Many edge devices per Google account can silently revoke older tokens, which is a problem for multi-site customers. The device flow only allows drive.file/drive.appdata.

Google's 750 GB/day per-user upload cap (~17 cameras at 4 Mbps 24/7) and a shared drive's 500,000-item cap (including trash) make Drive unsuitable for large continuous-recording sites. Position it as small-site, event-clip or archive storage.

OneDrive Personal has no permanentDelete, so rotated recordings sit in the recycle bin and still consume quota ('deleted' bytes). Retention math must account for this or users will hit 'full' unexpectedly.
Microsoft multi-tenant apps without publisher verification can be blocked from user consent in business tenants. SPA refresh tokens expire after 24 h, so browser-only designs fail.

Dropbox apps freeze new user linking two weeks after reaching 50 users unless Production approval is granted. Concurrent writes to one account trigger too_many_write_operations (namespace lock). Temporary links are documented as not for direct browser display.
Box refresh tokens are single-use. Two processes refreshing concurrently (e.g. backend and edge) will lock the user out until they re-authenticate. Refreshes must be centralised and serialised.

librclone is 'experimental', untested on iOS, cannot use operations/uploadfile, and rclone's internal Go packages are not a stable API, so upgrades can break the embedding. Pin versions and wrap rclone behind your own interface.
OpenDAL limitations (OneDrive Personal only, full 'drive' scope in its docs, no SMB/Box) would force workarounds if chosen as the single layer.

Wasabi (and possibly other S3 providers with minimum-duration billing) charges for objects deleted before 30/90 days, which conflicts with short CCTV retention. R2 rejects multipart uploads with unequal part sizes.
MinIO community edition was archived on 25 Apr 2026 (AGPLv3, no binaries), so it is risky to recommend or bundle for self-hosting.
Client-side encryption breaks direct provider playback and previews and needs client-side decryption on every platform, including web. If keys are lost, footage is unrecoverable.

iOS cannot run a continuous background recorder or uploader, so 'record to Google Drive from an iPhone' is not a realistic 24/7 feature. The storage engine must live on an always-on agent (PC, NAS, Docker, Android foreground service) or in the cloud.

Legal: CCTV footage is personal data under GDPR (Romania/EU). Storing it in third-party consumer clouds raises questions about controller/processor roles, data residency (EU buckets, pCloud EU region) and retention limits, as well as provider ToS on surveillance or commercial use.

Research gaps: web search was unavailable and several official domains were blocked by the proxy. Google/Microsoft/Dropbox facts came via Context7 mirrors of the official docs, and CASA pricing is unverified (low confidence).
questions_for_product_owner: Where does recording physically happen: an always-on edge agent (Windows PC, NAS, Docker, Raspberry Pi), the phone, or a cloud recorder pulling RTSP? This decides where the storage engine runs and which platforms need upload capability.
Is the first release a self-hosted/personal tool or a multi-tenant SaaS? In self-hosted mode, should users be able to bring their own OAuth client IDs (as rclone now requires for Drive)?
Continuous 24/7 recording, or event/motion clips only? Continuous recording at 2–4 Mbps per camera rules out Google Drive for more than about 15 cameras per account.
Expected cameras per user, bitrate/codec (H.264 or H.265) and retention days? These are needed to size the local spool, cloud quota and the default segment length.

Does the user need to pick any existing folder in Google Drive or OneDrive, or is an app-owned folder (e.g. 'Apps/YourApp/Recordings') acceptable? Choosing the app-owned folder keeps Google's scope non-sensitive and avoids the yearly CASA cost.
Is end-to-end (client-side) encryption a must-have, optional per destination, or not needed? It trades away provider previews and simple browser playback.
Which providers are must-have for the MVP in your target market (Romania/EU)? Is EU data residency a requirement (EU S3 regions, pCloud EU)?
Do you need tamper-evident or legally admissible storage (e.g. S3 Object Lock / WORM, hash chains) for evidence use cases?
Should the product also sell its own managed cloud retention (option E, own R2/S3 bucket) as a paid tier, with user clouds as export/archive targets?
What happens when a destination is full or unreachable: rotate the oldest early, pause and buffer locally (how many hours or GB of local buffer), or alert only?

Is there budget and a legal entity for provider compliance: Microsoft Partner Center publisher verification, Google brand verification (and CASA if broad Drive access is needed), Dropbox production review, privacy policy and ToS?

Must recordings remain readable without your app (e.g. plain MP4 in the user's Drive, or rclone-crypt so they can decrypt with stock rclone)? This is a data-portability and anti-lock-in promise worth deciding early.

area: Recording engine, events, playback, and lessons from existing NVR software (Frigate, Viseron, moonfire-nvr, MediaMTX, Kerberos, Shinobi, ZoneMinder, motionEye, Scrypted, Agent DVR, Home Assistant), plus motion/AI detection cost-benefit and licensing
summary: The mature open-source NVRs have settled on one recording pattern. They copy the camera's H.264/H.265 stream without re-encoding into short MP4/fMP4 segments, keep one database row per segment, and treat retention, events and pre-roll as metadata over a continuous local recording. Frigate (MIT) writes 10 s segments to a RAM cache and keeps a segment only if it matches the retention policy, which gives up to 60 s of pre-roll at no extra cost. Viseron (MIT) stores fMP4 .m4s segments and builds HLS playlists from its database on the fly. moonfire-nvr (GPL) stores raw samples and builds .mp4 files on request. For our hub (Windows plus Docker/Linux, commercial, closed source, no GPL/AGPL in the shipped product), the best permissive building blocks are MediaMTX (MIT, single Go binary for Windows, Linux and macOS). It records fMP4 with a 1 s recovery point, has segment-complete hooks, a time-range playback API, and documents an rclone upload recipe. Around it sit gortsplib/mediacommon (MIT), go2rtc (MIT), FFmpeg in its default LGPL build, and rclone (MIT). Licensing traps are real. Frigate's MIT image bundles nginx-vod-module (AGPL-3.0). Ultralytics YOLO is AGPL, the original YOLOv9 repo is GPL-3.0, and YOLO-NAS weights forbid commercial use. Shinobi uses a custom paid license for commercial use, and ZoneMinder, motionEye, moonfire and LightNVR are GPL. Frigate+ models need a separate commercial license for hosted or managed services. For motion, the cheapest MVP source is camera-side ONVIF events. Subscriptions need careful handling, because cameras leak subscriptions and stop sending events, as Home Assistant's code documents. Next comes pixel-diff on the decoded substream at about 5 fps, and later AI detection via OpenVINO or ONNX Runtime with Apache/MIT models. Frigate itself no longer recommends Coral for new installs. The gap this product can fill is clear: Frigate has no native apps, no Windows support and no cloud-drive storage. Shinobi and motionEye upload to Google Drive but not to OneDrive. Agent DVR covers Windows and the cloud but charges from $7.95/month for remote access, cloud storage and mobile apps. Nobody offers a consumer-friendly multi-vendor hub with native apps on all platforms plus Google Drive and OneDrive storage. Caveat: the shared WebSearch budget was used up and only GitHub, GitLab and developer.android.com could be reached. Facts about commercial apps (Blue Iris, tinyCam, Alfred, Hik-Connect, Reolink, Camect, Eufy) and their user complaints are therefore low confidence and were not re-verified.

facts.claim: Frigate is MIT-licensed. The Frigate name and logo are trademarks of Frigate, Inc. and are not covered by the MIT license.

Recent Frigate releases: 0.17.0 (27 Feb), 0.18.0 (12 Sep) and 0.18.2 (15 Oct), the last being a maintenance release with fixes for 3 security advisories. The page shows no years; the footer reads 2026, so these are almost certainly 2026 releases. 0.18 removed the DeGirum detector, deprecated DeepStack and moved to FFmpeg 8.

Frigate records with the FFmpeg segment muxer and no re-encoding: '-f segment -segment_time 10 -segment_format mp4 -reset_timestamps 1 -strftime 1 -c copy' (audio variants copy or convert to AAC). Only MJPEG/JPEG sources are encoded with libx264. For HEVC on Apple devices it forces the 'hvc1' tag.

Frigate's recording pipeline: 10 s segments are written to a small tmpfs cache (/tmp/cache) and validated with ffprobe. They move to disk only if they match the retention policy, being remuxed with '-c copy -movflags +faststart' plus a creation_time tag. The cache holds at most 6 segments (MAX_SEGMENTS_IN_CACHE=6), and MAX_PRE_CAPTURE is 60 s. The true start time is taken as file mtime minus probed duration.

Frigate retention: separate day counts for continuous and motion recordings (continuous is off by default). Alerts and detections each have their own retention with mode all, motion or active_objects. pre_capture/post_capture default to 5 s, with pre-capture capped at 60 s and limited by 10 s segment boundaries. When less than about 1 hour of headroom remains, an emergency cleanup deletes the oldest recordings regardless of retention. Exports are never removed by retention.

Frigate's timeline index (SQLite via peewee) stores one Recordings row per segment: camera, path, start/end, duration, motion, objects, dBFS, segment_size, a 16x16 motion_heatmap, keyframe ms offsets, stream_type and audio/video codec. There are also ReviewSegment rows (severity alert/detection, thumb_path), a Previews table, Export/ExportCase and a Timeline table.

Frigate plays recordings through Kaltura nginx-vod-module in 'mapped' mode. It serves HLS with an fMP4 container (vod_hls_container_format fmp4, HLS v6) assembled from the stored MP4 segments. nginx-vod-module is AGPL-3.0, so copying Frigate's playback stack into a closed product is a license risk.
Frigate exports clips by feeding the VOD playlist to FFmpeg's concat demuxer and writing MP4 with '-movflags +faststart'. The default custom export is a 25x timelapse.

Frigate's review UX: since 0.14, overlapping activity on one camera is grouped into a single 'review item', split into alerts (person/car by default) and detections. Items are shown as a grid of low-resolution, low-fps preview videos, and tapping one opens the full recording.

Frigate's dev-branch docs (not in the v0.18.2 docs, so likely an upcoming release) add 'Sub Stream Recording'. It records a second low-quality stream with its own retention and falls back to it automatically for playback and export.

Browser H.265 playback is limited. Per Frigate's docs, only Firefox 134+/136+/137+ (Windows/Mac/Linux and Android), Chrome 108+, Safari and Edge play H.265, and only some profiles. Per go2rtc, WebRTC H.265 needs Chrome 136+ or Safari 18+, desktop Firefox has no H.265, and iPhone MSE needs iOS 17.1+.
Frigate does not officially support Windows; some users run it under WSL or VirtualBox. It runs best in Docker on bare-metal Debian, and running in a VM is not recommended.

Frigate's 'app' is a PWA, not a native app. Notifications use WebPush/VAPID and need HTTPS plus external reachability of the server. Frigate's recording docs have no cloud-drive or S3 upload feature; the system is designed to run fully local.

Frigate's motion detection is a first-pass luminance-change filter (threshold, contour_area, lightning_threshold) that gates object detection. Detection runs on the decoded detect stream, ideally the substream, at a default 5 fps (10 fps is the recommended maximum). Motion regions are cropped to the model input (320x320). Frigate always decodes one stream, even for recording-only setups.

Frigate's hardware docs say 'The Coral is no longer recommended for new Frigate installations' (about 10 ms per inference). Reported times: Intel N100 with OpenVINO about 15 ms (MobileNetV2) and 30 ms (YOLOv9 s-320); Intel NPU about 6 ms (MobileNetV2); Hailo-8 about 6-7 ms; RTX 3050 YOLOv9 s-320 10 ms; Apple M1 via ONNX YOLOv9 t-320 3.3 ms; RK3588 YOLOv9-tiny about 35 ms. Max FPS = 1000 / inference ms.

Frigate+ subscription: includes 12 model trainings per year. Models stay usable after you cancel. Using Frigate+ models to provide a hosted or managed service, or to deploy at customers' sites, requires a separate commercial license.

Viseron is MIT-licensed. It stores recordings as short fMP4 '.m4s' segments, and the server API generates HLS playlists played through hls.js. The segments do not play on their own; a download produces an .mp4. It supports event, continuous and manual recordings, cron-based recording schedules per camera, and per-camera retention by max_age or max_size.

Viseron 'storage tiers' move files between storage locations when a tier's max age or size is reached. Options include drain, move_on_shutdown for a RAM-disk first tier, and polling for NTFS mounts. This is directly analogous to a local-then-cloud storage pipeline.

Viseron v3.7.0 ('ONVIF support', 17 Sep, year not shown, probably 2026) added an ONVIF component with PTZ and presets in the UI, FastALPR, and cron-based recording schedules, and dropped RPi3 support. v3.4.1 had a Hailo-8 hotfix.

moonfire-nvr is GPL-3.0-or-later with an OpenSSL linking exception and is pre-1.0. It does not transcode or decode video. It stores raw H.264 sample data on HDD and a per-frame index (delta-encoded varints) in SQLite on flash, and builds .mp4 or fragmented MP4 for any time range on demand. It handles six 1080p30 streams on a Raspberry Pi 2 at under 10% CPU. Recordings are about 1 minute. Crash safety uses the order fsync file, fsync directory, then insert row, and losing the last partial minute is an explicit non-goal. Timestamps use a 90 kHz clock. It has no motion detection.

MediaMTX is MIT-licensed and ships as a single dependency-free executable for Linux, Windows and macOS. It records to fMP4 (AV1, VP9, H.265, H.264, MJPEG; AAC, Opus, G.711 and more) or MPEG-TS. recordPartDuration (default 1 s) equals the recovery point; recordSegmentDuration defaults to 1h and recordDeleteAfter to 1d. It has hooks for runOnRecordSegmentCreate/Complete and a playback server with /list (recorded timespans as JSON) and /get?start=&duration=&format=fmp4|mp4, playable directly in a <video> tag.

MediaMTX's docs describe uploading recordings with rclone (sync or move) from the runOnInit and runOnRecordSegmentComplete hooks, covering S3, FTP, SMB, Google Drive and others. rclone is MIT-licensed.
MediaMTX's latest release is v1.21.2 (8 Oct, year not shown). It includes a security fix for free access to the playback server with legacy credentials. v1.21.0 added alwaysAvailableRecorded.

go2rtc is MIT-licensed. Its latest release is v1.9.14 (2026-01-19), which Home Assistant core lists as RECOMMENDED_VERSION. gortsplib and mediacommon (the RTSP and media libraries behind MediaMTX) are MIT, as are the Go ONVIF libraries use-go/onvif and kerberos-io/onvif.

FFmpeg docs: a normal MOV/MP4 'is undecodable if it is not properly finished'. A fragmented file stays decodable if writing is interrupted and needs less memory, but is less compatible. faststart runs a second pass to move the moov atom to the front and does not work for fragmented output. The 'hybrid_fragmented' movflag writes fragmented while recording and converts to a regular MP4 when finished. It appears in the docs of the release/7.1 and 8.0 branches but not 7.0, so it needs FFmpeg 7.1+.

In the FFmpeg segment muxer, every segment starts with a keyframe, so split times are only accurate if the camera's GOP aligns. Relevant options: segment_atclocktime (split at wall-clock intervals), reset_timestamps, strftime naming and segment_list. The Matroska muxer has 'live' and 'cluster_time_limit' options for streaming-safe writing.

FFmpeg concat demuxer inpoint/outpoint 'works best with intra frame codecs'. With H.264/H.265 you get extra packets before the In point, so a stream-copy clip export is keyframe-granular unless the edges are re-encoded.
FFmpeg decoder option skip_frame=nokey discards everything except keyframes. This is the cheap way to make per-segment thumbnails and sprite strips without fully decoding the stream.

FFmpeg is LGPL v2.1+ by default. Building with --enable-gpl, which x264/x265 and some filters need, turns the whole build into GPL v2+. A closed product should ship an LGPL build, dynamically linked or used as a separate process.

The ONVIF Core spec defines a PullPoint pattern (CreatePullPointSubscription, then PullMessages long-poll; devices must support a Timeout of at least 1 minute) so clients behind firewalls can get events in real time. The Analytics spec defines motion topics tns1:RuleEngine/CellMotionDetector/Motion and tns1:RuleEngine/MotionRegionDetector/Motion.

Home Assistant's ONVIF integration keeps subscriptions alive for 10 minutes and renews them every 8 minutes. The reason: ONVIF provides no way to list existing subscriptions, and a camera that hits its subscription limit stops sending events until the subscriptions expire or it reboots. HA uses a webhook (Notify) when reachable and falls back to PullPoint. Dependencies: onvif-zeep-async 4.3.0, onvif_parsers 2.5.0 and WSDiscovery 2.1.2. Home Assistant core is Apache-2.0.
Home Assistant's camera.record service has duration 1-3600 s (default 30) and lookback 0-300 s of pre-roll from the stream buffer. HA's stream component targets about 2 s HLS segments.

Scrypted: @scrypted/server is ISC-licensed (v0.148.0), and plugins such as prebuffer-mixin, onvif and objectdetector are Apache-2.0. The repo states licensing varies per directory and some plugins carry GPL-dependency obligations. No 'nvr' plugin exists in the public plugins directory, which suggests Scrypted NVR is closed and paid; the price was not verified.

Scrypted's Rebroadcast/Prebuffer plugin keeps persistent camera connections and buffers recent video for instant replay and faster stream start. It recommends a camera keyframe (IDR) interval of 4 s and High/Medium/Low streams of about 2000/500/100 Kbps.

Kerberos Agent is MIT-licensed (Go plus React). It records on motion by default with 10 s pre-recording and 20 s post-recording and a 30 s maximum length, and has a continuous option. Output is MP4, with an optional fragmented MP4 (8 s fragments) for HLS and AES-256 encryption at rest. Cloud targets are Kerberos Hub, Kerberos Vault and Dropbox; Google Drive, MinIO, Storj and FTP are listed as work in progress. Kerberos Hub is commercial: a license is required, with a free license for up to 8 agents.

Shinobi uses a custom 'Shinobi Open Source Software License Agreement'. Personal and non-commercial use is free. Commercial use, including selling hardware with Shinobi installed or running 15 or more active monitors outside schools and personal use, requires a paid subscription.

Shinobi's cloud uploaders cover Amazon S3, Backblaze B2, Google Drive, S3-compatible storage, SFTP, WebDAV and mounts; there is no OneDrive or Dropbox uploader. The Google Drive uploader uses the 'drive.file' OAuth scope, creates per-day folders, uploads each completed video and deletes cloud copies after a configurable number of days.

motionEye is GPL-3.0 (version 0.44.0 in the repo) and is a front-end for the 'motion' daemon. Its upload services are Google Drive, Google Photos, Dropbox, WebDAV, FTP, SFTP and S3; there is no OneDrive.
ZoneMinder is GPLv2 and Linux-only. The 1.38 series runs from 1.38.0 (1 Feb, inferred 2026) to 1.38.6 (5 Oct 2026). 1.38.5 fixed 19 reported vulnerabilities.
LightNVR is a new C NVR for 256 MB RAM devices and is GPLv3.

Agent DVR (iSpyConnect, closed source) is free for private local use. Remote access, cloud storage, mobile apps and business use require a subscription from $7.95/month. It runs on Windows 10+, macOS 11+, Linux (glibc 2.28+), Docker and Raspberry Pi 4+. It was rebuilt from iSpy in January 2022 and claims 2M+ users.

Object-detection model licenses: Ultralytics (YOLOv8/YOLO11) is AGPL-3.0; the original YOLOv9 repo (WongKinYiu/yolov9) is GPL-3.0; the MultimediaTechLab/YOLO reimplementation (v9/v7) is MIT; YOLOX, RF-DETR and D-FINE are Apache-2.0. The YOLO-NAS weight license forbids commercial or production use without a separate agreement with Deci, and Frigate has already removed the DeGirum detector because that company ceased operations.
Inference runtimes: ONNX Runtime is MIT and OpenVINO is Apache-2.0. DirectML is in maintenance mode, and Microsoft points Windows 11 24H2+ users to Windows ML.

Android 15 (API 35) limits the dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground-service types to 6 hours in any 24 h. Bringing the app to the foreground resets the budget. This matters for the later 'Android hub' (old phone or TV box) recording 24/7.

Cloud-upload limits that affect segment sizing: per rclone's docs, Google Drive allows about 750 GiB of uploads per user per day ('at the time of writing'). OneDrive/Graph upload sessions need each fragment under 60 MiB and a multiple of 320 KiB (327,680 bytes), and each uploaded fragment extends the session expiry.

Bandwidth and storage arithmetic: a 4 Mbps main stream is 0.5 MB/s, or about 43.2 GB/day per camera. Uploading it continuously needs a sustained 4 Mbps uplink per camera. The 15 GB free Google Drive tier holds about 8 hours of one such camera, and 750 GiB/day covers roughly 18 such cameras.

tinyCam Monitor PRO is an Android-only app that runs its own web server with a REST API partly compatible with Axis VAPIX. The developer also runs a separate tinyCam Cloud service. Pricing, ratings and feature set were not verified because the store and vendor sites could not be reached.

Commercial competitor landscape, from background knowledge and not re-verified (vendor sites, app stores, Reddit and news sites were unreachable): Blue Iris is a Windows-only commercial NVR sold as a one-time license. IP Cam Viewer and tinyCam are multi-brand mobile viewers with limited server-side recording. Alfred turns old phones into cameras on a freemium model with ads. Hik-Connect and the Reolink app are single-vendor apps with cloud add-ons. Camect is a hub with built-in AI whose current status is unknown. Eufy faced a widely reported controversy in late 2022 over unencrypted remote streams and cloud thumbnails despite 'local only' marketing. Recurring complaints across these apps: a separate app per brand, paywalled AI and cloud features, privacy and cloud dependence, unreliable P2P remote access, weak desktop and web clients, and ads in free tiers.
