facts.claim: The open eufy_security Home Assistant integration has about 206 open issues. Common themes are streams stuck in 'PREPARING', P2P lookup timeouts, missing motion events and worry about a vendor API deprecation. This illustrates the fragility of supporting cloud-only cameras, which the brief already excludes from the MVP.

options.name: A. Go hub + MediaMTX as a managed recording and live engine (sidecar binary)
options.description: The hub service, written in Go, ships MediaMTX next to it and drives it through the Control API and hooks. MediaMTX pulls RTSP from each camera with no transcoding, records fMP4 continuously (1 s parts, segments of a few minutes), and serves live WebRTC/HLS plus range playback (/get?format=fmp4|mp4). On runOnRecordSegmentComplete the hub probes the segment, indexes it in SQLite (start/end on the hub's wall clock, duration, keyframe offsets, codecs, size, motion/event flags, upload state) and queues it for upload. Retention, pre-roll and event-only mode are policies over this continuous local recording, the Frigate model.
options.license: MediaMTX MIT; gortsplib/mediacommon MIT; rclone MIT; FFmpeg LGPL (only if needed for thumbnails or remux)
options.maturity: MediaMTX is mature and actively released (v1.21.x in 2026). Recording plus playback is a documented, first-class feature.
pros: One permissively licensed binary that runs natively on Windows, Linux, macOS and ARM, matching the brief's hub targets
Crash-safe by design: fMP4 parts mean at most about 1 s is lost on power failure (recordPartDuration = RPO)
Live (WebRTC/HLS) and recording share a single camera connection
Playback API (/list, /get) already assembles time ranges into browser-playable fMP4 or MP4, so no AGPL nginx-vod is needed
The rclone hook recipe is documented upstream, and rclone covers Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox and S3
Go is strongly typed and matches the 'few languages, AI-maintainable' rule
cons: It is an external process, so the hub needs supervision, config generation, version pinning and a health watchdog
No built-in event model, retention-by-event or timeline database; the hub must build these
Only paths are toggled, with no RAM pre-roll; pre-roll comes from continuous local recording, which means continuous disk writes even in 'motion-only' mode
Its internal packages are not importable as a Go library; deep customization means forking or moving to option B
Playback-server auth needs care (v1.21.2 fixed an open-access bug), so keep it bound to localhost behind the hub's own auth

options.name: B. Custom Go recorder on gortsplib + mediacommon (MIT), modeled on moonfire, Frigate and Viseron
options.description: The hub embeds an RTSP client (gortsplib) and writes fMP4 itself with mediacommon. It keeps a per-camera in-memory GOP ring buffer for pre-roll, writes fMP4 segments with 1-2 s fragments and closes a segment every N minutes on a keyframe. It indexes per-segment and per-keyframe data in SQLite, generates HLS (EXT-X-MAP fMP4) playlists from the database like Viseron, and stitches MP4 ranges like moonfire. Live view uses go2rtc (MIT) or the same ingest.
options.license: MIT (gortsplib, mediacommon, go2rtc)
options.maturity: The libraries are mature and back MediaMTX, but the recorder, indexer and playback layer would be new code we own.
pros: Full control over segment boundaries, the RAM pre-roll buffer (true event-only recording without continuous disk writes, good for Raspberry Pi SD cards), dual-stream main and substream recording, and precise keyframe indexes
No sidecar process; one Go binary per hub
Timeline index and upload state can be designed together, with no impedance mismatch
cons: More code to write and test: RTSP edge cases (camera quirks, timestamp jumps, RTCP absence, reconnects), fMP4 muxing correctness and H.265 parameter sets
Reimplements much of what MediaMTX already handles well
Higher risk for an AI-maintained codebase unless test coverage against recorded camera captures is extensive

options.name: C. FFmpeg subprocess segmenting (Frigate pattern) + go2rtc for live
options.description: For each camera the hub runs an LGPL FFmpeg build with '-c copy -f segment -segment_time N' into a cache directory. It then validates each segment with ffprobe, keeps or discards it by policy, remuxes kept ones with '+faststart' (or uses fMP4 / hybrid_fragmented on FFmpeg 7.1+) and indexes them in SQLite. go2rtc re-streams to clients and to FFmpeg so the camera sees only one connection.
options.license: FFmpeg LGPL 2.1+ (must NOT be built with --enable-gpl); go2rtc MIT
options.maturity: Battle-tested by Frigate at large scale; FFmpeg 8 is current.
pros: Most proven approach in production NVRs
FFmpeg handles every codec and container quirk, and the same binary can do thumbnails (skip_frame nokey), exports and optional transcoding
Easy to reason about: recording is literally files plus a database
cons: Process-per-camera supervision, stderr parsing and restarts (Frigate 0.18.1 still needed back-off fixes for stale recording streams)
Shipping an LGPL FFmpeg build for Windows, x64 and arm64 with hardware acceleration is non-trivial, and LGPL compliance obligations apply
A tmpfs cache is not natively available on Windows; NTFS locking and antivirus scanning complicate move-and-rename flows
With non-fragmented MP4, an in-progress segment is lost on a crash

options.name: D. Build on top of Frigate (fork or bundle)
options.description: Use Frigate (MIT) as the hub engine and build native apps and a cloud-storage layer around its API.
options.license: MIT for Frigate code, but the Docker image includes nginx-vod-module (AGPL-3.0); Frigate+ models need a commercial license for managed services; the trademark is not licensed
options.maturity: Very mature (0.18.x, large community)
pros: Best-in-class detection, review UX and timeline out of the box
Large knowledge base
cons: Linux/Docker only; Windows is officially unsupported, which conflicts with the brief's Windows hub
Python plus nginx plus go2rtc stack: heavy, multi-language, hard to package for consumers
AGPL nginx-vod in the playback path, and the Frigate trademark cannot be used
No cloud-drive storage and no multi-tenant or remote-access layer, so we would still build most of the product

options.name: E. Reuse GPL or closed NVRs (ZoneMinder, Shinobi, moonfire-nvr, motionEye, LightNVR, Agent DVR, Blue Iris)
options.description: Integrate or white-label an existing NVR instead of building a recorder.
options.license: GPLv2 (ZoneMinder), GPLv3 (moonfire, motionEye, LightNVR), custom paid commercial (Shinobi), proprietary (Agent DVR, Blue Iris, Scrypted NVR)
options.maturity: Varies, from mature (ZoneMinder, Blue Iris, Agent DVR) to pre-1.0 (moonfire)
pros: Fastest route to a working NVR for a personal or self-hosted tool
cons: GPL/AGPL code must not ship in the product (project rule); Shinobi charges for commercial use
Proprietary engines create vendor dependency and per-seat costs
Use them only as design references (moonfire's storage design, Shinobi's and motionEye's upload services, Agent DVR's business model)

options.name: F. Motion/event source: camera ONVIF events (MVP)
options.description: The hub subscribes to each camera's ONVIF events: PullPoint by default, a Notify webhook when the camera can reach the hub. It maps tns1:RuleEngine/CellMotionDetector/Motion, MotionRegionDetector, VideoSource/MotionAlarm and vendor person/vehicle topics to event start and stop times. Short subscriptions are renewed regularly, following Home Assistant's 10-minute subscription and 8-minute renewal.
options.license: Spec under ONVIF no-derivatives license; Go clients use-go/onvif and kerberos-io/onvif are MIT
options.maturity: Universal on ONVIF Profile S/T cameras, but quality varies widely by vendor and firmware
pros: Almost zero hub CPU, so it scales to many cameras on a Raspberry Pi
Many cameras already run on-board person/vehicle AI, giving 'free' smart events
Same protocol as PTZ and presets, which the MVP needs anyway
cons: Subscriptions leak and cameras stop sending events at their limit (documented in HA's code)
Topic names, sensitivity and latency differ per vendor; some Tapo and Reolink models are partial or buggy
No uniform object classes; false positives from IR switching, rain and insects depend on the camera

options.name: G. Motion source: hub-side pixel-diff on the substream (v1.x fallback)
options.description: Decode the low-resolution substream (for example 640x360 at 5 fps) and run a Frigate-style luminance-diff with threshold, contour area, masks and lightning or IR-switch suppression. Use it for cameras without usable ONVIF events and as the gate for later AI.
options.license: Own code (Go plus a permissive decoder; FFmpeg LGPL or hardware decoders)
options.maturity: Proven approach (Frigate, Kerberos, motion)
pros: Works with any RTSP camera, with behavior that is consistent across vendors
Enables motion heatmaps and motion search on the timeline (Frigate stores a 16x16 heatmap per segment)
cons: Constant decode cost per camera, the main CPU consumer on small hubs; hardware decode differs per OS
Needs tuning UI (zones, masks, sensitivity); weather, shadows and headlights cause false alerts

options.name: H. AI object detection (post-MVP)
options.description: Run person, vehicle and animal detection on motion regions from the substream. On Windows use ONNX Runtime (MIT) with OpenVINO or Windows ML; on Linux use OpenVINO (Apache-2.0), Hailo or RKNN. Use only Apache/MIT models (YOLOX, RF-DETR, D-FINE, MIT YOLOv9 reimplementation) or our own fine-tuned weights.
options.license: Runtime: MIT/Apache. Avoid Ultralytics (AGPL), the original YOLOv9 repo (GPL-3.0), YOLO-NAS weights (non-commercial) and Frigate+ models (commercial license needed)
options.maturity: Hardware is mature (Intel iGPU and NPU at about 6-30 ms per inference); Coral is no longer recommended by Frigate
pros: Big reduction in false alerts, which drives event-only uploads to Drive and OneDrive and makes notifications useful
Target hubs (Intel N100/N150 mini PCs, Windows laptops) already have OpenVINO-capable iGPUs or NPUs
cons: Hardware fragmentation across Windows, Docker and ARM; a model and runtime test matrix is needed
Model licensing must be audited; training our own model needs a dataset, and camera images are GDPR-relevant
CPU-only inference is not viable at scale

recommendation:
For the MVP hub (Windows plus Docker/Linux, commercial and closed), start with option A: a Go hub service that supervises MediaMTX (MIT). Hide the recorder behind a small internal interface so it can later be swapped for option B (a custom gortsplib/mediacommon recorder) if a RAM pre-roll, dual-stream or precise indexing need it. Concretely:

(1) Never transcode. Record each camera's main stream continuously to local disk as fMP4 with about 1 s fragments. Close segments on a keyframe every 1-2 minutes as the local unit, and upload either those or 5-minute bundles to the cloud. Short local segments keep crash loss and pre-roll granularity small; larger cloud units reduce API calls against Google Drive (about 750 GiB/day per user) and OneDrive (fragments under 60 MiB in multiples of 320 KiB).

(2) Build the timeline index in SQLite on the hub, following Frigate's Recordings table. Store per segment: camera, stream, start and end on the hub's NTP-synced wall clock (not the camera clock, per moonfire's lessons), duration, keyframe offsets, codecs, bytes, motion and event flags, local state and per-destination upload state. Add an events table (start, end, source, label) and an append-only upload outbox, so an internet outage only delays uploads and never creates gaps.

(3) Treat 'motion-only' recording as policy over continuous local recording. Keep everything locally for a short ring (for example 1-24 h) and permanently keep or upload only segments that overlap events plus pre-roll and post-roll. Pre-roll then costs nothing and is bounded only by the ring, like Frigate's cache with its 60 s maximum. Default to 5-10 s pre-roll and about 10-20 s post-roll, similar to Kerberos and Frigate. Recommend a camera keyframe interval of 1-2 s (Scrypted suggests 4 s as a maximum) so cuts are accurate.

(4) Retention: separate day counts for continuous and event footage per destination. Add an emergency oldest-first cleanup when free space drops below a threshold, as Frigate does. Exports are never auto-deleted.

(5) Playback: generate HLS (fMP4, EXT-X-MAP) playlists from the database as Viseron does, or proxy MediaMTX /get. Never use nginx-vod-module (AGPL). Keep MediaMTX's playback and API bound to localhost behind the hub's auth.

(6) Export: concat with stream copy, aligned to keyframes, finished with +faststart MP4 (or MediaMTX /get?format=mp4). Re-encode only edges or timelapses, and only on request.

(7) Thumbnails: one keyframe image per segment and per event (decode keyframes only). Add a low-fps preview strip later for scrubbing, Frigate-style.

(8) Codecs: guide users to H.264 on the main stream and substream for web compatibility. Allow H.265 recording but flag clients that cannot play it (Firefox desktop WebRTC, older Chrome). Plan optional substream recording with longer retention, as in Frigate's dev docs, for remote playback over slow uplinks and cheap long history.

(9) Events in the MVP: ONVIF camera events with robust subscription lifecycle management (short terms, renewal, PullPoint fallback, a per-camera 'events healthy' indicator). Hub-side substream pixel-diff in v1.1. AI later via ONNX Runtime/OpenVINO with Apache/MIT models only.

(10) Licensing guardrails in CI: an SPDX scan that fails the build on GPL/AGPL, and an LGPL-only FFmpeg build if FFmpeg is shipped at all.

Run a 1-2 week spike first. MediaMTX on Windows and a Raspberry Pi 4/5 with SSD, 4-8 real cameras (Hikvision, Dahua, Reolink, Tapo), measuring CPU and RAM, segment integrity after hard power cuts, ONVIF event reliability per brand, and end-to-end upload to Drive and OneDrive during a simulated internet outage.
risks: License contamination. Frigate's MIT image bundles AGPL nginx-vod-module. Ultralytics is AGPL, the original YOLOv9 repo is GPL-3.0, and YOLO-NAS weights are non-commercial. Shinobi charges for commercial use. ZoneMinder, motionEye, moonfire and LightNVR are GPL. An FFmpeg build with --enable-gpl becomes GPL. Frigate+ models need a commercial license for hosted services. Mitigate with an SPDX/license scan in CI and an approved-dependency list.

H.265 playback. Many cameras default to H.265, which desktop Firefox WebRTC cannot play, and Chrome needs 108+ (136+ for WebRTC) plus hardware support. Recording without transcoding then yields footage some clients cannot play. Server-side transcoding on a Raspberry Pi or weak Windows box is expensive.

ONVIF event unreliability. Cameras cap subscriptions, and leaked subscriptions silently stop events until reboot (documented in Home Assistant's code). Topics and quality vary by vendor and firmware, so 'motion recording' may silently miss events. Needs health monitoring and a pixel-diff fallback.

Upload bandwidth vs. continuous recording. One 4 Mbps camera produces about 43 GB/day; consumer uplinks and Google Drive's roughly 750 GiB/day per-user cap make continuous cloud upload of several cameras infeasible for many users. Cloud should default to event-only or substream upload, with clear UI about the bandwidth needed.

Crash and power-loss data loss. Non-fragmented MP4 is undecodable if not finalized, so use fMP4 or hybrid_fragmented (FFmpeg 7.1+), fsync ordering (moonfire) and startup reconciliation between files and database rows (Frigate media sync aborts if more than 50% would be deleted).
Disk-full and SD-card wear on Raspberry Pi hubs. Continuous writes wear out SD cards. Require or strongly recommend an SSD or HDD, and add emergency oldest-first cleanup.

Clock drift and timestamps. Camera clocks drift, jump, or arrive without RTCP sender reports. Index on the hub's NTP-synced wall clock and store raw stream timestamps too (moonfire lesson), or timelines and exports will misalign.

Windows-specific file semantics. Open-file locking, antivirus scanning of new segments and NTFS change-notification quirks (Viseron needs polling on NTFS mounts) can break rename, move and upload flows that work on Linux.
Keyframe-granular cuts. With stream copy, pre-roll, segment boundaries and exports snap to GOP boundaries. Cameras with 4-10 s GOPs give imprecise clips unless their IDR interval is lowered.

Mobile platforms cannot be the recorder. iOS does not allow continuous background recording, which is general knowledge not verified this session. Android 15 caps dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services at 6 h per 24 h, so the future Android hub needs a different service type or must stay in the foreground.
Coral, DeGirum and similar accelerator ecosystems are churning: Frigate no longer recommends Coral and removed DeGirum after the company ceased operations. AI hardware support is a moving target.

GDPR. Recordings, thumbnails and event metadata in third-party clouds are personal data, so retention defaults, deletion propagation to Drive and OneDrive, and data processing disclosures must be designed in.

Research gap. The WebSearch budget was exhausted and most non-GitHub domains (vendor sites, app stores, news, Reddit) were unreachable in this session, so the commercial competitor analysis and user-complaint themes are low confidence and should be re-verified.
questions_for_product_owner: Should the cloud (Google Drive/OneDrive) receive continuous 24/7 footage, or only event clips plus optional low-resolution substream footage? Continuous upload of a 4 Mbps camera is about 43 GB/day, which is beyond many users' uplinks and Drive's ~750 GiB/day cap at scale.
When the internet is up and a segment has uploaded, should the local copy be deleted ('move') or kept for N days ('sync')? Is the local disk the primary archive or only a buffer?

What is the acceptable data loss on a hub crash or power cut: about 1 second (fMP4 fragments) or up to one segment (1-5 minutes)? This also fixes the local segment length ('a few minutes' in the brief).

For 'motion-only' users, do we accept continuous writes to a short local ring buffer (simple, gives free pre-roll), or must the hub avoid continuous disk writes (for example Raspberry Pi with an SD card), which needs a custom RAM pre-roll recorder?
What default pre-roll and post-roll should events have (e.g. 5-10 s before, 10-20 s after), and is a user-configurable value up to 60 s enough?
Do we require users to set cameras to H.264, or must H.265 recordings play everywhere (web, Firefox, older devices)? The latter implies optional on-hub transcoding and stronger minimum hardware.
Should the hub record the camera substream as well (cheap long retention, smooth remote playback), as Frigate's upcoming sub-stream recording does?
What minimum hub hardware and camera count will we officially support (e.g. Raspberry Pi 5 + SSD for 4 cameras, Intel N100 mini PC for 8-16, any Windows 10/11 PC)?
Is clip export/sharing (download MP4, share link) needed in the MVP, or only timeline playback?
Should users be able to play back recordings directly from Google Drive/OneDrive when the hub is offline? That needs the app to read cloud files itself, with an index stored in the cloud too.
Is using the camera's own SD card as a backup (ONVIF Profile G or vendor APIs) desirable as a gap-filler when the hub is down, or out of scope?

For the later AI phase: which accelerators do we target first (Intel iGPU/NPU via OpenVINO is the most common in mini PCs), and are we willing to train or fine-tune our own Apache/MIT-licensed model instead of licensing Frigate+ or Ultralytics?

area: Security, privacy and legal (GDPR/Romania, threat model, E2EE, OAuth, app-store and platform policies, EU Cyber Resilience Act) for a cross-platform multi-camera IP camera app built by a Romanian developer
summary:
The biggest lever for both legal exposure and security risk is whether your servers ever see plaintext video or camera credentials. Design the product local-first: an always-on hub (Windows service, Docker or NAS) pulls RTSP/ONVIF, records, and encrypts each segment before uploading it to the user's own Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, S3 or local disk. Your cloud then only does accounts, signaling, TURN relay and push. With that design you are a small data processor for business users and largely outside the video processing for home users. The alternative, a full cloud NVR, makes you a large-scale video processor. That brings an Art. 28 DPA for every business customer, a likely DPO, DPIAs and Ring/Verkada-style insider and breach liability.

GDPR applies to home users as soon as a camera sees public space or a neighbour's property (CJEU Ryneš). Romania adds its own rules. Employee monitoring under Law 190/2018 Art. 5 is capped at 30 days of retention and needs prior information and union consultation. Businesses that must have guarding under Law 333/2003 / HG 301/2012 have minimum-retention and licensed-installer requirements. The Criminal Code (art. 226) punishes recording inside homes. So the app needs per-camera retention settings, privacy masks, audio off by default, and a signage/notice helper.

Several platform rules force architecture decisions:
- **iOS:** ONVIF WS-Discovery needs Apple's approval for the multicast entitlement plus NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription. iOS blocks local-network traffic for apps in the background, so a phone cannot be the recorder.
- **Android:** 15+ limits dataSync/mediaProcessing foreground services to 6 h per 24 h. Android 17 (targetSdk 37) enforces the ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK permission.
- **Chrome:** Local Network Access puts a permission prompt in front of a cloud-hosted web UI that tries to reach LAN devices directly.

The EU Cyber Resilience Act matters now. Its vulnerability and incident reporting duties have applied since 11 Sep 2026, and full obligations (CE marking, SBOM, at least 5 years of security updates) apply from 11 Dec 2027. A draft technical description lists "hardware and software intended to centrally control" home security cameras as a Class I important product, which may mean third-party conformity assessment.

For OAuth, Google's drive.file and drive.appdata scopes avoid the yearly CASA security assessment that restricted scopes require. Microsoft's Files.ReadWrite.AppFolder works for personal accounts without admin consent. Dropbox freezes new user links 2 weeks after an app reaches 50 users unless it has production approval.

Research limits: the web search budget was used up and most EU/Romanian legal sites (eur-lex, edpb, dataprotection.ro, legislatie.just.ro, ftc.gov, cisa.gov) could not be reached from this session. Apple/Android/Google/Microsoft/Dropbox facts come from official docs; Romanian legal points and incident numbers come from prior knowledge and are marked medium or low confidence. Romanian counsel should check them.

facts.claim: On iOS, outgoing TCP to a LAN address, sending UDP unicast/multicast/broadcast, receiving multicast/broadcast, resolving .local names and any Bonjour browse/register all require local network access (user prompt). Listening for incoming TCP and receiving unicast UDP do not. Traffic from WKWebView, SFSafariViewController and Safari is exempt.

On iOS, sending or receiving IP multicast or broadcast (which ONVIF WS-Discovery to 239.255.255.250:3702 needs) requires the com.apple.developer.networking.multicast entitlement (iOS/iPadOS 14+, visionOS 1+). Apple must approve it via the Multicast Networking Entitlement Request form. The entitlement is not required on macOS.

NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription must be in Info.plist for any app that uses the local network directly or indirectly, including Bonjour and direct unicast/multicast connections to local hosts (iOS 14+, macOS 11+). For app extensions, the key goes in the container app's Info.plist.

When an iOS app is in the background, local network operations are denied silently, without showing the alert. A backgrounded iOS app therefore cannot pull RTSP from LAN cameras for recording. macOS 15 introduced per-user local network privacy, from which launchd daemons and root processes are exempt.

App Review Guideline 2.5.4: background services may only be used for their intended purposes (VoIP, audio playback, location, task completion, local notifications). Guideline 2.5.14 requires explicit consent and a clear visual/audible indicator when recording, which applies to two-way-talk microphone use. Guidelines page last updated 16 Oct 2026.

Apple 5.1.1(i) requires a privacy policy link in App Store Connect and inside the app, covering retention/deletion and how to revoke consent. 5.1.1(v) requires in-app account deletion when accounts can be created. Under 4.8, if a third-party login (e.g. Google Sign-In) is the primary account, an equivalent privacy-preserving login must also be offered, unless the app uses only its own account system.

iOS 15+ supports Picture-in-Picture for live remote video via AVPictureInPictureVideoCallViewController with AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer. This is the sanctioned way to keep a live view visible when the app goes to the background, instead of abusing background audio.

iOS apps and third-party SDKs must ship a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy manifest declaring collected data types, tracking domains and required-reason API use. Apple has enforced this for new apps and updates since around May 2024; the enforcement date is from memory.

Android 14+ requires a declared foreground service type plus the matching FOREGROUND_SERVICE_* permission. The 'camera' type requires the CAMERA runtime permission and is meant for the device's own camera, not IP streams. 'connectedDevice' can be satisfied by CHANGE_WIFI_MULTICAST_STATE. 'specialUse' needs a written justification. Apps targeting 14+ must declare their FGS types in Play Console (Policy > App content).

For apps targeting Android 15+, all dataSync foreground services together may run at most 6 hours in any 24 hours; mediaProcessing has its own separate 6 h/24 h budget. BOOT_COMPLETED receivers may not start dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, mediaProjection or microphone foreground services. Continuous 24/7 recording or uploading from an Android phone is therefore not viable.

Android local network protection is opt-in on Android 16 (NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES). It is mandatory for apps targeting Android 17 (API 37), which must hold the new ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK runtime permission (NEARBY_DEVICES group) or use a system picker. This covers outgoing and incoming TCP, UDP unicast/multicast/broadcast, mDNS/SSDP and NsdManager, across all networking libraries including OkHttp and Cronet. Google names the runtime-permission path as the one for 'home automation or IoT device management'.

Google Play requires new apps and updates to target API 36 from 31 Aug 2026, with an extension available to 1 Nov 2026. By the yearly pattern, API 37, and with it enforced ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK, will likely be required around Aug 2027; that date is an inference.

For apps targeting Android 17, certificate transparency is enabled by default, which can break connections to cameras or NVRs with self-signed certificates. Custom trust anchors in the Network Security Config skip CT checks. Cleartext HTTP has been disabled by default since Android 9 and must be allowed per domain. Android 17 also recommends FLAG_SECURE for sensitive windows and tightens background audio, which affects two-way talk.

Android Keystore keys stay out of the app process and can be hardware-bound (TEE or StrongBox). Keys can require user authentication through BiometricPrompt. This is the right place for a key that wraps camera credentials and OAuth refresh tokens on Android.

Google Drive scopes: drive.file (only files the app created or the user opened with it) and drive.appdata are described as recommended, non-sensitive scopes. Full 'drive' scopes are restricted. One Google page calls drive.file 'sensitive'; either way it does not require a security assessment.

Apps that request Google restricted scopes and can access the data from or through a third-party server must pass a CASA security assessment by a Google-empanelled assessor (App Defense Alliance) and re-verify at least every 12 months. Sensitive-scope verification requires a scope justification and a video demonstration.
Unverified Google OAuth apps are capped at 100 users. Refresh tokens issued while the consent screen is in 'Testing' status expire after 7 days. Both points are from memory and were not re-fetched.

Microsoft Graph Files.ReadWrite.AppFolder (delegated) needs no admin consent and is available to personal Microsoft accounts. The folder is created at /drive/special/approot, which maps to Apps/{Entra app name}.

Microsoft publisher verification requires a Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program (formerly MPN) account and a work/school-registered app; apps registered with a personal Microsoft account cannot be verified. Where risk-based step-up consent is enabled, users in other tenants cannot consent to most unverified multitenant apps registered after 8 Nov 2020. This matters for business OneDrive customers.
Dropbox apps in development status can link at most 500 users. Once an app links 50 users, it has two weeks to obtain production approval, or new linking is frozen until approval.

OAuth 2.1 (consolidating RFC 9700 security BCP): PKCE is mandatory, redirect URIs must match exactly, the implicit and password grants are removed, and public-client refresh tokens must be sender-constrained (DPoP/mTLS) or rotated on every use.

Chrome Local Network Access (which replaces Private Network Access) gates public-to-local and public-to-loopback requests behind a user permission and requires a secure context. WebSockets are covered, and WebRTC local ICE candidates are dropped without the permission. In my recollection the prompt shipped by default around Chrome 142 (late 2025); I did not re-verify the version.

WebRTC Encoded Transform (RTCRtpScriptTransform) lets an app add its own encryption layer (e.g. SFrame, RFC 9605) on top of DTLS-SRTP. However, the explainer itself warns it cannot yet do this without exposing keys to JavaScript.

Packaged Windows (MSIX/AppContainer) apps need the privateNetworkClientServer capability to reach home or work networks through the firewall; internetClient gives no LAN access. Full-trust Win32 apps (runFullTrust) do not run in an AppContainer.

Microsoft Store Policies v7.19 (effective 14 Oct 2025): 10.5.1 requires a privacy policy whenever personal data is handled (always for Win32/Desktop Bridge apps), and 10.5.4 requires personal information to be stored and transmitted securely with modern cryptography.

CRA (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) timeline: in force Dec 2024; conformity-assessment-body provisions from 11 Jun 2026; Art. 14 reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents from 11 Sep 2026 (already in effect today); all other obligations from 11 Dec 2027.

CRA scope includes software products such as mobile apps, plus remote data processing solutions needed for a product to perform its functions. Pure SaaS and websites are out of scope unless they process data for a CRA-regulated product.

CRA Annex III Class I item 'Smart home products with security functionalities, including ... security cameras'. The draft Commission technical description (2025) extends it to 'hardware and software intended to centrally control such products'. A camera hub or management app could therefore be a Class I important product, which can only self-assess (Module A) by applying harmonised standards in full; otherwise third-party assessment is required. The final implementing-regulation wording should be checked.

CRA Art. 14 reporting runs through ENISA's single reporting platform to the national CSIRT (in Romania, DNSC): early warning within 24 h, notification within 72 h, then a final report. Fines go up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of worldwide turnover for breaching essential requirements. The support period must be at least 5 years unless the product's expected use is shorter. All three points are from memory.

GDPR Recital 18: the household exemption covers the private individual, but the GDPR still applies to controllers or processors that provide the means for household processing. A vendor that hosts or relays home users' video is therefore subject to the GDPR.

CJEU C-212/13 Ryneš (2014): a home camera that covers even part of a public space is not 'purely personal or household' processing. CJEU C-708/18 TK v Asociația de Proprietari bloc M5A (2019, a Romanian case) allowed CCTV in apartment-block common areas on legitimate interest, subject to a necessity and proportionality balancing test.

EDPB Guidelines 3/2019 on video devices (v2.0, adopted 29 Jan 2020) say: interpret the household exemption narrowly; use layered transparency with a first-layer warning sign (controller identity, purpose, rights, where to find full information); keep storage short, with retention beyond about 72 hours needing more justification; treat biometric/face recognition as Art. 9 special-category data.

Romanian Law 190/2018 Art. 5: video monitoring of employees on legitimate-interest grounds is lawful only with prior complete information to employees, prior consultation of the union or employee representatives, proof that less intrusive means failed, and storage proportionate to the purpose and not longer than 30 days, except as provided by law or in duly justified cases.

Romanian Law 333/2003 and its implementing norms (HG 301/2012) cover businesses obliged to have guarding: a physical-security risk analysis, design and installation of alarm/CCTV systems by police-licensed companies, and minimum technical requirements including a minimum recording retention (about 20 days, from memory; the exact value and scope need checking). Together with Law 190's 30-day cap, Romanian business users effectively need retention in a configurable 20–30 day window.

ANSPDCP Decision 174/2018 lists processing that requires a DPIA, including large-scale systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas (e.g. CCTV in malls, parks) and large-scale biometric processing. This mirrors GDPR Art. 35(3)(c).

Romanian Criminal Code art. 226 (violation of private life) criminalises, without right, taking images or audio recordings of a person inside a home or its annexes, and recording private conversations. Audio recording and cameras aimed at neighbours carry criminal as well as GDPR exposure for users, so the ToS and defaults should discourage both.

GDPR fines: up to EUR 10M or 2% of turnover for Art. 25/28/32/33 failures (security, privacy by design, processor duties, breach notification), and up to EUR 20M or 4% for breaches of principles or data-subject rights. Breach notification to ANSPDCP is due within 72 h.

GDPR Art. 37(1)(b): a DPO is mandatory when core activities include regular and systematic monitoring on a large scale; WP29/EDPB DPO guidance cites CCTV as an example. A cloud NVR operator processing many customers' video would likely need a DPO, while a local-first design probably would not.

The EU-US Data Privacy Framework survived its first court challenge: the General Court dismissed Latombe v Commission (T-553/23) on 3 Sep 2025. An appeal to the CJEU was expected or pending, so US-hosted sub-processors such as TURN, push or analytics still carry transfer risk. Prefer EU hosting with SCCs as a fallback.

EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(e), applicable since 2 Feb 2025, prohibits creating or expanding facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. Remote biometric identification is high-risk under Annex III(1)(a). The timing of high-risk obligations was subject to the Nov 2025 Digital Omnibus delay proposal; its status should be checked.

The new Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 treats software as a 'product'. Member States must transpose it by 9 Dec 2026. Manufacturers face strict liability for defects, including cybersecurity defects and missing security updates, and for destroyed or corrupted data of consumers.

The EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) has applied since 12 Sep 2025. Its access-by-design duties for connected products and related services apply mainly if you sell hardware or a bundled service. Its cloud-switching chapter (export in a machine-readable format; switching fees phased out by 12 Jan 2027) may apply if you sell cloud recording as a data processing service.

Ring (FTC, May 2023, USD 5.8M): employees and contractors had broad access to customer videos, including one who viewed thousands of private videos, and weak defences against credential stuffing (MFA came late) let attackers reach roughly 55,000 US customers' accounts and live feeds. The order required deleting data products derived from improperly accessed video and running a security program that includes MFA.

Verkada (Mar 2021): attackers used an exposed 'super admin' credential to reach about 150,000 customer cameras (hospitals, prisons, schools). The FTC settled in Aug 2024 for a USD 2.95M penalty, formally under CAN-SPAM, plus a mandated information-security program.

Wyze: in Sep 2023 and again in Feb 2024, a cloud caching/client-library bug during an AWS outage showed users thumbnails and events from other customers' cameras. About 13,000 users were affected in Feb 2024 and about 1,500 opened the foreign footage. Separately, Wyze left a reported camera vulnerability unpatched for about 3 years (disclosed 2022).

Eufy/Anker (Nov 2022): devices marketed as 'local storage only' and 'end-to-end encrypted' were shown to upload thumbnails and face data to the cloud, and live streams could be opened unencrypted from a URL in VLC. Anker later acknowledged the issues. The lesson: privacy claims in marketing become legal liability (GDPR transparency, unfair commercial practices).

CISA joint advisory AA25-141A (May 2025): Russian GRU unit 26165 accessed more than 10,000 internet-exposed IP cameras near Ukrainian border crossings, military sites and rail stations, mostly via RTSP with default or brute-forced credentials. Romania had a notable share, about 10% in my recollection. For a Romanian product, camera feeds are of real interest to state actors.

Hikvision CVE-2021-36260 is a critical unauthenticated command injection in the camera web server and has been widely exploited. The GitHub Advisory DB lists many more Hikvision CVEs in 2025–2026, including CVE-2025-66176 and CVE-2025-66177 (High, stack overflows in the device 'Search and Discovery' feature, published 13 Jan 2026) and several High-rated camera firmware buffer overflows (Jul 2026). Discovery protocols and camera responses are attack surface for the client too.

Licences of useful security building blocks: rclone (MIT; Drive/OneDrive/S3/Dropbox backends plus a 'crypt' client-side encryption backend), libsodium (ISC), Headscale (BSD-3-Clause, self-hosted Tailscale control server), coturn TURN server (BSD-3-Clause, from memory). All are compatible with a closed-source commercial product.
OWASP MASVS, the mobile app security verification standard to use as a checklist, is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

options.name: A. Local-first hub + zero-knowledge cloud relay (hybrid)
options.description: An always-on hub runs on the user's own machine (Windows service, Docker, NAS or mini-PC). It discovers cameras with ONVIF, pulls RTSP, records, and encrypts every segment on the hub before writing to local disk or uploading to the user's own Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox or S3 (envelope encryption: per-segment AES-256-GCM or XChaCha20-Poly1305 data keys wrapped to each authorised device's X25519 key). Camera credentials never leave the hub; they are sealed with DPAPI/TPM, Keychain or Keystore. Your cloud only handles accounts, device pairing, WebRTC signaling, TURN relay (which sees only SRTP ciphertext) and E2EE-capable push. Clients pin the hub's identity key at pairing (QR code on the LAN), so a compromised signaling server cannot man-in-the-middle the DTLS session.
options.license: Architecture; components: libsodium ISC, Google Tink Apache-2.0, coturn BSD-3, Pion WebRTC MIT, rclone MIT
options.maturity: Proven pattern (Apple HomeKit Secure Video uses on-hub analysis with E2EE cloud storage; Ring offers opt-in E2EE); you build the integration yourself
pros: Your servers never hold plaintext video or camera passwords, so a breach of your cloud cannot leak footage (avoids the Verkada/Ring/Wyze failure classes)
GDPR footprint is small: you are a processor only for relay metadata, accounts and push; video stays in the user's own storage. The DPA stays short and a DPO is probably not needed
Google drive.file / drive.appdata and OneDrive AppFolder scopes are enough, so no restricted scopes and no yearly CASA assessment; OAuth tokens can stay on the hub
Fits platform limits: phones and the web are viewers only, and the hub does 24/7 recording (no Android FGS 6 h limit, no iOS background local-network issue)
EU residency is easy: host only small signaling/TURN servers in the EU
cons: Users must run a hub; a 'cameras only, no hub' customer needs a cloud fallback
Key management UX is hard: device loss means key loss; recovery needs a recovery key, passkey PRF or multi-device escrow, and revoking a share means re-wrapping future keys
No server-side thumbnails, search or AI unless done on the hub; encrypted files in Drive cannot be previewed in the Drive UI

Hub software probably counts as CRA Class I ('software intended to centrally control' security cameras): from Dec 2027 that brings CE marking, an SBOM, 5+ years of updates, and possibly a notified body
The web client needs keys in the browser (WebCrypto non-extractable keys); WebRTC E2EE beyond DTLS exposes keys to JS

options.name: B. Pure self-hosted / no vendor cloud
options.description: The hub and apps talk only over the LAN or a user-managed overlay VPN (WireGuard, Tailscale, or self-hosted Headscale). Accounts are local. Storage goes to local disk or to cloud drives using the user's own OAuth client.
options.license: WireGuard (kernel GPLv2; wireguard-go MIT; wireguard-apple MIT; wireguard-android Apache-2.0), Headscale BSD-3, Tailscale client BSD-3
options.maturity: Mature (Frigate, Home Assistant, Blue Iris users do this today)
pros: Smallest legal footprint: you are not a controller or processor of any user video; GDPR obligations sit with the user
No relay costs and no attack surface that you operate
Attractive to privacy-conscious and prosumer users
cons: Poor UX for non-technical users (VPN setup); push notifications still need APNs/FCM, which routes through a vendor
The CRA still applies if the software is commercial; only a non-monetised open-source release escapes it
Hard to monetise; no multi-tenant sharing across households without infrastructure

options.name: C. Full cloud NVR SaaS (server-side recording, AI and sharing)
options.description: Cameras or the hub stream to your cloud media servers (SFU or recorder). The cloud stores recordings or pushes them to the user's Drive using server-held OAuth tokens, and runs detection and AI. Camera credentials are held by the cloud.
options.license: n/a (proprietary backend; media servers such as MediaMTX MIT, go2rtc MIT)
options.maturity: Mature commercial model (Verkada, Eagle Eye, Ring, Wyze)
pros: Best UX: works without a hub (for cameras that can push), with cloud AI, instant sharing and web playback
Easier to charge recurring revenue
cons: You become a large-scale processor of video: an Art. 28 DPA for every business customer, a likely DPO (Art. 37), DPIA support, and data-subject access requests involving footage
Insider-access and tenant-isolation risk; the Ring, Verkada and Wyze incidents all arose in this model

Server-side storage of Google tokens with broad scopes triggers restricted-scope verification and yearly CASA; drive.file still needs careful encryption at rest of refresh tokens (KMS envelope, per-tenant)
Significant cost for EU hosting, egress bandwidth, and likely ISO 27001 or SOC 2 for B2B sales
Cameras would need to be reachable from the cloud (port forwarding is unacceptable), so a hub or camera-push protocol is needed anyway

options.name: D. Remote access via WebRTC P2P with TURN fallback and pinned hub identity
options.description: The hub opens an outbound WebSocket to your signaling server. Clients connect with WebRTC (DTLS-SRTP), and the TURN relay forwards encrypted packets only. The hub's DTLS certificate fingerprint is signed by a long-term hub identity key that each client pinned at LAN pairing. PTZ and control commands go over an authenticated DataChannel.
options.license: Pion MIT / libwebrtc BSD-3 / coturn BSD-3
options.maturity: Mature
pros: No inbound ports on the user's router; works through NAT
The same transport serves web, Android, iOS and Windows
Live-view confidentiality is effectively end to end between hub and viewer even through TURN
cons: Without pinning, the signaling server could man-in-the-middle the session; pinning adds pairing UX
Chrome Local Network Access affects direct LAN ICE candidates and fetches from a cloud-hosted page; TURN usage costs bandwidth
coturn lacks some RFC 8489 auth features; use short-lived TURN credentials (REST API shared secret)

options.name: E. Remote access via port forwarding, UPnP or camera vendors' P2P clouds
options.description: Expose the hub's or cameras' HTTP/RTSP ports to the internet, or rely on each camera's own vendor cloud.
options.license: n/a
options.maturity: Common but discredited
pros: Trivial to implement
cons: The direct cause of Mirai and of the AA25-141A camera compromises; exposes cameras with chronic critical CVEs (e.g. Hikvision CVE-2021-36260)
Vendor P2P clouds route feeds through third parties (often outside the EU), a GDPR transfer and trust problem
Conflicts with CRA 'secure by default' expectations. Recommendation: reject; actively warn users and recommend blocking camera internet egress on a VLAN

options.name: F. Storage connectors with least-privilege scopes
options.description: Google Drive uses drive.file (or drive.appdata for hidden storage) with the Google Picker, OneDrive uses Files.ReadWrite.AppFolder, and Dropbox uses App-folder access. S3-compatible storage uses user-supplied, bucket-scoped keys. Local storage writes to disk or SMB/NFS. The hub can hold tokens, or the tokens can be device-held. All payloads are client-side encrypted. rclone's backends and crypt format can serve as a reference or embedded library.
options.license: rclone MIT; Google/Microsoft/Dropbox SDKs Apache-2.0/MIT
options.maturity: Mature APIs
pros: Avoids restricted scopes and CASA; per-app folders limit the blast radius if tokens leak
OneDrive AppFolder works for personal accounts without admin consent
cons: Dropbox needs production approval before more than 50 users (2-week grace period); Microsoft publisher verification is needed for smooth business-tenant consent
Google brand/app verification is still needed before public launch (unverified apps are capped at about 100 users; Testing-mode refresh tokens expire after 7 days)
Consumer Drive and OneDrive regions cannot be controlled, so tell users that their own provider choice determines where data resides

recommendation:
Build Option A: a local-first hub with a zero-knowledge relay, using Option D for transport and Option F for storage. Reject Option E. Treat Option C (cloud NVR) as a later, separately priced tier, only after you have a DPA, DPO and ISO 27001 roadmap.

1) **Architecture rules.** Only the hub talks to cameras.
   - Camera credentials stay on the hub, sealed with DPAPI or TPM on Windows, Keychain on Apple and Keystore on Android.
   - Encourage a separate low-privilege ONVIF 'User' account for streaming and an 'Operator' account for PTZ.
   - Phones and the web are viewers and controllers only. iOS denies background local-network access and Android 15+ limits dataSync to 6 h per 24 h, so they cannot be recorders.
   - Recordings are encrypted per segment on the hub (libsodium secretstream or Tink AEAD) with data keys wrapped to device keys before upload. Never store plaintext in Drive or OneDrive, and never claim 'E2EE' or 'local only' unless it is literally true (the Eufy lesson).
2) **Remote access.**
   - Use outbound-only WebRTC with TURN in the EU and short-lived TURN credentials.
   - Pin the hub identity key at QR pairing so your own servers cannot man-in-the-middle the session.
   - Do no port forwarding or UPnP. Advise users to put cameras on a VLAN with no internet egress.
   - Parse all camera, ONVIF and RTSP input as hostile: use memory-safe parsers and fuzz them (Hikvision 'Search and Discovery' CVEs show discovery is attack surface).
3) **Access control.**
   - Use per-camera roles: owner, admin, operator (PTZ), live viewer, playback viewer.
   - Shares should be time-limited, and revocation should rotate keys.
   - Your own staff get no standing access to customer data (the Ring and Verkada lessons).
   - Require MFA or passkeys and add credential-stuffing protection.
   - Keep a tamper-evident audit log of live views, playbacks, exports, PTZ and configuration changes, with its own retention limit.
4) **GDPR and Romanian compliance features.**
   - Per-camera retention defaults: short for home users; a 20–30 day preset for Romanian businesses, to be confirmed with counsel.
   - Privacy masks, audio off by default, and a warning when the field of view covers public space (Ryneš).
   - Generate signage and first-layer notices.
   - Provide DSAR export with redaction or blurring of other people.
   - Provide a DPA template plus a sub-processor list (hosting, TURN, APNs/FCM, email) for business users.
   - Write a DPIA template for users who monitor public areas, per the ANSPDCP 174/2018 list.
   - No face recognition at launch. If it is ever added: on-device only, opt-in, and never build databases from footage (AI Act Art. 5(1)(e)).

CRA reporting has already applied since 11 Sep 2026. An actively exploited vulnerability in shipped hub or app software with no 24 h/72 h process in place is an immediate compliance failure.
Apple may refuse or delay the multicast entitlement. Fallback: manual IP entry, unicast ONVIF probing of a subnet (still needs local network permission), or discovery done by the hub.

Android 17 enforcement (ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK for targetSdk 37, likely mandatory on Play around Aug 2027): a denied permission silently breaks LAN viewing, so a hub-relayed fallback is needed even on the LAN.
Chrome Local Network Access and mixed-content rules break a cloud-hosted web UI that talks directly to LAN hubs or cameras over plain HTTP.
E2EE key loss means permanent loss of recordings, which drives support load and reputational risk; the recovery design is critical.
Overclaiming privacy ('E2EE', 'local only', 'GDPR compliant') while thumbnails or push previews go to the cloud is the Eufy failure mode. It creates GDPR transparency and consumer-law exposure.
Insider or support-tool access to customer streams (Ring, Verkada) and tenant-isolation bugs in caches or CDNs (Wyze) if any cloud media path is added later.

Camera ecosystem insecurity: compromised cameras can attack the client (malformed RTSP/ONVIF), and default-credential cameras are targeted by state actors (AA25-141A). The product may be blamed for breaches it did not cause.

questions_for_product_owner: Who is the primary customer: home users, prosumers or self-hosters, or businesses (shops, offices, apartment associations, companies under Law 333/2003)? This decides your GDPR role (none, processor, or large-scale processor) and the retention presets.
Will your servers ever need to see plaintext video, for example cloud recording without a hub, server-side AI, thumbnails in push notifications or sharing links? Or can we commit to zero-knowledge?

Will you sell or bundle hardware, such as a hub box or rebranded cameras? That brings in CRA Class I for hardware, the Radio Equipment Directive, the Data Act connected-product duties, WEEE and UK PSTI.
Is a hub (always-on PC, NAS, Raspberry Pi-class device or Windows service) acceptable for users, or must the product work with cameras plus phone only?
Do you want AI features? Person or vehicle detection is low risk. Face recognition and licence-plate recognition bring GDPR Art. 9, AI Act and ANSPDCP DPIA obligations.
Should audio recording and two-way talk be supported? Default off is recommended for legal reasons.
Business model: paid, freemium, or open source? A non-monetised open-source release changes CRA status; monetisation makes you a manufacturer.

Through which legal entity will you publish (an SRL is needed for the Microsoft partner programme, the Apple organisation account and DPAs), and who is the security and privacy contact for ANSPDCP and DNSC reporting?
Is permanent loss of encrypted recordings acceptable when a user loses all devices and the recovery key, or do you want an optional escrow, which would weaken the zero-knowledge claims?
